teile.einleitung: The Dead Sea Scrolls are very old manuscripts that were found in caves near Qumran from 1947 onwards. They are among the most important finds in archaeology and contain the oldest known Bible texts.
wichtigste: The first scrolls were discovered in 1947.
Scrolls or fragments were found in 11 caves.
Most of it is written in Hebrew.
The Great Isaiah Scroll contains the Book of Isaiah almost complete.
The biblical texts are about 1,000 years older than the oldest complete manuscripts known until then.
Not a single fragment of the Book of Esther was found.

abschnitte.text: In **1947**, Bedouins discovered old clay jars with scrolls in a cave near **Qumran** by the Dead Sea. In the following years researchers kept searching. In all, scrolls or fragments were found in **11 caves**. Many texts survive only in small pieces, which had to be laboriously put together.

About a quarter of the texts are **biblical texts**. The best known is the **Great Isaiah Scroll** from Cave 1. It contains the Book of **Isaiah** almost complete. The Qumran texts are **about 1,000 years older** than the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts from the Middle Ages known until then. They show how carefully the text was copied over a long time. Only of the Book of **Esther** was not a single fragment found.

Most of it is written in **Hebrew**, other texts in Aramaic or Greek. Besides biblical texts there are rules of a community, prayers and commentaries. Special is the **Copper Scroll**: it is scratched into metal and **lists hiding places of treasures**. Whether these treasures ever existed is not known.

The community of Qumran is most often linked with the **Essenes**. They were a Jewish group who lived very strictly by religious rules. This interpretation is not undisputed among researchers, however. Today important scrolls are on display in the **Shrine of the Book** at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem. The roof of the building has the shape of a jar lid.

gewusst: The texts date from roughly the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD.
In all, remains of about 900 different manuscripts from Qumran are known.

teile.einleitung: The annunciation to the shepherds is part of the Christmas story in the Gospel of Luke. In the night an angel appears to simple shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem. He tells them first of all that Jesus has been born.
wichtigste: The story is in the Gospel of Luke, in chapter two.
Shepherds in the fields were the first to hear of the birth of Jesus.
The angel came in the night, and the shepherds were afraid.
As a sign he named a child in swaddling clothes lying in a manger.
Then a great crowd of angels praised God.
The shepherds found the child and told everyone about it.

abschnitte.text: Near **Bethlehem**, **shepherds** were keeping watch over their flock at night. The Bible speaks only of a flock. In pictures and in nativity scenes, though, they are almost always **sheep**. Shepherds were simple people with hard work. It was to them that the message was brought first.

Suddenly **an angel** stood beside them, and it became bright all around them. The shepherds were **very afraid**. The angel said first: “Do not be afraid!” Then he announced great joy: today in the city of David the **Saviour** has been born.

The angel gave the shepherds a **sign by which to recognise him**. They would find a child wrapped in **swaddling clothes** and lying in a **manger**. A manger is a feeding trough for animals. In this way the shepherds could recognise the right child.

After the first angel, a **great crowd of angels** appeared. They praised God with the words: “**Glory to God in the highest**, and peace on earth.” These words can still be heard today in many Christmas carols and services.

The shepherds set off at once. They found **Mary**, **Joseph** and the child in the manger. Afterwards they **told** everyone what they had heard. People were amazed at their words. Then the shepherds returned and praised God.

gewusst: The angels' song of praise is called “Gloria in excelsis Deo” in Latin.
In many nativity plays the shepherds are among the most popular parts for children.

teile.einleitung: “Sola gratia” means “by grace alone”. According to this principle of the Reformation, people cannot earn salvation. They receive it as a free, undeserved gift from God.
wichtigste: “Sola gratia” means “by grace alone”.
According to this principle, salvation is an undeserved gift from God.
The Reformers appealed especially to Augustine.
In 1517 Luther criticised the sale of indulgences.
In 1525 Luther answered Erasmus with “De servo arbitrio”.
The Reformers rejected Pelagianism.

abschnitte.text: In theology, **grace** means God's free turning towards human beings. The principle **“sola gratia”** says: people cannot earn salvation through achievement. They are given it without deserving it. Together with “sola fide” and “sola scriptura”, this principle is one of the core ideas of the Reformation. Luther also spoke of **alien righteousness**, “iustitia aliena”, which comes from Christ and is granted to the person.

People were already arguing about this question in the 5th century. The monk **Pelagius** stressed that people could live good lives by their own will. The Church Father **Augustine** of Hippo countered that people depend entirely on God's grace. The teaching of Pelagius is called **Pelagianism** and was rejected by the Church. The Reformers appealed especially to Augustine. Luther was also a monk in the order of the Augustinian Hermits.

In Luther's time the Church sold **indulgences**. They were meant to shorten the punishments for sins. Preachers such as Johann Tetzel promoted them. In 1517 Luther criticised this practice in his **95 Theses**. In his view it made God's grace seem something that could be bought, but forgiveness could not be acquired with money.

The scholar **Erasmus of Rotterdam** published a work on free will in 1524, “De libero arbitrio”. He thought that people could cooperate in their salvation. In 1525 Luther answered with **“De servo arbitrio”**, “On the Bondage of the Will”. In it he wrote that in matters of salvation the will is not free but depends entirely on God's grace. The dispute showed how differently humanists and Reformers saw the human being.

gewusst: Erasmus lived and worked in Basel for many years and is buried in Basel Minster.
The well-known song “Amazing Grace” is also about God's undeserved grace.

teile.einleitung: The New Testament is the second part of the Christian Bible. It tells of Jesus Christ and of the first Christian communities. It consists of 27 books, which were originally written in Greek.
wichtigste: The New Testament has 27 books.
It begins with the Gospel of Matthew.
At its centre are the life, death and resurrection of Jesus.
The writings arose in the 1st and early 2nd century AD.
More than three quarters of the books are letters.
It was originally written in Greek.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning stand the four **Gospels** according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They tell of the life, the death and the resurrection of Jesus. After them follows the **Acts of the Apostles** about the first Christians. Then come 21 **letters**, many of them by Paul. The end is formed by the **Revelation of John**. Altogether there are **27 books**.

More than three quarters of the books are **letters**. They are addressed to communities or to individual people. In them the authors explain the faith and give advice for living together in the community. The letters of **Paul** are even older than the Gospels. In this way one learns much about the first Christian communities.

Jesus himself wrote nothing down. Only in the decades after his death did Christians write the texts down. Most of them come from the **1st century AD**, the youngest probably from the early 2nd century. They were written in **Greek**, the language widely spoken at that time. Which writings exactly belong to it was fixed by the churches up to the 4th century. This list is called the **canon**.

The New Testament has been translated into thousands of languages. **Martin Luther** published a German translation in 1522. In Zurich, under **Huldrych Zwingli** and Leo Jud, the **Zurich Bible** came into being, which was printed complete in 1531. It is revised again and again to this day. Together with the Old Testament, the New Testament forms the Christian Bible.

gewusst: The word “testament” here means “covenant”, meaning the new covenant between God and human beings.
The word “gospel” translated means “good news”.

teile.einleitung: The blessing of the children is a short story from the Gospels. People bring children to Jesus so that he may bless them. The story shows how important children are to Jesus.
wichtigste: People brought children to Jesus so that he would bless them.
The disciples turned the children away.
Jesus became indignant at this.
He said: “Let the children come to me!”
The kingdom of God belongs to people like children.
Jesus took the children in his arms and laid his hands on them.

abschnitte.text: The story is in the **Gospel of Mark** and also in Matthew and Luke. People bring **children** to Jesus so that he may touch them and **bless** them. The **disciples** find this a nuisance and **turn them away**. Perhaps they thought Jesus had more important things to do. Children did not count for much in society then.

abschnitte.titel: Let the children come to me
abschnitte.text: Jesus becomes **indignant** when he sees this. He says: **“Let the children come to me and do not stop them!”** Then he explains that the **kingdom of God belongs to people like children**. Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God **like a child** will not enter it. Children trust and let themselves be given gifts, and that is what Jesus means by it.

In the Gospel of Mark **Jesus takes the children in his arms**. He **lays his hands on them** and blesses them. **To be blessed** means: **God wishes a person well** and accompanies them. The story shows that **children are important to Jesus**. That is why it is often read at baptisms and children's services.

In some churches today there is a **blessing of children** as a celebration of its own. Especially in free churches, children are blessed instead of being baptised as babies. At children's services or at the start of school too, pastors often bless children. In doing so they lay a hand on the head and speak a blessing.

gewusst: The picture of Jesus with the children was painted by many painters, including Lucas Cranach.

teile.einleitung: The Septuagint is the oldest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. It came into being from the 3rd century BC for Jews who spoke Greek. Later it became the Old Testament of the first Christians.
wichtigste: The Septuagint is a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.
According to tradition it came into being in Alexandria in Egypt.
First the Torah, that is, the five Books of Moses, was translated.
The name means “seventy”; the abbreviation is LXX.
According to the Letter of Aristeas, 72 translators worked on it.
The early Christians adopted it as their Old Testament.

abschnitte.text: After the conquests of Alexander the Great, **Greek** became the most important language in the eastern Mediterranean. Many Jews lived outside Israel and no longer understood Hebrew well. So their holy writings were translated into Greek. First, in the 3rd century BC, the translation of the **Torah**, the five Books of Moses, was made. The other books followed over the course of about two centuries.

In **Alexandria** in Egypt lived a large Jewish community that spoke Greek. An old text, the **Letter of Aristeas**, tells a legend: King Ptolemy II Philadelphus wanted the translation for his famous library. Six scholars came from each of the twelve tribes of Israel, 72 in all. They finished the work in 72 days. Historians regard this story as largely legendary.

“Septuaginta” is the Latin word for **seventy**. The number recalls the roughly seventy translators of the legend. The abbreviation is written **LXX**, which is seventy in Roman numerals. Scholars still use this abbreviation today. The Septuagint also contains some books that are missing from the Hebrew Bible.

abschnitte.titel: The Bible of the first Christians
abschnitte.text: The early Christians often spoke Greek and therefore read the Septuagint. The **New Testament** often quotes the Old Testament in its version. A well-known example is Isaiah 7:14: in Hebrew it says “alma”, young woman, but in the Septuagint “parthenos”. The Gospel of Matthew quotes this Greek version in the Christmas story. In the Orthodox Church the Septuagint is still regarded as the authoritative form of the Old Testament.

Important texts of the Septuagint survive in great **manuscripts** from the 4th and 5th centuries. One of the most famous is the **Codex Sinaiticus**. The scholar Konstantin von Tischendorf discovered it in the 19th century in St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai. In 1844 he found the first leaves, and in 1859 he received the main part. The codex also contains the complete New Testament.

gewusst: The Codex Sinaiticus is now spread over several places; the largest part is in London.
Many words of the Septuagint such as “Genesis” or “Exodus” are still the names of biblical books today.

teile.einleitung: Theodosius I was a Roman emperor in the 4th century. Under him Christianity became the state religion of the Roman Empire. He was the last emperor to rule over the whole empire.
wichtigste: Theodosius came from Hispania, now Spain.
In 380, with the edict “Cunctos populos”, he made Christianity the state religion.
In 391 and 392 he banned the sacrifices and cults of the old gods.
Bishop Ambrose of Milan demanded public penance from him.
After his death in 395 the empire was finally divided into west and east.
His son Honorius received the west, Arcadius the east.

abschnitte.text: Theodosius was born around **347** in **Hispania**, now Spain. He came from a family of officers and himself became a successful general. In 379 he became emperor in the east of the empire. Later he ruled as the **last emperor** over the whole Roman Empire. Because of his importance he is also called “Theodosius the Great”.

In the year **380**, Theodosius issued an edict that is called **“Cunctos populos”** after its opening words in Latin, “all peoples”. It is also called the Edict of the Three Emperors. All peoples were to accept the faith taught by **Bishop Damasus of Rome** and **Bishop Peter of Alexandria**. Anyone who believed otherwise was regarded as a heretic. In this way Christianity became the **state religion**.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the old cults
abschnitte.text: In the years **391 and 392**, Theodosius banned sacrifices to the Roman gods. Temples were closed, and the old cults lost their protection. According to the traditional view, the ancient **Olympic Games** also ended around this time, about 393. The exact end is disputed among historians, however. For many people it was a great upheaval.

In the year 390 an uprising broke out in **Thessalonica**. Theodosius then had very many people killed. **Bishop Ambrose of Milan** therefore excluded the emperor from worship. Only when Theodosius did public **penance** was he allowed to take part again. The story shows how much influence the Church now had, even over the emperor.

Theodosius died in the year **395** in Milan. After his death the Roman Empire was finally **divided**. His son **Honorius** received the west, his other son **Arcadius** the east. Both were still young when their father died. The Western Roman Empire fell in the 5th century, while the Eastern Roman Empire lasted for about a thousand years more.

gewusst: Under Theodosius the Council of Constantinople met in 381 and developed the creed further.
The Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital Constantinople, lasted until 1453.

teile.einleitung: Constantine the Great was a Roman emperor in the 4th century. Under him Christians were allowed to live their faith freely, and Christianity became ever more important in the Roman Empire.
wichtigste: In 312 Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge.
Before the battle he is said to have put a sign of Christ on the shields.
He promoted Christianity and had many churches built.
In 321 he established Sunday as a day of rest.
In 330 he made Constantinople, today's Istanbul, the new capital.
His mother Helena travelled to the Holy Land.

abschnitte.titel: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
abschnitte.text: In Constantine's time there were several rulers in the Roman Empire who fought each other. On **28 October 312** Constantine defeated his rival **Maxentius** outside Rome at the **Milvian Bridge** over the Tiber. Maxentius drowned in the river while fleeing. After that Constantine ruled the west of the Empire. From 324 he was sole ruler.

The Christian writer **Lactantius** reports that Constantine was told in a dream before the battle to put a sign of Christ on the shields. The **Christogram** consists of the Greek letters **Chi and Rho**, the first letters of “Christ”. Constantine attributed his victory to the God of the Christians. In 313 he agreed with Licinius in Milan on religious freedom for all.

Constantine had great churches built, for example in Rome and in Jerusalem. There the **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** arose above the place where Jesus is said to have been buried. It was consecrated in 335. In 325 he summoned the bishops to the **Council of Nicaea**. In the year **321** he decreed that courts and craftsmen should rest on **Sunday**. Constantine was baptised only shortly before his death in the year 337.

Constantine magnificently expanded the old city of **Byzantium** on the Bosporus. In the year **330** it was inaugurated as the new capital and named **Constantinople** after him. Today it is called **Istanbul** and lies in Turkey. The city remained the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for over 1,000 years.

Constantine's mother **Helena** travelled to Palestine around 326 and promoted the building of churches there. A legend tells that she found the cross of Jesus. Because of his great importance for the Empire and for Christianity, Constantine is called **the Great**. In the Orthodox Church he is venerated as a saint.

gewusst: Sunday as a day of rest goes back to a law of Constantine from the year 321.
Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his soldiers in the city of Eboracum, today's York in England.

teile.einleitung: The church year is the annual calendar of the Church. It arranges the Christian festivals and seasons across the whole year. It does not begin on 1 January, but with the first Sunday of Advent.
wichtigste: The church year begins with the first Sunday of Advent.
The Catholic church year has three parts: the Christmas cycle, the Easter cycle and Ordinary Time.
Easter is on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring.
Easter Sunday is at the earliest on 22 March.
Pentecost is on the 50th day of the Easter season.
Candlemas is on 2 February, the Annunciation on 25 March.
The Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer is on the third Sunday in September.

abschnitte.text: The **church year** begins with the **first Sunday of Advent**, that is, four Sundays before Christmas. The Catholic church year has three great parts. The **Christmas cycle** covers Advent and the Christmas season. The **Easter cycle** runs from Lent to Pentecost. The remaining time is called **Ordinary Time**.

Christmas is every year on **25 December**. Exactly nine months earlier, on **25 March**, the Church celebrates the **Annunciation**. In this it recalls how the angel Gabriel announced to Mary the birth of Jesus. On **2 February**, 40 days after Christmas, is **Candlemas**. On this day the candles are often blessed.

Easter has no fixed date. It is on the **Sunday after the first full moon of spring**. So Easter can be at the earliest on **22 March** and at the latest on **25 April**. Many festivals depend on the date of Easter, for example Ascension Day and Pentecost. **Pentecost** is on the **50th day** of the Easter season, counting Easter Sunday. The word Pentecost comes from the Greek word for “the fiftieth”.

In Switzerland there is a special public holiday: the **Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer** (Bettag). It is on the **third Sunday in September**. It has been celebrated throughout Switzerland since 1832. It is a holiday for all denominations. In many families people traditionally eat plum tart on this day.

gewusst: The liturgical colours change in the church year: purple in Advent, white at Christmas and Easter, red at Pentecost, green in Ordinary Time.
The last Sunday of the Catholic church year is the Feast of Christ the King.

teile.einleitung: In the course of history Christianity has split into many churches and denominations. Ecumenism is the effort that these churches understand each other better, work together and find more unity again.
wichtigste: The Greek word “oikoumene” means “the whole inhabited earth”.
The World Council of Churches was founded in 1948 in Amsterdam and has its seat in Geneva.
The Roman Catholic Church is not a member, but works closely with the Council.
The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity takes place every year from 18 to 25 January.
In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the mutual excommunications from the Middle Ages.
In Switzerland the churches work together in the Working Group of Christian Churches (AGCK).

abschnitte.text: The word **ecumenism** comes from the Greek “oikoumene”. In antiquity it meant the **whole inhabited earth**. Today it means the movement that wants to bring together Christians of different churches. This includes joint services, conversations about questions of faith and cooperation in social tasks. The aim is to reduce what divides and strengthen what is shared.

abschnitte.titel: The World Council of Churches in Geneva
abschnitte.text: The most important association is the **World Council of Churches** (WCC). It was founded in **1948**, shortly after the Second World War, in **Amsterdam**. Its seat is in **Geneva**. Over 300 churches from all over the world belong to the Council, among them Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant ones. The **Roman Catholic Church** is not a full member, but cooperates in individual commissions.

In 1054 the churches of Rome and Constantinople had excommunicated each other. In **1965** Pope **Paul VI** and Patriarch **Athenagoras** withdrew these excommunications. In **1999** the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed in **Augsburg** a joint declaration on the **doctrine of justification**. With this a central point of dispute from the time of the Reformation was largely settled.

abschnitte.titel: Taizé and the Week of Prayer
abschnitte.text: The Swiss **Brother Roger** founded the community of **Taizé** in 1940 in French Burgundy. There brothers from different denominations live together. Every year thousands of young people from many countries come to sing, pray and reflect. Also known worldwide is the **Week of Prayer for Christian Unity**. In the Northern Hemisphere it takes place every year from **18 to 25 January**.

In Switzerland it is above all Reformed and Catholic Christians who often live in the same village. Many parishes celebrate ecumenical services, for example on the Bettag (Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer) or in schools. Since **1971** there has been the **Working Group of Christian Churches in Switzerland** (AGCK). In it Catholic, Reformed, Old Catholic, Orthodox and other churches work together.

gewusst: Brother Roger, the founder of Taizé, came from Switzerland, from the canton of Vaud.
That the world headquarters of ecumenism is in Geneva is also connected with Geneva's history as a city of the Reformation and of international organisations.

teile.einleitung: Akbar I was one of the most important rulers of the Mughal Empire in India. He ruled for almost 50 years, from 1556 to 1605. He is known for his openness towards different religions.
wichtigste: Akbar ruled the Mughal Empire from 1556 to 1605.
He came to the throne at about the age of 13.
In 1564 he abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims.
In the Ibadat Khana he had representatives of many religions discuss.
He created the teaching of Din-i Ilahi.
He had the residential city of Fatehpur Sikri built.
Abul Fazl wrote the chronicle “Akbarnama”.

abschnitte.text: The **Mughal Empire** was a large empire in northern India, founded by Akbar's grandfather **Babur**. Akbar came to the throne in **1556** at about **13 years** old. He ruled until **1605**, almost 50 years. Under him the empire grew greatly. He also reorganised the **administration** and the tax system.

Most people in the empire were **Hindus**, while the rulers were **Muslims**. In **1564** Akbar abolished the **jizya**. This was a poll tax on non-Muslim subjects. In this way he won the support of the Hindu majority. He also married into Hindu princely families and gave Hindus high offices.

Akbar had the **Ibadat Khana** built, the “House of Worship”. There **Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Parsis** and Christian **Jesuits** discussed with one another. Akbar was looking for shared truths among the religions. From this came the teaching **Din-i Ilahi**, the “divine faith”. It combined elements from several religions but had only a few followers at court.

From about **1571**, Akbar had the city of **Fatehpur Sikri** built of **red sandstone** as a new residence. He left it again as early as 1585, usually thought to be because of a **lack of water**. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The court historian **Abul Fazl**, a confidant of Akbar, wrote the chronicle **“Akbarnama”**. Its part **Ain-i Akbari** describes the administration of the empire in detail.

gewusst: Fatehpur Sikri was used as a residence for only about 15 years.
A grandson of Akbar, Shah Jahan, later had the Taj Mahal built.

teile.einleitung: Al-Khwarizmi was a great scholar who lived in Baghdad around 800. He wrote important books on mathematics, astronomy and geography. Two words that we often use today go back to him: algebra and algorithm.
wichtigste: Al-Khwarizmi lived from about 780 to 850.
He worked at the court of the caliphs in Baghdad.
His name means “the one from Khwarazm”.
The word algebra comes from the title of one of his books.
The word algorithm comes from his name.
His arithmetic book made the new numerals known in Europe.
He was also an astronomer and geographer.

abschnitte.text: **Al-Khwarizmi** means “the one from **Khwarazm**”. This region lies in **Central Asia** on the **Amu Darya** river. He lived from about **780 to 850**. He worked in **Baghdad** at the court of the **Abbasid caliphs**. Baghdad was at that time a centre of science, where many scholars did research and translated books.

Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on **solving equations**. Its title contained the word **“al-jabr”**, which means roughly **“completing”**. This means doing the same thing on both sides of an equation so that it stays in balance. From “al-jabr” came the name **algebra**. An example: with **3x + 4 = 19**, you first calculate 19 minus 4 equals 15. Then you divide 15 by 3 and get **x = 5**.

Another book explained **written calculation** with the numerals from India in the **place-value system**. In this system the value of a digit depends on its position. The book was translated into **Latin** and began with the words **“Dixit Algorizmi”**, that is, “Algorizmi said”. In this way many Europeans got to know calculating with the new numerals.

abschnitte.titel: From a name to the algorithm
abschnitte.text: In Latin his name became **“Algoritmi”**. From it came the word **algorithm**. An algorithm is an exact **step-by-step set of instructions** for solving a task. Today the word is very important in **computer science**, because every computer program follows algorithms.

Al-Khwarizmi was a **versatile scholar**. He drew up **astronomical tables** with which the movements of the sun, moon and planets could be calculated. He also wrote a **description of the known world** with many place details. With it, maps could be drawn.

gewusst: The word “algorithm” goes back to the name al-Khwarizmi.
The numerals we write today are also called Arabic numerals, although they originally come from India.

teile.einleitung: The Abbasids were a dynasty of caliphs who ruled a large part of the Islamic world from 750. They founded Baghdad, which soon became one of the largest cities in the world. Under them trade, science and culture flourished.
wichtigste: The name goes back to al-Abbas, an uncle of Muhammad.
The uprising against the Umayyads began in Khorasan.
Caliph al-Mansur founded the city of Baghdad in 762.
The core of Baghdad was laid out as a perfect circle.
Harun al-Rashid exchanged embassies with Charlemagne.
From 836 to 892 Samarra was the residence of the caliphs.
From 945 the Buyids held the real power in Baghdad.

abschnitte.text: The **Abbasids** derived their claim from **al-Abbas**, an **uncle of the Prophet Muhammad**. From 747 the general **Abu Muslim** gathered followers in the eastern province of **Khorasan**. They marched west under **black banners**. In the year 750 they overthrew the **Umayyad** dynasty. Black remained the court colour of the Abbasids, while the Umayyads were linked with white.

In **762**, Caliph **al-Mansur** had the city of **Baghdad** on the **Tigris** laid out as the new capital. Its location linked important trade routes between Mesopotamia and Iran. The city centre was **perfectly circular**: the **“Round City”** had double walls and four gates. In the middle stood the palace and the main mosque. Baghdad became a centre of **science** and translation.

A famous caliph was **Harun al-Rashid**. Frankish sources report that around 800 he exchanged **embassies** with **Charlemagne**. As a gift, Charlemagne is said to have received an **elephant** named **Abul Abbas**. Harun also appears in the stories of **“One Thousand and One Nights”**.

In the year **751** the Abbasids fought at the **Talas** River in Central Asia against an army of the Chinese **Tang dynasty** and won. According to tradition, **papermaking** then reached the Islamic world. Paper was cheaper than parchment. It helped to spread books and knowledge widely.

abschnitte.titel: Samarra and the loss of power
abschnitte.text: Caliph **al-Mutasim** moved the residence to **Samarra**, partly because of tensions with his Turkish troops in Baghdad. From **836 to 892** the caliphs lived there. Famous is the mosque with the **spiral minaret**. In the year **945** the Shia **Buyids** from Iran occupied Baghdad. The caliphs formally remained in office but had hardly any political power left.

gewusst: Charlemagne is said to have received an elephant named Abul Abbas from Harun al-Rashid.
The spiral minaret of Samarra winds upwards like a snail shell.

teile.einleitung: The Last Supper is the meal that Jesus celebrated with his disciples on the evening before his death. Christians remember it on Maundy Thursday and in every Lord's Supper or Eucharist.
wichtigste: Jesus celebrated the meal in a room on the upper floor of a house in Jerusalem.
According to Luke, Peter and John prepared it.
At the bread Jesus said: “This is my body.”
According to John, Jesus washed the disciples' feet.
Jesus predicted that one of them would betray him.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the famous wall painting in Milan.

abschnitte.text: The Last Supper took place in **Jerusalem** at the time of the Jewish **Passover**. According to Luke, Jesus sent **Peter and John** ahead to prepare the meal. According to Mark, the disciples found a large **room on the upper floor** of a house, already furnished with cushions. There Jesus ate with the twelve disciples.

During the meal Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to the disciples. He said: **“This is my body.”** Then he handed them a cup of wine and spoke of his blood. By this he meant that he gives himself for human beings. From this arose the celebration of the **Lord's Supper** or the **Eucharist**, which Christians still celebrate today.

abschnitte.titel: Foot washing and a new commandment
abschnitte.text: The **Gospel of John** tells that Jesus **washed his disciples' feet**. That was a job for servants at the time. By this Jesus showed that people should serve one another. He also gave them a **new commandment**: “Love one another!” As he had loved them, they were to love one another. On Maundy Thursday the washing of feet is re-enacted in some churches.

At the meal Jesus sadly predicted: **“One of you will betray me.”** The disciples were alarmed. According to the Gospel of Matthew, the betrayer Judas received **30 pieces of silver** from the chief priests. At the end of the meal Jesus and the disciples sang a **hymn**. Then they went out into the night to the Mount of Olives.

abschnitte.titel: The Last Supper in art and church
abschnitte.text: The most famous picture of it was painted by **Leonardo da Vinci** over 500 years ago as a large wall painting in a monastery in **Milan**. In the Reformation **Luther** and **Zwingli** also argued over the meaning of the Lord's Supper. For Zwingli the meal was above all a meal of remembrance. Luther stressed that Christ is really present in the bread and wine.

gewusst: Leonardo's Last Supper is so delicate that visitors may look at it only in small groups and for a short time.
In 1529 Luther and Zwingli met in Marburg, but could not agree about the Lord's Supper.

teile.einleitung: Mary is the mother of Jesus and one of the most important women in Christianity. Many Christians venerate her, and there are numerous feasts, churches and pictures dedicated to her.
wichtigste: The mother of Jesus is called Mary.
She lived in Nazareth in Galilee.
She visited her relative Elizabeth.
In many pictures she rides on a donkey to Bethlehem.
The Immaculate Conception is celebrated on 8 December.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Gospel of Luke**, **Mary** lived in **Nazareth** in Galilee. That is why Jesus is later also called Jesus of Nazareth. The Bible tells that the angel **Gabriel** came to Mary and told her she would become the mother of the Son of God. Mary was engaged to **Joseph**, a carpenter. Afterwards she visited her relative **Elizabeth**, the mother of John the Baptist.

Because of a census, Mary and Joseph travelled to **Bethlehem**. There Jesus was born, according to the Bible in a stable, and was laid in a **manger**. The Bible mentions no animal to ride. In many pictures and in nativity plays, however, Mary rides on a **donkey**. Donkeys were common pack animals at that time.

The Gospels tell that Mary accompanied Jesus all his life. At the wedding at Cana she asked him for help when the wine ran out. According to the Gospel of John she also stood beneath the **cross** when Jesus died. Many Christians see in Mary a model of trust and faith. The well-known prayer **“Ave Maria”** begins with the angel's greeting.

The Catholic and the Orthodox churches venerate Mary in a special way. There are many **Marian feasts**. The **Immaculate Conception** is celebrated on **8 December** in Advent. In some Catholic cantons of Switzerland it is a public holiday. A famous place of pilgrimage is the monastery of **Einsiedeln** in the canton of Schwyz with its **Black Madonna**.

gewusst: Mary is one of the few women who are also named in the Koran, where she is called Maryam.
Many churches in Switzerland bear the name Marienkirche or Liebfrauenkirche (Church of Our Lady).

teile.einleitung: The Tower of Babel is a story from the first book of the Bible. People want to build a tower up to heaven. God confuses their language, and they scatter over the whole earth.
wichtigste: The story is in the first Book of Moses, also called Genesis.
At that time all people spoke the same language.
They built a city and a tower of baked bricks.
They wanted to make a name for themselves with it.
God confused their language, and they were scattered over the earth.
Babel is another name for Babylon, which was in what is now Iraq.

abschnitte.text: The Bible tells that in the beginning all people had **the same language**. So they could understand one another well and work together. They moved to a plain and settled there. There they made a great plan.

The people wanted to build a city with a **tower** whose top reaches to the sky. For this they baked **bricks** of clay. As mortar they used **bitumen**, a kind of tar. They said they wanted to make a name for themselves. So they wanted to become famous and not be scattered over the earth.

God saw the city and the tower. He **confused their language** so that nobody understood anyone else. Now they could not carry on building. The people went their separate ways and **scattered** over the whole earth. In its own way the story explains why there are so many languages.

**Babel** is the Hebrew name for **Babylon**. This old city lay on the River Euphrates, and its ruins are now in **Iraq**. In Babylon there was a huge stepped temple, a so-called **ziggurat**. Many researchers suspect that such buildings inspired the story of the tower.

When many languages are spoken all at once, people today speak of **Babylonian confusion of tongues**. The story has also occupied many artists. Famous is the painting “The Tower of Babel” by **Pieter Bruegel the Elder**. It shows a gigantic tower that rises like a mountain into the clouds.

gewusst: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted the Tower of Babel more than once.
In Switzerland, with four national languages, translations are often needed in everyday life so that there is no confusion of tongues.

teile.einleitung: Samuel is an important figure in the Old Testament. Even as a child he heard the voice of God. Later he became a prophet and anointed the first kings of Israel.
wichtigste: Samuel's mother was called Hannah.
Hannah had asked God for a child for a long time.
Samuel grew up with the priest Eli in the sanctuary.
In the night he heard a voice calling his name.
He answered: “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
As a prophet, Samuel anointed Saul as the first king of Israel.

abschnitte.text: Samuel's mother was called **Hannah**. For a long time she had no child and was very sad about it. In the sanctuary at Shiloh she prayed to God and asked **for a child**. She promised that the child would serve God. When Samuel was born, her joy was great. She thanked God with a song.

When Samuel was still small, Hannah brought him to the sanctuary, to the priest **Eli**. Samuel grew up there and helped with the service. Every year his mother brought him a new robe. Samuel learned how to serve God.

One night Samuel heard **a voice calling his name**. He ran to Eli, but Eli had not called. This happened **three times**. Then Eli realised that God was calling the boy. He told Samuel to answer: **“Speak, for your servant is listening.”** That is how God spoke to Samuel for the first time.

When Samuel was grown up, he became a **prophet**. A prophet announces what God wants to say to people. Samuel also led the people of Israel as a judge. When the people wanted a king, Samuel anointed **Saul** as the first king. Later he anointed the young **David**, who became king after Saul.

gewusst: Two books of the Bible bear Samuel's name: the first and the second Book of Samuel.
The name Samuel is often explained as “God has heard”.

teile.einleitung: The Star of Bethlehem is part of the Christmas story. According to the Gospel of Matthew, it led wise men from the East to the newborn Jesus. To this day the star on the Christmas tree recalls this story.
wichtigste: Only the Gospel of Matthew tells of the star.
The wise men first looked for the new king in Jerusalem.
The star stopped over the place where the child was.
When they saw the star again, they were overjoyed.
Painters often show it like a comet with a tail.
Some researchers suspect Jupiter and Saturn close together behind it.

abschnitte.text: Only the **Gospel of Matthew** tells of the star. Wise men from the East saw a star rise and took it as a sign of a new king. They set out on a long journey. First they looked for the child in the capital, **Jerusalem**, at the court of King Herod. There they learned that the expected king was to be born in **Bethlehem**.

When the wise men travelled on, they saw the star again. The Bible says that they had **very great joy**. The star went ahead of them and **stopped** over the place where the child was. So they found Jesus and his mother Mary. They knelt down and brought their gifts.

Many painters show the star like a **comet** with a long, shining tail. A famous example is a fresco by the painter **Giotto** in Padua from the early 14th century. That is why the star is often shown with a tail on nativity scenes too. The Bible says only that it was a star.

Researchers have long wondered what might lie behind the star. Some think of the planets **Jupiter and Saturn**, which stood close together in the sky a few years before the start of our calendar. The astronomer **Johannes Kepler** already put forward this idea. Others think of a comet or a new bright star. Nobody knows for certain, and many see in the star above all a picture of God's guidance.

At Christmas we meet the star everywhere. Many people put a **star on top of the Christmas tree**, some a glass tip instead. Stars hang in windows and decorate streets. Around Epiphany, the **star singers** carry a star from house to house. It recalls that the star showed the way to the child.

gewusst: A European space probe that visited Halley's Comet in 1986 was named after the painter Giotto.
In the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, a silver star marks the place where Jesus is said to have been born.

teile.einleitung: A blessing is a good wish that points to God. Whoever blesses wishes a person good things from God and entrusts them to his protection. There are blessings in church services, at parting, before a meal or before a journey.
wichtigste: To bless means to wish a person good things from God.
In a church service the blessing comes at the end.
A very old blessing begins with “The Lord bless you and keep you”.
During a blessing the hands are often raised or spread out.
At Christmas and Easter the Pope gives the blessing “Urbi et orbi”.
Greetings such as “God keep you” also contain a small blessing.

abschnitte.text: The German word for **bless**, “segnen”, comes from the Latin “signare”, which means “to mark with a sign”. This usually means the sign of the cross. Whoever blesses asks God to protect a person and give them good things. So a blessing is a wish that does not come from a person alone but trusts in God. Pastors can bless, but so can parents, grandparents or friends.

In many churches the **service** ends with the blessing. The pastor lifts the hands or spreads them out over the congregation. The gesture shows that the blessing comes from God and is meant for everyone. Then people go home with this good wish and into the new week. In the Reformed churches of Switzerland this is just as usual as in Catholic ones.

One of the oldest blessings is in the Old Testament, in the 4th Book of Moses. It is called the **Aaronic blessing** because it was entrusted to Aaron and his sons, the priests. It begins with the words “The Lord bless you and keep you”. It goes on to say that God makes his face shine upon you and gives you peace. This blessing is still spoken today in Jewish and Christian services.

At Christmas and Easter the Pope gives a special blessing. It is called **“Urbi et orbi”**, which means “to the city and to the world”. This means the city of Rome and the whole world. The Pope speaks it from the balcony of St Peter's Basilica. Many people all over the world follow it on television or on the internet.

There are blessings in everyday life too. At parting, in some regions people say **“Behüt dich Gott”**, which means: may God protect you. Before a meal people wish each other “Gesegnete Mahlzeit”, a blessed meal. Before a journey one can speak a **travel blessing** and ask God to protect the travellers. Even the greeting “Grüss Gott” originally contains a good wish.

gewusst: The words “Grüss Gott” originally mean “God greet you”, so they are a small blessing.
The Aaronic blessing is over 2,000 years old and is still spoken in almost exactly the same words today.

teile.einleitung: Holy water is water that has been blessed by a priest. It is used above all in the Catholic Church. Many believers make the sign of the cross with it when they enter a church.
wichtigste: Holy water is blessed water.
It stands ready in the holy water stoup at the entrance of Catholic churches.
Many make the sign of the cross with it.
Holy water recalls one's own baptism.
A priest or deacon blesses the water.
In the Easter Vigil the water is blessed especially solemnly.

abschnitte.text: **Holy water** is water that has been **blessed**. In the Catholic Church a **priest** or **deacon** blesses the water. Only then does it become holy water. It looks like ordinary water. But for believers it is a sign of God's closeness.

Right at the **entrance** of a Catholic church, holy water stands ready. The little vessel is called a **holy water stoup**. It is often made of stone and fixed to the wall. Many people dip their fingers in as they go in. Then they make the **sign of the cross** with it.

Water is used at **baptism**. Holy water reminds believers of their own baptism. In many religions water stands for cleansing and new life. With the sign of the cross, people show that they belong to Christ.

Sometimes the priest sprinkles holy water over the people. To do this he dips an **aspergillum**, a holy water sprinkler, into the water and flicks small drops. In this way he blesses people or things. This happens, for example, at services, at the blessing of houses or at a funeral.

Water is blessed especially solemnly in the **Easter Vigil**. In this celebration before Easter, the **baptismal water** is blessed. Many believers also take some holy water home from it. Some have a small holy water stoup by the door at home.

gewusst: In some churches there are holy water dispensers from which you can fill your own bottles.
In Orthodox churches too water is blessed, especially on the feast of the Baptism of Jesus in January.

teile.einleitung: The rosary is a prayer chain made of beads. Especially in the Catholic Church many people pray with it, alone or together.
wichtigste: A rosary is a chain for prayer.
It consists mainly of beads.
The beads help in counting the prayers.
A group usually has ten beads.
Most often one prays the “Hail Mary”.
October is the month of the rosary.

abschnitte.text: A **rosary** is a chain of **beads**. At the end there usually hangs a **small cross**. The beads help in **counting the prayers**: at each bead one says a prayer and moves the chain along a little. So you do not have to count and can concentrate entirely on praying.

Most often one says the prayer **“Hail Mary”**, also called the Ave Maria. The beads are usually arranged in groups of **ten**. Such a group is called a **decade**. Between the groups one prays the **Our Father**. For each decade one thinks of an event from the life of Jesus and Mary.

The rosary is widespread above all in the **Catholic Church**. One prays it alone, in the family or together in church. Many people carry a rosary with them or hang one up. The calm, repeated praying helps them to become still.

In the Catholic Church **October** is the **month of the rosary**. On 7 October the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary is celebrated. In many parishes, also in Switzerland, people meet in October to pray the rosary together.

gewusst: The name recalls a garland of roses that one symbolically gives to Mary with the prayers.
Prayer chains also exist in other religions, for example in Islam and Buddhism.

teile.einleitung: Vatican City is the smallest state in the world. It lies in the middle of Rome and is the seat of the pope, the head of the Catholic Church. The pope is guarded by the Pontifical Swiss Guard.
wichtigste: In area, Vatican City is the smallest state in the world.
It is completely surrounded by the city of Rome.
Since the Lateran Treaties of 1929 it has been a state of its own.
People pay there with the euro.
The official language of the Holy See is Latin.
The Swiss Guard protects the pope.

abschnitte.text: **Vatican City** is smaller than half a square kilometre. That makes it the **smallest state in the world**. Only a few hundred people live there. It is an **enclave** in the middle of **Rome**, that is, completely surrounded by the city. The pope is at once Bishop of Rome and head of state of the Vatican.

For a long time the pope owned a large territory in Italy, the Papal States. In the 19th century it was absorbed into the new Kingdom of Italy. Only in **1929** did the Holy See and Italy come to an agreement in the **Lateran Treaties**. In them Vatican City was recognised as a **sovereign state**.

In the Vatican people pay with the **euro**. This is based on an agreement with the European Union, and the Vatican even mints its own euro coins. The Holy See publishes the most important official documents in **Latin**. In everyday life most people in the Vatican speak **Italian**.

The best-known building is **St Peter's Basilica** with the great St Peter's Square in front of it. It is one of the largest churches in the world. In the **Vatican Museums** you can see famous works of art. They include the **Sistine Chapel** with ceiling paintings by Michelangelo. There the cardinals also elect a new pope.

The **Pontifical Swiss Guard** was founded in 1506. Guards must be Catholic Swiss men and have completed **recruit school** in the Swiss Army. New guards are sworn in every year on **6 May**. On that day in 1527 the Guard defended the pope, and 147 guards died. In 2018 Pope Francis enlarged the Guard from 110 to **135** men.

gewusst: Vatican City has a railway station of its own, one of the smallest in the world.
The uniform of the Swiss Guard shines in blue, yellow and red.

teile.einleitung: The Second Vatican Council was a great assembly of the bishops of the Catholic Church held in Rome from 1962 to 1965. It brought important renewals, such as worship in the local language. Its aim is often summed up in the word “aggiornamento”.
wichtigste: Pope John XXIII opened the Council in 1962.
Pope Paul VI brought it to a close in 1965.
The slogan of the Council is “aggiornamento”.
The Mass could now be celebrated largely in the local language.
The Council recognised the right to religious freedom.
The Swiss theologian Hans Küng took part as an adviser.

abschnitte.text: A **council** is an assembly of the bishops that discusses important questions of the Church. Pope **John XXIII** unexpectedly announced the Council in 1959. He opened it on **11 October 1962** in St Peter's Basilica. He died in 1963, before it was finished. His successor **Paul VI** continued the Council and ended it on 8 December 1965.

The aim of the Council is often described with the Italian word **aggiornamento**. It means roughly “bringing up to date”. The Church was to translate its message into the present. The Council wanted to open itself to the modern world and enter into conversation with it.

A visible innovation came through the Constitution on the Liturgy, **Sacrosanctum Concilium**. Instead of Latin only, the Mass could now be celebrated largely in the **local language**. The aim was for the congregation to be able to take an active part. Since then, in Swiss churches the Mass has been heard in German, French, Italian or Romansh.

The declaration **Nostra aetate** deals with the relationship to non-Christian religions. It rejects any collective guilt of the Jews for the death of Jesus and condemns every form of antisemitism. In **Dignitatis humanae** the Council recognised the **right to religious freedom**. The Pastoral Constitution **Gaudium et spes** deals with the Church in the world of today. It begins with the words “Joy and hope”.

The theologian **Hans Küng** came from **Sursee** in the canton of Lucerne. As a young professor in Tübingen he was named an official adviser to the Council in 1962. Later he came into conflict with Rome. In 1979 he lost his Church licence to teach. But he remained a widely read theologian.

gewusst: More than 2,000 bishops from all over the world took part in the Council.
The First Vatican Council had taken place almost a hundred years earlier, in 1869 and 1870.

teile.einleitung: Catholic social teaching is the teaching of the Catholic Church about a just life together in society. It deals with work, poverty, property, the state and the economy. The most important texts are circular letters of the popes, the encyclicals.
wichtigste: Catholic social teaching asks what a just society looks like.
One principle is the universal destination of goods: the goods of the earth are there for everyone.
The principle of subsidiarity was expressly formulated in 1931 in “Quadragesimo anno”.
John XXIII wrote “Mater et magistra” in 1961.
Paul VI wrote “Populorum progressio” in 1967 about the development of peoples.
John Paul II published “Centesimus annus” in 1991.
Since 2004 there has been a Compendium of the Social Doctrine.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century **industrialisation** changed the lives of many people. Many workers lived in great poverty. In **1891** Pope **Leo XIII** published the encyclical **“Rerum novarum”** on the condition of the workers. It is regarded as the beginning of modern Catholic social teaching. An **encyclical** is a circular letter from the Pope to the whole Church.

One principle is the **dignity of every person**. Another is the **universal destination of goods**: the goods of the earth are intended for **all people**, not only for a few. Added to these are **solidarity**, that is, standing up for one another, and the **common good**. Also important is the **principle of subsidiarity**: what smaller communities such as the family or the municipality can do themselves should not be taken over by the larger one. This principle is also known from Swiss federalism.

In **1931** Pope Pius XI expressly formulated the principle of subsidiarity in **“Quadragesimo anno”**. In **1961** came **“Mater et magistra”** by **John XXIII**. Pope **Paul VI** wrote **“Populorum progressio”** in **1967** about the **development of peoples** and the plight of poor countries. In **1991**, a hundred years after “Rerum novarum”, **John Paul II** published **“Centesimus annus”**. The title means “the hundredth year”.

Since **2004** there has been the **Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church**. This book sums up the teaching systematically. It deals with themes such as family, work, the economy, politics, the environment and peace. Whoever wants to get to know social teaching finds an overview in it. Later popes also wrote new social encyclicals, for example on the protection of the environment.

In **2025** Robert Francis Prevost was elected Pope and called himself **Leo XIV**. He explained that he chose the name partly because of Leo XIII. Just as the latter responded to the first industrial revolution, he sees in **artificial intelligence** a **new industrial revolution**. Social teaching is also meant to give answers to this.

gewusst: The titles of encyclicals are usually the first Latin words of the text.
“Rerum novarum” means “of new things”.

teile.einleitung: Transubstantiation is a teaching of the Catholic Church about the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist. It says that bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ while their appearance remains. The Reformers saw this differently, and it was argued about for a long time.
wichtigste: In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council used the term in official teaching for the first time.
The substance changes; the accidents such as appearance and taste remain.
According to Catholic teaching, the change happens at the consecration.
Luther's teaching is often called consubstantiation.
Zwingli understood the Lord's Supper as a memorial meal.
Calvin and Bullinger reached agreement in 1549 in the Consensus Tigurinus.

abschnitte.text: The term **transubstantiation** means “change of essence”. According to Catholic teaching, the **substance**, that is, the inner essence, of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ. The outer properties such as appearance, smell and taste remain. They are called **accidents**. The terms come from the philosophy of Aristotle.

In the 11th century, **Berengar of Tours** understood the Lord's Supper more as a sign. He denied a change and so triggered the **second Eucharistic controversy**. In 1059 he had to recant in Rome but later held to his view. The **Fourth Lateran Council** under Pope Innocent III used the term “transsubstantiatio” in official teaching for the first time in 1215. In this way it became binding for the Church.

In the Catholic Mass, the priest speaks Jesus's **words of institution** during the Eucharistic Prayer: “This is my body” and “This is my blood”. This part is called the **consecration**. According to Catholic teaching, bread and wine are changed at this moment. The solemn feast of **Corpus Christi** celebrates in particular the lasting presence of Christ in the Eucharist. Pope Urban IV introduced it in 1264, and in Catholic cantons of Switzerland there are processions for it.

The Reformers rejected transubstantiation but did not agree among themselves. **Luther** taught that Christ is really present “in, with and under” bread and wine, but that bread and wine remain. This teaching is often called **consubstantiation**, although Luther hardly used the word. The Zurich Reformer **Huldrych Zwingli** understood Jesus's words in the sense of “This signifies my body”. For him the Lord's Supper was a **memorial meal**; bread and wine are signs.

After Zwingli's death, **Heinrich Bullinger** carried on the Zurich Reformation. In 1549 he reached agreement with **John Calvin** of Geneva in the **Consensus Tigurinus**, the Zurich Consensus. In it they teach a spiritual communion with Christ in the Lord's Supper, without any change of the elements. The consensus joined the Zurich and Geneva Reformations. It became important for the Reformed churches worldwide.

gewusst: “Tigurinus” comes from the Latin name for the area around Zurich.
In 1529 Luther and Zwingli met in Marburg but could not agree on the question of the Lord's Supper.

teile.einleitung: The Quest for the historical Jesus asks what can be known by scholarly means about the historical Jesus. It began in the 18th century and has strongly shaped theology to this day.
wichtigste: Lessing published the critical fragments of Reimarus from 1774 to 1778.
David Friedrich Strauss interpreted many Gospel accounts as myths.
His appointment to Zurich triggered the Züriputsch in 1839.
Albert Schweitzer wrote the history of this research in 1906.
Ernst Käsemann opened the new quest for the historical Jesus in 1953.
The Third Quest understands Jesus as a Jew of his time.

abschnitte.text: The research asks: what was **Jesus** really like as a person of his time? Between 1774 and 1778, **Gotthold Ephraim Lessing**, as librarian in Wolfenbüttel, published writings by **Hermann Samuel Reimarus**. They appeared as Fragments of an Anonymous Author. Reimarus distinguished between what Jesus wanted and what the disciples later taught about him. With this the critical question of the **historical Jesus** began.

In 1835 **David Friedrich Strauss** published the book “The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined”. He interpreted many accounts of the Gospels as **myths**. In 1839 he was to become a professor at the University of **Zurich**. There was great resistance among the people to this. The **Züriputsch** followed, and the liberal Zurich government was overthrown. In France, **Ernest Renan** wrote his successful book “Vie de Jésus” in 1863.

**William Wrede** coined the term **Messianic Secret** in 1901. He interpreted Jesus's commands to be silent in the Gospel of Mark as a theological construction. **Martin Kähler** held in 1892 that faith depends on the proclaimed **Christ of the Bible**, not on a reconstruction. **Albert Schweitzer** showed in 1906 in “From Reimarus to Wrede” that many pictures of Jesus reflected the ideals of their authors.

For a long time people were sceptical about whether much can be known about the earthly Jesus. In 1953 **Ernst Käsemann**, a pupil of Rudolf Bultmann, gave the lecture “The Problem of the Historical Jesus”. He demanded that people again ask historically about Jesus. With this the **new quest** for the historical Jesus began. An important tool was the **criterion of dissimilarity**: it holds a saying of Jesus to be authentic if it can be derived neither from Judaism nor from early Christianity.

Since the 1980s people have spoken of the **Third Quest**. It uses findings from **archaeology** and social history. It consistently understands Jesus as a **Jew** in Galilee in the 1st century. Critics of the criterion of dissimilarity object that it artificially separates Jesus from Judaism.

gewusst: Albert Schweitzer was not only a theologian but also a doctor and organist, and in 1953 he received the Nobel Peace Prize for the year 1952.
The Züriputsch of 1839 is one of the few examples in which a theology book contributed to the fall of a government.

teile.einleitung: The Pauline Epistles are letters in the New Testament that name the apostle Paul as sender. Paul wrote them to Christian communities and to individual people. They are among the oldest texts of Christianity.
wichtigste: Thirteen letters in the New Testament name Paul as sender.
Seven of them are regarded by scholars as certainly written by Paul himself.
The Letter to the Romans is the longest and stands first.
The Letter to Philemon, with only one chapter, is the shortest.
The letters to Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Epistles.
The Hymn to Love stands in the First Letter to the Corinthians.

abschnitte.text: Paul founded and visited Christian **communities** in many cities, for example in Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica. When he travelled on, he advised them by **letters** from a distance. Most of the Pauline letters are addressed to such communities. Some go to individuals. The letters were read aloud in the community.

**Thirteen letters** begin with the name of Paul. Scholars, however, regard only **seven** of them as certainly genuinely his. These are the Letter to the Romans, the two Letters to the Corinthians, the Letter to the Galatians, the Letter to the Philippians, the First Letter to the Thessalonians and the Letter to Philemon. The others were probably written by pupils in his name. The letters are arranged roughly **by length**, which is why the long **Letter to the Romans** comes first.

In chapter 13 of the **First Letter to the Corinthians** stands the **Hymn to Love**: “Love is patient and kind.” This text is often read at weddings and funerals. In the **Letter to the Galatians** Paul writes that there are no longer Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, but that all are **one in Christ**. With this he stresses that all the baptised are of equal worth.

The letters to **Timothy and Titus** are called the **Pastoral Epistles**. Pastor is Latin and means shepherd. The letters give advice on how to lead a community like a good shepherd. Other letters are called the **Captivity Epistles**, among them the Letter to the Philippians. In it Paul mentions that he is in prison, and yet encourages the communities.

The **Letter to Philemon** is the shortest Pauline letter, with only one chapter. It is about a runaway slave named **Onesimus**. Paul asks his owner **Philemon** to take Onesimus back like a brother. The little letter shows how Paul stood up for individual people.

gewusst: The Pauline letters are older than the four Gospels.
Paul dictated many letters to a scribe and sometimes added a greeting at the end in his own hand.

teile.einleitung: The Council of Chalcedon was a great assembly of bishops in the year 451. It dealt with the question of how Jesus Christ can be both God and man.
wichtigste: The council met in the year 451 and is regarded as the fourth ecumenical council.
Chalcedon is today the Kadıköy district of Istanbul.
Emperor Marcian summoned the council.
It taught: Christ has two natures in one person.
It rejected Monophysitism.
The Oriental Orthodox churches still do not recognise Chalcedon today.

abschnitte.text: **Chalcedon** lay on the Asian shore of the Bosporus, opposite Constantinople. Today it is the Istanbul district of **Kadıköy**. The Eastern Roman emperor **Marcian** and his wife **Pulcheria** had the council summoned in the autumn of 451. They wanted to end the disputes after the Synod of Ephesus in 449. It is regarded as the fourth **ecumenical council**, that is, an assembly of the whole Church.

The council decided an important formula of faith. Christ is **true God and true man** in one person. His two **natures** are **without confusion, without change, without division and without separation**. This means: God and man do not flow into one another in him, but are also not separated from each other. The formula is still valid in many churches today.

Pope **Leo the Great** had sent a doctrinal letter, the **“Tome of Leo”** (Tomus ad Flavianum). In it he explained the teaching of the two natures. The council fathers accepted it. They are said to have cried out that Peter had spoken through Leo. What was rejected was **Monophysitism**, the teaching that Christ had only a single nature.

**Canon 28** of the council gave the Bishop of Constantinople, as bishop of the “new Rome”, privileges immediately after Rome. Pope Leo I rejected this decision. The dispute over the rank of the great episcopal sees strained the relationship between East and West for a long time.

Not all Christians accepted the council. The **Coptic**, **Armenian**, **Syriac** and **Ethiopian** churches separated from the imperial church. Today they are called the **Oriental Orthodox churches**. Since the 20th century there have been talks, and many experts think that the sides are closer in faith than was once thought.

gewusst: The formula of Chalcedon is recognised by the Catholic, the Orthodox and most Protestant churches.
Several hundred bishops took part in the Council of Chalcedon, almost all from the east of the Empire.

teile.einleitung: The Agreement of Milan of 313 was a turning point for Christians in the Roman Empire. After long persecution they were now allowed to live their faith freely and openly.
wichtigste: The agreement was concluded in 313 in Milan.
The emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed on it.
It granted religious freedom to all people.
Christians received back confiscated meeting places.
It is also known as the Edict of Toleration of Milan.
It did not yet make Christianity the state religion.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of **313** the emperors **Constantine** and **Licinius** met in **Milan**, which was then called **Mediolanum**. In the 4th century Mediolanum was for a time an imperial residence in the west. The two rulers shared the empire: Constantine governed the west, Licinius the **east**. In Milan they agreed on a common religious policy.

The agreement allowed all people to choose their **religion freely**. That applied to Christians as much as to followers of the old Roman gods. Christianity was put on an **equal footing** with the other religions. It became the **state religion**, however, only several decades later, towards the end of the 4th century under Emperor Theodosius.

During the great **persecution of Christians** the state had confiscated churches, buildings and land belonging to Christians. After the Agreement of Milan these **confiscated meeting places** were to be returned. Already in 311 Emperor **Galerius**, shortly before his death, had issued an **edict of toleration** and ended the persecution, although earlier he had himself persecuted Christians.

In the past people mostly spoke of the **Edict of Toleration of Milan**. An edict is a decree of a ruler. Because no actual edict was issued in Milan, experts today often speak of an **agreement**. Its content is known above all through a letter that Licinius later had published in the east. Later there was war between Licinius and Constantine, which Licinius lost.

gewusst: In 2013 the 1,700th anniversary of the Agreement of Milan was celebrated in Milan and other cities.
The Agreement of Milan is regarded as one of the earliest examples of religious freedom in history.

teile.einleitung: The Romanesque is a building style of the Middle Ages. Typical are thick walls, small windows and round arches. Many old churches in Switzerland and in Europe are Romanesque.
wichtigste: Romanesque building was done in Europe from about 1000 to 1250.
Typical are round arches.
Romanesque churches have thick walls and small windows.
The barrel vault, which looks like a half tube, is common.
Speyer Cathedral is regarded as the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world.
The Grossmünster in Zurich is a well-known Romanesque building.

abschnitte.text: The name **Romanesque** was invented only much later. It means that the style recalls **Roman buildings**. Like the ancient Romans, the master builders used round arches and mighty walls. Romanesque building was done in Europe from about **1000 to 1250**. After it came the **Gothic**.

The most important feature is the **round arch** over doors and windows. Romanesque churches have **thick walls** and **small windows**. That is why it is often rather dark inside. The ceiling is often a **barrel vault**, which looks like a tube cut in half. The heavy stone vaults needed strong walls to carry them.

Many Romanesque churches have a long main space, the **nave**. At the end there is usually the **apse**, a semicircular end behind the altar. Often beneath it there is a **crypt**, a room for tombs or relics. The churches look strong and calm, almost like a fortress of God.

**Speyer Cathedral** in Germany is regarded as the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world. It belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage. In Switzerland the **Grossmünster in Zurich** is a well-known Romanesque building. Parts of Basel Minster and many small village churches, for example in Graubünden, are also Romanesque.

Most people at that time could not read. That is why pictures on walls and ceilings told stories from the Bible. In the church of St Martin in **Zillis** in Graubünden there is a famous painted wooden ceiling from the 12th century. Stone figures on pillars and portals also showed biblical scenes.

gewusst: The wooden ceiling of Zillis consists of 153 painted panels.
In Speyer Cathedral several emperors and kings of the Middle Ages are buried.

teile.einleitung: The Letter to the Romans is a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christian community in Rome. It is the longest Pauline letter in the New Testament and has strongly shaped the history of Christianity.
wichtigste: According to the prevailing view, Paul wrote the letter from Corinth.
Central is the sentence “The righteous shall live by faith”, a quotation from Habakkuk.
For Paul, Abraham serves as an example of righteousness through faith.
Luther translated Romans 3:28 with the addition “alone” through faith.
Augustine and Karl Barth were strongly shaped by the Letter to the Romans.
At the end the scribe Tertius sends greetings and Phoebe is recommended.

abschnitte.text: Paul had not yet visited the community in **Rome** when he wrote the letter. According to the prevailing scholarly view he wrote it in **Corinth**, probably around the year 56 or 57. He introduced himself to the community and explained his faith at length. He dictated the letter: the scribe **Tertius** even adds a greeting of his own in Romans 16:22.

The main theme is the **righteousness of God**. In Romans 1:17 Paul quotes the prophet **Habakkuk**: “The righteous shall live by faith.” According to Paul a person becomes righteous not through his own achievements, but through faith. As an example he names in chapter 4 **Abraham**: God counted his faith to him as righteousness.

The Church Father **Augustine** heard a voice in a garden: “Take up and read.” He opened a passage in the Letter to the Romans and was converted. For **Martin Luther** the letter was the key to the Reformation. In Romans 3:28 he inserted into his translation the word **“alone”**: a person is made righteous “by faith alone”. People argued over this for a long time.

The Swiss theologian **Karl Barth** was pastor in Safenwil in Aargau when he wrote a commentary with the title **“The Letter to the Romans”**. It appeared in 1919 and made him known. Barth stressed that God is wholly other than man. In this way he helped to found **dialectical theology**, which was very influential in the 20th century.

In the last chapter Paul greets many people in Rome by name. In Romans 16:1 he recommends **Phoebe** of **Cenchreae**, a port city near Corinth. She served the community there. Presumably she brought the letter to Rome. The many names show that women too had important tasks in the first communities.

gewusst: The Letter to the Romans has 16 chapters and stands in the Bible as the first of the Pauline letters.
Karl Barth revised his “Letter to the Romans” so strongly that the second edition of 1922 was almost a new book.

teile.einleitung: The Sistine Chapel is a famous chapel in the Vatican in Rome. Michelangelo painted its ceiling and the altar wall with huge pictures from the Bible. Here the cardinals also elect a new pope.
wichtigste: The Sistine Chapel stands in the Apostolic Palace in the Vatican.
It is named after Pope Sixtus IV, who had it built from 1475.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling from 1508 to 1512.
The best-known picture is “The Creation of Adam”.
On the altar wall Michelangelo painted “The Last Judgement”.
The conclave to elect the pope takes place in the chapel.

abschnitte.text: The Sistine Chapel is part of the **Apostolic Palace** in the Vatican. Pope **Sixtus IV** had it built from 1475, which is why it bears his name. The room is about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide. Soon famous artists such as Botticelli and Perugino painted the side walls. Today the chapel is part of the **Vatican Museums** and is visited by millions of people every year.

From 1508 to 1512, **Michelangelo** Buonarroti painted the enormous ceiling. He actually saw himself mainly as a sculptor. He often worked on a high scaffold with his head tilted back. The nine main pictures in the middle show stories from **Genesis**, the first Book of Moses. They include the creation of the world and the story of Noah.

The most famous picture on the ceiling is **“The Creation of Adam”**. God stretches out his finger to give life to the first human being. The fingertips of God and Adam almost touch. These two hands are among the best-known motifs in the history of art. Today they can be seen on posters, mugs and in many films.

Michelangelo painted in the technique of **fresco**. The paint is applied to lime plaster that is still damp. As it dries, it bonds firmly with the wall and lasts for centuries. Because the plaster dries quickly, a piece had to be finished every day. Later, from 1536 to 1541, Michelangelo painted the huge fresco **“The Last Judgement”** on the altar wall, with Christ as the judge.

When a new pope is elected, the cardinals gather in the Sistine Chapel. This assembly is called the **conclave**, from the Latin “cum clave”, with a key. The cardinals are shut off from the outside world. After each round of voting the ballot papers are burned. **White smoke** from the chimney shows that a new pope has been elected; black smoke means: no agreement yet.

gewusst: From 1980 to 1994 the frescoes were cleaned, and afterwards the colours shone much brighter than before.
The Swiss Guard protects the pope and so also the Apostolic Palace.

teile.einleitung: The ontological argument is a famous argument from philosophy. It tries to show, by thinking alone about the concept “God”, that God exists. For almost a thousand years thinkers have argued over whether the argument holds.
wichtigste: Anselm of Canterbury formulated the argument in the work “Proslogion”.
Anselm defines God as that than which nothing greater can be thought.
The monk Gaunilo criticised him with the example of a perfect island.
René Descartes took the argument into his “Meditations”.
Immanuel Kant wrote against it: “Being is evidently not a real predicate.”
In the 20th century Kurt Gödel developed a version using modal logic.

abschnitte.text: **Anselm** was born around 1033 in **Aosta**, not far from the Swiss border. He became a monk in the monastery of Bec in Normandy and later **Archbishop of Canterbury**. Around 1077/78 he wrote the **Proslogion**. In it he defines God as “that than which nothing greater can be thought”. If this being existed only in our thoughts, one could think of a greater one that also really exists. So God must really exist, says Anselm.

Already in Anselm's time there was objection. The monk **Gaunilo of Marmoutiers** said: by this logic the most perfect conceivable island would also have to exist, merely because one imagines it. That is obviously false. Anselm replied that his argument applies **only to God**, because only God is the greatest thing of all.

In the 17th century **René Descartes** took up the argument again. In the fifth of his **“Meditations”** he concludes from the concept of a perfect being to its existence. He compared that with a **triangle**: just as the sum of its angles belongs to a triangle, existence belongs to God. Without existence God would not be perfect.

The philosopher **Immanuel Kant** criticised the argument in the “Critique of Pure Reason”. He wrote: **“Being is evidently not a real predicate.”** By this he meant that existence adds no new property to a concept. His example: **a hundred real thalers** contain in the concept no more than a hundred merely possible thalers. The name “ontological argument” also comes from Kant.

In the 20th century the logician **Kurt Gödel** concerned himself with the argument. He worked out a version using concepts of **modal logic**, a logic about the possible and the necessary. His proof was published only in **1987**, nine years after his death. To this day philosophers discuss whether such proofs are convincing. Believers and non-believers come to different results here.

gewusst: The word “ontological” comes from the Greek “on”, that which is.
With his argument Anselm did not want to replace faith, but to understand it better with reason.

teile.einleitung: The collection is a gathering of money during the service. With the money the churches often help people in need, in Switzerland and all over the world.
wichtigste: In the collection, money is gathered during the service.
The word comes from Latin and means gathering.
The collection is voluntary.
Often the money is put in a little basket or bag or collected at the exit.
The money often goes to aid organisations such as Caritas or HEKS.

abschnitte.text: In the **collection**, churches gather money during or after the service. The word comes from the Latin **collecta** and means gathering.
