In many churches the collection is part of every service. Already in the Bible the Apostle Paul tells how he gathered money for the poor congregation in Jerusalem.

Often someone goes through the rows with a **little basket** or a **small bag** on a pole. In many churches the collection also stands **by the exit**, and you put the money in as you leave. Some churches today also offer the possibility of giving with a mobile phone. How much someone gives is usually seen by nobody.

The collection is **voluntary**. Nobody has to give anything, and everyone gives as much as they can and wish. Even a small amount helps. In Christianity, sharing with others is regarded as an important sign of love of one's neighbour.

Often it is announced beforehand what the collection is intended for. The money often goes to **aid organisations**. **Caritas** is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church. **HEKS** is the aid organisation of the Protestant Reformed Church of Switzerland. Both help people in need at home and abroad. Sometimes the collection is also intended for the parish's own needs.

gewusst: In Switzerland many church members also pay a church tax, but the collection is a voluntary donation.
On certain Sundays all the churches of a country collect for the same purpose.

teile.einleitung: Moses is one of the most important people of the Bible. According to the story, he led the people of Israel out of Egypt into freedom. Even his rescue as a baby in a little basket on the Nile is a well-known story.
wichtigste: According to the Bible, Moses was born in Egypt while the people of Israel were oppressed there.
Pharaoh wanted the newborn boys of the Hebrews to be killed.
His mother hid Moses in a little basket among the reeds on the Nile.
Pharaoh's daughter found him and took him in.
His own mother was allowed to care for him as a nurse.
According to the Bible, the name Moses means “drawn out of the water”.

abschnitte.text: The story is in the **second book of Moses**, also called **Exodus**. The people of Israel lived in Egypt and were forced to do hard labour there. **Pharaoh**, the king of Egypt, was afraid that the people would become too large and too strong. So he ordered the newborn boys of the Hebrews to be killed. In this dangerous time Moses was born.

His mother first hid her baby for three months. Then she wove a little box out of **reeds** and made it waterproof with bitumen and **pitch**. She laid the child in it and hid the basket in the reeds on the bank of the **Nile**. The **sister** of Moses stood nearby and watched from a distance to see what would happen.

**Pharaoh's daughter** came down to the river to bathe. She saw the basket and heard the child crying. She felt pity and took him in. Then the sister asked whether she should fetch a woman who could look after the child. She fetched the child's own mother. So the mother was allowed to bring up her son as a **nurse**, and was even paid for it.

When Moses was older, his mother brought him to Pharaoh's daughter. She adopted him as her son and gave him the name **Moses**, for she said: “I drew him out of the water.” So a child from the oppressed people grew up, of all places, **at the royal court**. Later Moses became the leader of his people.

According to the Bible, Moses led the people of Israel out of Egypt and through the desert. On Mount **Sinai** he received the **Ten Commandments**. In Judaism Moses is the most important prophet. He is also venerated in Christianity and in Islam, where he is called Musa. Whether and when exactly Moses lived cannot be said with certainty by historical scholarship.

gewusst: Later the Bible mentions a sister of Moses named Miriam, and tradition sees in her the girl at the Nile.
In many pictures Moses carries the two stone tablets with the Ten Commandments.

teile.einleitung: The Saint Thomas Christians are one of the oldest Christian communities in the world. They live mainly in the state of Kerala in south-west India. According to their tradition, the apostle Thomas brought the faith to them.
wichtigste: Most Saint Thomas Christians live in Kerala on the Malabar Coast.
According to tradition, the apostle Thomas landed in Muziris in the year 52.
His tomb is honoured in Mylapore in present-day Chennai.
Their liturgy was in Syriac for centuries.
In 1599 the Portuguese enforced Latinisation with the Synod of Diamper.
The largest church of the Saint Thomas Christians today is the Syro-Malabar Church.

abschnitte.text: The **Saint Thomas Christians** live mainly on the **Malabar Coast** in the state of **Kerala** in south-west India. Their mother tongue is **Malayalam**. They are among the oldest Christian communities of all. They are named after the apostle **Thomas**, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus. Today they are divided among several churches.

According to tradition, the apostle Thomas came to India in the year **52**. He is said to have landed in **Muziris**, an important trading port near present-day Kodungallur. In antiquity, trade routes between Rome and India ran through this port. Thomas is said to have founded congregations and later died as a martyr. His tomb is honoured in **Mylapore**, a district of present-day Chennai. Today the San Thome Basilica stands over it.

For a long time the Saint Thomas Christians were closely linked with the **Church of the East** in Mesopotamia. Their bishops often came from there. That is why they celebrated the liturgy in **Syriac**, a form of Aramaic. Aramaic was also the language that Jesus spoke. So in their tradition Indian and oriental roots come together.

In the 16th century the **Portuguese** came to India. They wanted to bring the Saint Thomas Christians into line with the Roman Catholic Church. In 1599, with the **Synod of Diamper** under Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes, they enforced Latinisation. Syriac books were burned and Latin customs introduced. In 1653 many Saint Thomas Christians broke away from the Portuguese with the **Oath of the Leaning Cross** in Mattancherry. They held on to ropes that were tied to a cross.

These events led to a lasting **split**. Today there are several churches of the Saint Thomas Christians, some linked with Rome, others Orthodox or independent. The largest is the **Syro-Malabar Church**. It is linked with Rome but celebrates in a rite of its own, the East Syriac rite. It has several million members.

gewusst: Kerala has a particularly high share of Christians compared with India as a whole.
The apostle Thomas is also known as “doubting Thomas” because he doubted the resurrection.

teile.einleitung: The Psalms are a book of the Bible with prayers and songs. Jews and Christians have prayed and sung them for many centuries, at services and at home.
wichtigste: The Book of Psalms contains 150 psalms.
The Hebrew name “Tehillim” means songs of praise.
Psalm 23 begins with “The Lord is my shepherd”.
The longest psalm is Psalm 119, the shortest Psalm 117.
The book is traditionally divided into five smaller books.
The Swiss national anthem is called the Swiss Psalm (Schweizerpsalm).

abschnitte.text: The **Psalms** stand in the Old Testament. The book contains **150** songs and prayers. In Hebrew it is called **“Tehillim”**, which means **songs of praise**. Many psalms praise God, others lament, ask or give thanks. They tell of joy, fear, grief and trust, that is, of feelings that all people know.

The best-known psalm is probably **Psalm 23**. It begins with the words **“The Lord is my shepherd”** and compares God with a good shepherd who cares for his sheep. The longest psalm is **Psalm 119** with 176 verses. The shortest is **Psalm 117** with only two verses. Many psalms are ascribed to King **David**.

The Book of Psalms is traditionally divided into **five smaller books**. Each ends with a short doxology. It is thought that this division is meant to recall the five books of Moses. The psalms arose over a long time and were only later collected into one book.

In the Psalms the Hebrew word **“Hallelujah”** often occurs. It means **“Praise God”**. Today it is sung in many hymns. The Reformed in Switzerland for a long time sang above all **metrical psalms**, that is, psalms turned into rhymed verses.

The Swiss national anthem is called the **Swiss Psalm** (Schweizerpsalm). Its name recalls the Book of Psalms, for the text is like a prayer and addresses God. The melody was written by the monk **Alberich Zwyssig** in 1841. Since 1981 the Swiss Psalm has been officially the national anthem.

gewusst: Psalm 117 is not only the shortest psalm, but also one of the shortest chapters of the whole Bible.
Psalm 119 is built on the Hebrew alphabet: each group of eight verses begins with the same letter.

t1gdw8wc.t: On the Freedom of a Christian

teile.einleitung: “On the Freedom of a Christian” is a famous work by Martin Luther from the year 1520. In it he explains how a Christian can be at once completely free and completely ready to serve. The work is one of the most important texts of the Reformation.
wichtigste: Luther wrote the work on freedom in the year 1520.
It is one of the three main Reformation writings.
There is a German and a Latin version, “De libertate christiana”.
Luther places two seemingly contradictory theses at the beginning.
The inner person is free in faith, the outer person serves in love.
An accompanying letter was addressed to Pope Leo X.

abschnitte.titel: Two sentences that seem to contradict each other
abschnitte.text: Luther begins with two theses. The first is: “A Christian is a **free lord** of all things and subject to no one.” The second is: “A Christian is a **dutiful servant** of all things and subject to everyone.” At first both sound like a contradiction. Luther relies here on **1 Corinthians 9:19**. There Paul writes that he is free from everyone and yet has made himself a servant to everyone.

Luther resolves the contradiction by distinguishing two sides of the human being. The **inner person** is free before God through **faith**. He does not have to earn salvation through good works. The **outer person** lives together with others. Out of **love** he serves his neighbour freely.

For the relationship between Christ and the believing soul, Luther uses the image of **bride and bridegroom**. As in a marriage, the two share everything with each other. Christ takes the sin upon himself, and the soul receives his righteousness. Luther calls this the **joyful exchange**.

Luther wrote the work at the same time in **German** and in **Latin**. The Latin version is called “De libertate christiana” and was addressed to scholars throughout Europe. He dedicated it to Pope **Leo X** with an open letter. In it he attacked the Roman Curia sharply, but wanted to spare the pope personally.

In **1520**, Luther wrote three fundamental programmatic works. Besides the work on freedom, they are “To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation” and “On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church”. Together they are regarded as the **main Reformation writings**. Thanks to printing, they spread quickly.

gewusst: The work on freedom is quite short and is regarded as one of Luther's most understandable writings.
In the same year, 1520, the pope threatened Luther with excommunication.

teile.einleitung: “Sola fide” is Latin and means “by faith alone”. The principle comes from the Reformation: a person is made right with God because they believe, not because of their good works. It is one of the most important ideas of Martin Luther.
wichtigste: “Sola fide” means “by faith alone”.
It is about justification: God declares the sinner righteous.
For Luther the Bible passage Romans 1:17 was central.
In Romans 3:28 Luther added the word “alone”.
He called the Letter of James an “epistle of straw”.
According to Luther, the believer is “simul iustus et peccator”.

abschnitte.text: **Justification** is a theological technical term. It means that God **declares** sinful people **righteous**, that is, accepts them and forgives them. The question was: how does this happen? According to Reformation teaching, by **faith** in Jesus Christ alone and not through one's own achievements. “Sola fide” belongs together with “sola gratia” and “sola scriptura” among the well-known principles of the Reformation.

For a long time Luther suffered from the fear of not being good enough before God. While working on the Bible he came across **Romans 1:17**: “The righteous shall live by faith.” There Paul quotes the prophet Habakkuk. Luther now understood that God's righteousness makes a person righteous through faith. He later called this liberating insight his **tower experience**, after a tower room in the monastery at Wittenberg. When exactly it happened is disputed among researchers.

In his translation of the Bible, Luther wrote in **Romans 3:28** that a person is made righteous “without the works of the law, by faith alone”. The word **“alone”** is not in the Greek text. His opponents therefore accused him of falsifying it. Luther defended his choice in 1530 in the “Open Letter on Translating”. He said that this is how one speaks in German and that the sense was rightly captured.

The **Letter of James** says that faith without works is dead. Luther found little of the gospel of justification in it and scornfully called it an **“epistle of straw”**. For Luther, good works were not unimportant, but they are the result of faith, not its precondition. The Catholic Church, on the other hand, stressed that faith and works belong together. In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics signed a joint declaration in which they moved closer together on basic questions of justification.

abschnitte.titel: Righteous and a sinner at the same time
abschnitte.text: Luther described the believing person with the formula **“simul iustus et peccator”**. That means “at the same time righteous and a sinner”. Before God the believer is declared righteous. In himself, however, he remains a person who makes mistakes. According to Luther, this tension is part of Christian life.

gewusst: The joint declaration on the doctrine of justification was signed in Augsburg in 1999.
In some editions of Luther's Bible, the sentence from Romans 1:17 is especially highlighted.

teile.einleitung: Al-Andalus is the Arabic name for the areas of the Iberian Peninsula that were ruled by Muslims. This period began in 711 and ended in 1492 with the fall of Granada. In Al-Andalus, science, art and architecture flourished.
wichtigste: Al-Andalus covered Muslim-ruled parts of present-day Spain and Portugal.
The conquest began in 711 across the Strait of Gibraltar.
Gibraltar is named after the general Tariq ibn Ziyad.
Muslims, Christians and Jews lived together for a long time.
The Christian reconquest is called the Reconquista.
In 1492 Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, fell.
The philosopher Ibn Rushd is known in Europe as Averroes.

abschnitte.text: In the year **711**, Muslim troops from **North Africa** crossed the **Strait of Gibraltar**. This strait separates Morocco and Spain and is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. The troops defeated the kingdom of the **Visigoths**. Within a few years they conquered almost the whole peninsula. Their leader was **Tariq ibn Ziyad**.

The name **Gibraltar** comes from the Arabic **“Jabal Tariq”**, which means “mountain of Tariq”. So the rock still recalls the general today. The name **Andalusia** for a region in southern Spain also comes from Al-Andalus. Many Spanish words likewise come from Arabic.

In Al-Andalus, **Muslims, Christians and Jews** lived side by side for a long time and exchanged knowledge. Christians and Jews, however, had **fewer rights** than Muslims. Cities such as **Córdoba** became centres of learning. The philosopher **Ibn Rushd** lived in the 12th century and explained the works of the Greek **Aristotle**. In Europe he was called **Averroes**.

Christian kingdoms from the north expanded step by step towards the south. This **reconquest** is called **Reconquista** in Spanish. In the end only the kingdom of **Granada** remained, with the magnificent fortress **Alhambra**. In January **1492**, the **Catholic Monarchs** Isabella and Ferdinand conquered the city. The last ruler, **Boabdil**, handed it over without a fight and went into exile in North Africa.

gewusst: In the same year as the fall of Granada, 1492, Columbus sailed to America.
The name Gibraltar originally means “mountain of Tariq”.

teile.einleitung: The Lutheran churches go back to the Reformation of Martin Luther in the 16th century. They are among the largest Protestant churches in the world.
wichtigste: With his 95 Theses Luther criticised the sale of indulgences.
An important principle is called “Sola scriptura”, Scripture alone.
In 1521 Luther did not recant his writings at the Diet of Worms.
The Augsburg Confession of 1530 is the foundation of the Lutherans.
Scandinavia is predominantly Lutheran.
The Lutheran World Federation has its seat in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: **Martin Luther** was a monk and a professor in Wittenberg. In 1517 he published his **95 Theses**. They were directed above all against the **sale of indulgences**. With letters of indulgence one could supposedly buy oneself free from the punishment for sins. Luther criticised that forgiveness was in this way becoming a business. In 1521 at the **Diet of Worms** he refused, before Emperor Charles V, to recant his writings.

An important principle of Luther is called **“Sola scriptura”**, which means “Scripture alone”. For Luther the **Bible** stood above the traditions and decisions of the Church. Just as important to him was that a person is saved by God's grace alone and by faith. The most important confession of the Lutherans is the **Augsburg Confession**. It was presented to the emperor in 1530 at the Diet of Augsburg.

Luther wanted the whole **congregation** to sing in German at the service. That is why he wrote many hymns. “**A Mighty Fortress Is Our God**” came into being around 1529 and became the hymn of the Reformation. His seal was the **Luther rose**: a black cross in a red heart on a white rose. Today it is a sign of many Lutheran churches.

Especially many Lutherans live in **Scandinavia**. In Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland the Lutheran church is the largest church, and in some countries it was long the state church. There are also large Lutheran churches in Germany, in the USA and in Africa. The **Lutheran World Federation** was founded in 1947 and has its seat in the Ecumenical Centre in **Geneva**.

In Switzerland it was above all the **Reformed** movement that prevailed, which goes back to **Zwingli** in Zurich and **Calvin** in Geneva. There are only a few Lutheran congregations in Switzerland. Lutherans and Reformed have much in common, however. Since 1973 they have mutually recognised each other as churches through the **Leuenberg Agreement**. Leuenberg lies in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.

gewusst: The Reformation began in 1517 and was celebrated in 2017 with a great jubilee.
After the Diet of Worms, Luther was secretly taken to the Wartburg to protect him.

teile.einleitung: Zacchaeus is a rich chief tax collector from Jericho of whom the Gospel of Luke tells. Because he is short, he climbs a tree to see Jesus. The meeting with Jesus changes his life.
wichtigste: The story is in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 19.
Zacchaeus is chief tax collector in Jericho and rich.
Because he is short, he climbs a sycamore fig tree.
Jesus wants to be his guest, which many people grumble about.
Zacchaeus gives half of his possessions to the poor.
Anyone he has cheated, he pays back four times over.

abschnitte.text: **Zacchaeus** lives in the town of **Jericho**. He is the town's top tax collector, a **chief tax collector**. Tax collectors gathered levies for the Romans. Many took more than they were allowed to. That is why tax collectors were often unpopular and regarded as cheats. The Gospel of Luke says that Zacchaeus was **rich**.

One day **Jesus** passes through Jericho. Zacchaeus very much wants to see him. But he is **short**, and the crowd is large. So he runs ahead and climbs a **sycamore fig tree**. From above he can see Jesus well.

When Jesus comes to the tree, he looks up. He calls Zacchaeus by **name** and says he should **come down** quickly. Today he must stay at his **house**. Zacchaeus hurries down from the tree and welcomes Jesus with great joy.

Many people do not agree with Jesus. They **grumble** and say that Jesus is going to be the guest of a **sinner**. For them a tax collector was not good company. But Jesus goes to Zacchaeus anyway. In this way he shows that he also seeks out the people whom others reject.

Zacchaeus stands up and makes a big promise. He wants to give **half** of his possessions to the **poor**. Anyone he has cheated, he wants to pay back **four times over**. In this way he wants to do more than make up for his wrong. Jesus says that today salvation has come to this house.

gewusst: The sycamore fig tree is also called the sycamore and grows in warm regions.
At the end of the story Jesus says that he came to seek and to save what was lost.

teile.einleitung: Church bells hang high up in the church tower. With their sound they call people to the service and accompany important moments in life. In Switzerland you hear them in almost every village.
wichtigste: Church bells are mostly cast from bronze.
The clapper strikes the bell on the inside.
On Sunday morning the bells call people to the service.
In the past the bells were rung by hand with a rope.
Today most bells are rung electrically with a motor.
The bells hang in the bell chamber.
At a bell hoisting, children pull new bells up into the tower.

abschnitte.text: Church bells are mostly **cast from bronze**. Bronze is a mixture of a lot of **copper** and some **tin**. The liquid metal is poured into a mould and then has to cool slowly. How high a bell sounds depends on its size and shape. In Switzerland there is the Rüetschi bell foundry in Aarau, which has been casting bells for centuries.

Inside the bell hangs the **clapper**. When the bell swings, **it strikes the rim** and the bell sounds. The bells hang in the tower in the **bell chamber**. This has large openings so that the sound carries far outside. Many churches have several bells, which together form a **peal**.

abschnitte.titel: By hand and with a motor
abschnitte.text: In the past the bells were rung **by hand with a rope**. The sexton pulled hard on it until the bell swung. Today most church bells are rung **electrically with a motor**. A control system makes sure they ring at the right time. Often the bells also strike the **hours**.

On **Sunday morning the bells call people to the service**. They also ring on festivals such as Christmas and Easter, at a baptism and at a wedding. At a **funeral** the bell rings to pay the dead their last respects. In the evening, in many villages, the evening bell recalls prayer. In this way the bells accompany the day and the lives of the people.

When a church gets new bells, there is often a big celebration: the **bell hoisting**. In it **children** pull the bells up into the church tower **with ropes**. Beforehand the bells are blessed and often given a name. For the whole village it is a special day that many remember for a long time.

gewusst: On many bells there are inscriptions, names and the year in which they were cast.
Large church bells can weigh several tonnes.

teile.einleitung: Pietism was a movement of renewal in Protestant Christianity that began in the 17th century. For its followers a living, personal faith was more important than fixed doctrines.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Latin “pietas”, piety.
Philipp Jakob Spener, with his writing “Pia Desideria” of 1675, is regarded as the founder.
Believers met in house groups, the “collegia pietatis”.
August Hermann Francke built up large school and social institutions in Halle.
From 1722 the Moravian Church (Herrnhuter Brüdergemeine) arose, from which the “Losungen” come.
Basel was an important centre, for example with the Basel Mission of 1815.

abschnitte.text: **Philipp Jakob Spener** is regarded as the founder of Lutheran Pietism. In his reform writing **“Pia Desideria”** of 1675, which means “pious wishes”, he demanded a renewal of the Church. The believers were to read the Bible themselves and live their faith in everyday life. For this they met, alongside the service, in private house groups, the **collegia pietatis**.

At the centre stood personal **rebirth**. This means the experience that a person is made new inwardly by God and consciously decides for faith. Prayer, Bible reading and an exemplary life were also important. Pietists often campaigned for the poor, the sick and orphans.

**August Hermann Francke** began in 1698 in **Halle** with an orphanage. From it grew the large **Francke Foundations** with schools, workshops, a pharmacy and a printing house. Many children were taught here, also from poor families. Halle thus became a centre of Pietism.

From 1722 **Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf** took in religious refugees on his estate in Upper Lusatia. So the place Herrnhut and the **Herrnhuter Brüdergemeine** (Moravian Church) came into being. From them come the **Losungen** (Daily Watchwords): for every day of the year a Bible verse is drawn by lot. The little book appears every year and is read in many languages, also in Switzerland.

In Switzerland too Pietism found followers, especially in **Basel**. There the **Basel Mission** was founded in 1815, which sent missionaries to Africa and Asia. The Basel man **Christian Friedrich Spittler** founded in 1840 the **Pilgermission St Chrischona** near Basel. From it a training institution for preachers emerged.

gewusst: The Losungen of the Moravians have appeared without interruption every year since 1731.
The Francke Foundations in Halle still exist today.

teile.einleitung: According to custom, the Easter Bunny hides eggs and sweets at Easter. Children look for them in the garden or in the flat. But the hare was not always the animal that brought the eggs.
wichtigste: According to custom, the Easter Bunny hides eggs for the children.
The Easter Bunny is first mentioned in 1682 in a book.
In the Emmental it used to be the cuckoo that brought the eggs.
In parts of Westphalia people spoke of the Easter fox.
In France, according to old belief, the church bells bring the eggs.
Children often collect the eggs in an Easter nest.

abschnitte.text: At Easter children look for the eggs and sweets that the **Easter Bunny** is supposed to have hidden. Often they collect their finds in an **Easter nest**. That is a little basket filled with hay, moss or grass. Of course a hare does not lay eggs. The custom is a cheerful story that parents tell their children.

The Easter Bunny is first mentioned in the year **1682** in a book. A doctor described in it the custom in areas on the Upper Rhine. After that the Easter Bunny spread slowly. Where the idea comes from exactly, nobody knows for sure. For Christians the hare has long been a sign: the Church Father **Ambrose** saw in it an image of the **resurrection**.

In the past quite different animals brought the eggs in some places. Even in the 19th century in parts of Switzerland such as the **Emmental** it was the **cuckoo**. In **Westphalia** in Germany people spoke of the **Easter fox**. In France and other countries, according to old belief, the **church bells** bring the eggs. They fall silent from Maundy Thursday and come back in the Easter night. On the way they let eggs fall into the gardens.

Since **sugar** and cocoa became cheaper, there are many hares and eggs made of **chocolate**. Before Easter the shelves in the shops are full of them. Switzerland is known for its chocolate, and chocolate bunnies are a firm part of Easter here. Many families today hide painted eggs and chocolate together.

gewusst: That the Easter Bunny caught on also has to do with picture books and postcards in the 19th century.
According to the French legend, the church bells fly to Rome over Easter.

teile.einleitung: The Ahmadiyya is a religious movement that came into being in 1889 in British India. Its followers regard themselves as Muslims, but most other Muslims do not recognise them as such. Its motto “Love for all, hatred for none” is well known.
wichtigste: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founded the Ahmadiyya in 1889.
It arose in the Punjab in British India.
The founder saw himself as the promised Messiah and Mahdi.
The motto is “Love for all, hatred for none”.
In 1974 Pakistan declared the Ahmadis non-Muslims.
The head of the largest community bears the title of caliph.
Its headquarters is now in Great Britain.

abschnitte.text: The movement was founded by **Mirza Ghulam Ahmad**, and its name is derived from his name. On **23 March 1889**, the first followers swore allegiance to him in **Ludhiana**. At that time the area belonged to the **Punjab** in **British India**. Today this region lies in **India** and **Pakistan**.

The founder regarded himself as the **promised Messiah** and **Mahdi**. According to Islamic tradition, the Mahdi is a renewer guided by God. Most other Muslims reject this teaching. The Ahmadiyya stresses that faith should be spread without violence. Its well-known motto is **“Love for all, hatred for none”**.

After the founder's death, the community chose a successor in **1908** with the title **caliph**. There have been five caliphs to date. Since **2003**, **Mirza Masroor Ahmad** has led the largest Ahmadiyya community. A smaller group, the Lahore Ahmadiyya, split off early and has no such caliphate.

In **Pakistan**, a constitutional amendment declared the Ahmadis a **non-Muslim minority** in **1974**. Since then they have been heavily discriminated against there. Because of this persecution the leadership moved to **London** in **1984**. Since **2019** the seat has been in **Tilford** in southern England. The community has followers in many countries.

In Switzerland too there is a small Ahmadiyya community. In **Zurich** stands the **Mahmood Mosque**, which opened in 1963. It is regarded as the first purpose-built mosque in Switzerland. Its minaret can be seen from afar.

gewusst: According to its own figures, the Ahmadiyya is now present in over 200 countries.
The name Ahmadiyya is derived from the name of the founder.

teile.einleitung: Grace before meals is a short prayer at mealtime. People thank God for the food on the table and ask for his blessing. Many families, camps and kindergartens say or sing it together.
wichtigste: Grace is mostly said before the meal, sometimes after it too.
People thank God for the food.
A prayer usually ends with “Amen”, which means roughly “so be it”.
Many people fold their hands when they pray.
A well-known grace is “Come, Lord Jesus, be our guest”.
Many graces are sung.

abschnitte.text: **Grace** is mostly said **before the meal**, when everyone is sitting at the table. Sometimes people also pray afterwards. In the prayer people **thank** God for the food. They remember that food is not something to be taken for granted and that many people have worked to produce it. Grace is also a lovely moment in which everyone calms down.

Many people **fold** their **hands** when they pray. In this way they become calm and can concentrate on the prayer. At the end everyone says **“Amen”**. The word comes from **Hebrew** and means roughly “so be it” or “truly”. With the Amen, everyone agrees to the prayer.

A very well-known grace goes: **“Come, Lord Jesus, be our guest and bless what you have given us.”** In it Jesus is invited to the table as a guest. The **Lord's Prayer** also fits a meal. In it we say: “Give us today our daily bread.” Bread here stands for everything we need to live.

Many graces exist as short **songs**. In families, **camps** and kindergartens they are often sung together, sometimes as a round. Some songs have funny movements to go with them. Other families simply keep a moment of silence. Afterwards, in Switzerland, people often wish each other **“En Guete”**, enjoy your meal.

gewusst: In Judaism and Islam too there are prayers and words of blessing before or after eating.
The word “Amen” has stayed the same in a great many languages of the world.

teile.einleitung: The East-West Schism is the great split between the Church in the East and the Church in the West. The year 1054 is regarded as its beginning. From it arose the Orthodox and the Roman Catholic churches.
wichtigste: Schism is a Greek word and means split.
In 1054 representatives of Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other.
The Patriarch of Constantinople at the time was Michael Cerularius.
The papal envoys laid the bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia.
An important point of dispute was the addition “Filioque” in the creed.
The Eastern Church became the Orthodox Church, the Western Church the Roman Catholic Church.

abschnitte.text: The Roman Empire had long been divided into a western part and an eastern part. In the west, **Rome** with the Pope was the centre, and the language of the Church was Latin. In the east, **Constantinople**, today's Istanbul, was the capital of the Byzantine Empire and seat of the Patriarch. There people spoke Greek. Over the centuries customs and ways of thinking drifted further and further apart.

abschnitte.titel: A quarrel over faith and power
abschnitte.text: An important point of dispute was the **Filioque**, which means “and from the Son”. The West added to the creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father **and from the Son**. The East rejected this addition. It was also disputed how much power the **Pope** has over the whole Church. In addition there were differences in worship, for example over the bread for communion.

In 1054 envoys of the Pope under **Cardinal Humbert** travelled to Constantinople. They quarrelled fiercely with the Patriarch **Michael Cerularius**. In the end they laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of **Hagia Sophia**, the main church of the empire. The Patriarch in turn excommunicated the envoys. At that time many people did not yet think that the separation would last so long.

In 1204 crusaders from the West conquered and plundered Constantinople. That deepened the mistrust greatly. From then on East and West were finally separated. Only in 1965 did **Pope Paul VI** and **Patriarch Athenagoras** lift the mutual excommunication of 1054. The two churches are not united again, but today they speak to each other in a friendly way.

gewusst: The word “orthodox” means “of right belief”, and the word “catholic” means “universal” or “all-embracing”.
The excommunication of 1054 was directed against persons, not against the whole other Church.

teile.einleitung: Nazareth is the town in which, according to the Gospels, Jesus grew up. In his time it was only a small village. Today Nazareth is a large city in the north of Israel.
wichtigste: Nazareth lies in Galilee, a hilly region in the north of Israel.
In the time of Jesus probably only a few hundred people lived there.
The family of Jesus had to flee from King Herod and afterwards lived in Nazareth.
In everyday life people in Galilee spoke Aramaic.
At about 30 years old Jesus left Nazareth and began to preach.
The Basilica of the Annunciation was consecrated in 1969.

abschnitte.text: Nazareth lies in **Galilee**, in the north of present-day **Israel**. In the time of Jesus it was only a small village. Researchers estimate that only a few hundred people lived there at that time. The people were farmers and craftsmen. Joseph, the husband of Mary, was according to the Gospels a carpenter or builder.

According to the Gospel of Luke, **Mary** received in Nazareth from the angel Gabriel the message that she would become the mother of Jesus. The Gospel of Matthew tells that the family had to flee from **King Herod**. He was afraid of a new king. Afterwards the family settled in Nazareth. In everyday life Jesus here spoke **Aramaic**, the language of the people in Galilee.

At **about 30 years old** Jesus began to work publicly. When he preached in the **synagogue** of Nazareth, the people rejected him and drove him out of the town. Jesus said of this: a prophet is without honour in his own country. In the Gospel of John, **Nathanael** asks doubtfully whether anything good can come out of Nazareth. Even so, Jesus was named after the place: Jesus of Nazareth.

Today Nazareth is a large city with many Arab inhabitants, Christians and Muslims. Every year many **pilgrims** come. The most important church is the **Basilica of the Annunciation**, which was consecrated in 1969. It stands at the place where, according to tradition, Mary received the angel's message. It is regarded as the largest church in the Middle East.

gewusst: Because Jesus came from Nazareth, his followers were in the past also called Nazarenes.
In the Basilica of the Annunciation hang depictions of Mary from many countries of the world.

teile.einleitung: A nativity scene shows the birth of Jesus in the stable at Bethlehem with figures. It includes Mary, Joseph, the child, shepherds, angels and animals such as the ox and donkey. Many families and churches set up a nativity scene in Advent.
wichtigste: A nativity scene shows the birth of Jesus with figures.
The ox and donkey stand in almost every nativity scene.
In 1223 Francis of Assisi celebrated in Greccio with a manger and real animals.
Nativity figures are especially often made of wood.
In many families the baby Jesus is added only on Christmas Eve.
In the nativity play, children act out the Christmas story.

abschnitte.titel: What belongs in a nativity scene
abschnitte.text: The nativity scene usually shows a simple **stable** with a roof. In it lie animals, straw and the child. Around the child stand **Mary** and **Joseph**. In addition there are **shepherds** with sheep and **angels**. Often the three kings with their gifts are added later.

The **ox and donkey** have belonged to almost every nativity scene for a very long time. They stand beside the child in the stable. In Luke's Christmas story they are not mentioned at all. They come from an old interpretation of a verse in the Book of Isaiah, and in this way they became fixed figures of the nativity scene.

In the year **1223**, **Francis of Assisi** celebrated Christmas in a special way in the village of **Greccio** in Italy. He set up a manger with a real ox and a donkey. In this way he wanted to show the story come alive. This celebration is regarded as one of the first nativity scenes of this kind.

Many **nativity figures** are carved from **wood**. But there are also figures of clay or cloth. Some nativity scenes are very small, others fill a whole room. Many families set up the nativity scene already in **Advent** but leave it empty. The **baby Jesus** is added only on **Christmas Eve**.

In the **nativity play**, children act Mary, Joseph, the shepherds and the angels. It is often performed in church. In a **living nativity**, people portray the figures. Often real sheep or donkeys are there too. In this way the story becomes vivid for everyone.

gewusst: Especially famous are the magnificent nativity scenes from Naples with many scenes of everyday life.
The German word “Krippe” actually means feeding trough.

teile.einleitung: The Kulturkampf was a fierce dispute between the state and the Catholic Church in Switzerland in the 19th century. It lasted above all in the 1870s and shaped the relationship between church and state for a long time.
wichtigste: The trigger was the dogma of papal infallibility of 1870.
In 1873 the diocesan cantons deposed Bishop Eugène Lachat of Basel.
Gaspard Mermillod was expelled from Switzerland in 1873.
In 1873 the Federal Council broke off relations with the Holy See.
In 1874 compulsory civil marriage was introduced.
Only in 1920 did a nuncio return to Bern.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century the **liberals** wanted a modern state in which the Church has less influence. The Catholic Church resisted this. In 1870 the First Vatican Council proclaimed the **infallibility of the Pope** in matters of faith. Many liberals saw in this a danger to the state. So began an open dispute, which is called the **Kulturkampf**.

The Bishop of Basel, **Eugène Lachat**, proclaimed the new dogma despite a ban. In 1873 most cantons of the diocese declared him deposed. In the same year Rome appointed **Gaspard Mermillod** Apostolic Vicar of Geneva. The Federal Council saw this as interference in the diocesan order and expelled Mermillod. In December 1873 the Federal Council **broke off** relations with the **Holy See**.

In the **Jura**, then part of Bern, many Catholic priests refused to recognise the deposition of their bishop. In 1874 the canton of Bern expelled about 97 priests. In 1875 the Confederation declared this expulsion unconstitutional. During this time the **Christ Catholic Church** also arose, which rejected the dogma of infallibility.

The new **Federal Constitution of 1874** contained several **confessional exception articles**. New dioceses now needed the approval of the Confederation. Clergy could not be elected to the **National Council**, until 1999. With a federal law, **compulsory civil marriage** was introduced in 1874. Only a marriage concluded before the **registry office** was now valid.

From the 1880s the dispute calmed down. In 1884 the Confederation and the Vatican agreed on the restoration of the **Diocese of Basel**. The parishes of Ticino were detached from the dioceses of **Como and Milan**. Only in **1920** did a papal **nuncio** return to Bern. The last exception articles were repealed much later.

gewusst: The ban on new dioceses without the consent of the Confederation was only repealed in 2001 in a popular vote.
Since the Kulturkampf, couples in Switzerland marry first at the registry office, and a church wedding can follow afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Teresa of Ávila was a Spanish nun and mystic of the 16th century. She renewed the order of the Carmelite nuns and wrote famous books on prayer. In 1970 she was the first woman to be named a Doctor of the Church.
wichtigste: Teresa was born in 1515 in Ávila in Spain.
She entered a Carmelite convent and reformed the order.
Her reform gave rise to the Discalced Carmelite nuns and friars.
She worked closely with John of the Cross.
Her best-known book is called “The Interior Castle”.
In 1970 she became the first woman Doctor of the Church.

abschnitte.text: Teresa was born in **1515** in **Ávila** in Castile, a town with mighty walls. As a young woman she entered a convent of the **Carmelite nuns** in Ávila. For a long time she was often ill and struggled with her faith. Then she had deep experiences of God in prayer. That is why she is called a **mystic**.

Teresa found that life in the convent had become too comfortable. She wanted to return to simplicity, silence and prayer. In 1562 she founded a first small convent in Ávila according to her rules. The sisters wore simple sandals instead of shoes, which is why they are called **Discalced Carmelite nuns**. Before her death Teresa founded many more convents throughout Spain.

In her reform, Teresa worked closely with the young monk **John of the Cross**. He carried the renewal over to the male Carmelites. Like Teresa, he was a great mystic and poet. Both met with resistance, including within their own order. Today both are regarded as saints and Doctors of the Church.

Teresa wrote several books that are still read today. In the best known, **“The Interior Castle”**, she compares the soul to a castle of crystal with many rooms. In the middle lives **God**. The path of prayer leads step by step inwards to him. Her prayer **“Nada te turbe”**, “Let nothing disturb you”, is also well known; the Taizé community sings it as a song.

Teresa died in October **1582**, in exactly the night when Spain introduced the **Gregorian calendar**. The 4th of October was followed directly by the 15th of October. In 1622 she was canonised. In **1970** Pope Paul VI made her the **first woman** to be a **Doctor of the Church**. Catherine of Siena followed shortly afterwards.

gewusst: Her feast day is on 15 October, that is, the day after her death in the new calendar.
Teresa wrote with a lot of humour; some of her letters are really funny.

teile.einleitung: The Diet of Worms of 1521 was an important moment of the Reformation. Martin Luther had to answer there before the emperor and refused to recant his writings.
wichtigste: In 1521 Luther had to answer in Worms before Emperor Charles V.
He was asked to recant his writings.
The sentence “Here I stand, I can do no other” is ascribed to Luther.
The Edict of Worms placed him under the imperial ban.
Frederick the Wise had him hidden at the Wartburg.
There, as “Junker Jörg”, Luther translated the New Testament.

abschnitte.text: A **Diet** (Reichstag) was an assembly of the princes and cities of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1521 it took place in the city of **Worms**. There Martin Luther had to answer before the young **Emperor Charles V**. The Pope had already excluded him from the Church, because Luther had sharply criticised the Church.

Luther was asked to **recant his writings**. Luther asked for time to think. The next day he declared that he could recant only if he were refuted from the Bible or with clear reasons. The famous sentence **“Here I stand, I can do no other”** is ascribed to him. Whether he said it exactly like that is not certain.

After the Diet the emperor issued the **Edict of Worms**. It placed Luther under the **imperial ban**. With it he was an outlaw, nobody was allowed to protect him, and his books were to be burned. But many princes and cities did not enforce the edict.

Luther's prince, **Frederick the Wise** of Saxony, had him staged as if attacked on his way home. Luther was secretly taken to the **Wartburg** near Eisenach. There he lived under the assumed name **Junker Jörg** (Knight George) and let his beard grow. In only a few weeks he translated the **New Testament** from Greek into German.

gewusst: Luther's translation of the New Testament appeared in 1522 and was called the “September Testament” because of the month of publication.
At the Wartburg you can still visit today the room in which Luther worked.

teile.einleitung: The Trinity is a central teaching of Christianity. It says that the one God lives in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This teaching was formulated in long debates in the first centuries after Christ.
wichtigste: Trinity means that God is one and yet consists of three persons.
The term “trinitas” comes from the Church writer Tertullian.
The Council of Nicaea in 325 called the Son “homoousios”, of one being with the Father.
Nicaea condemned the teaching of Arius that the Son was a creature.
The Council of Constantinople in 381 reaffirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit.
The addition “filioque” still divides the Western and Eastern churches today.

abschnitte.text: Christians believe in **one single God**. At the same time they speak of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The teaching of the **Trinity** tries to explain how this fits together. The three are not three gods but three persons of the one God. The Latin Church writer **Tertullian** of Carthage introduced the term “trinitas” around 200. The formula of one substance and three persons also comes from him.

The Alexandrian presbyter **Arius** taught that the Son was created by God and not eternal like the Father. The **Council of Nicaea** in the year 325 was directed against this. It declared that the Son is “homoousios”, that is, of one being with the Father. A group seeking a middle way later preferred the word “homoiousios”, of similar being. The difference is only one letter, but theologically very important.

The **First Council of Constantinople** in the year 381 reaffirmed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit. From it came the **Nicene-Constantinopolitan** Creed. In the West the word **filioque** was added later, which means “and from the Son”. According to this, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Eastern Church rejects this addition; it strained relations up to the schism of 1054.

In the 4th century the **Cappadocians** shaped the formula “one essence, three hypostases”. They included Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa. **Augustine** wrote the work “De trinitate”. He compared the Trinity to the human mind, which consists of memory, understanding and will. This is called his psychological doctrine of the Trinity.

Not every explanation was accepted. **Modalism**, also called Sabellianism, saw Father, Son and Spirit only as three modes of appearance of a single God. The Church rejected this teaching because it removes the distinction between the persons. The technical term **perichoresis**, by contrast, describes how the three persons wholly interpenetrate one another.

gewusst: Perichoresis literally means roughly “moving around one another”.
The teaching of Nicaea and Constantinople is still prayed in the services of many churches today.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican and one of the most important thinkers of the Middle Ages. He wanted to show that faith and reason fit together. His works shape Catholic theology to this day.
wichtigste: Thomas was born around 1225 near Aquino in Italy.
Against his family's wishes he became a Dominican.
He relied heavily on the philosopher Aristotle.
He taught as a professor at the University of Paris.
He is regarded as the most important representative of Scholasticism.
Shortly before his death he compared everything he had written to straw.

abschnitte.titel: A nobleman becomes a begging friar
abschnitte.text: Thomas was born around **1225** in the castle of Roccasecca near **Aquino**, between Rome and Naples. His noble family wanted him to become abbot of a rich monastery. But Thomas joined the young order of the **Dominicans**, a mendicant order that valued study and preaching. For that reason his brothers held him **prisoner** in a castle for over a year. In the end the family let him go.

Thomas studied, among other places, in Cologne under the famous scholar **Albert the Great**. Because he was tall, strong and quiet, fellow students called him the **“dumb ox”**. Albert is said to have said that the bellowing of this ox would one day be heard by the whole world. Later Thomas became a master of theology at the **University of Paris**. He also taught in Italy, for example in Naples.

Thomas relied especially on the Greek philosopher **Aristotle**. He combined his thinking with the Christian faith. For him **faith and reason** do not contradict each other but complement each other. This way of thinking of the Middle Ages is called **Scholasticism**: people thought through the faith with careful questions and logical arguments. Thomas is regarded as its most important representative.

Thomas wrote a great deal. The **Summa contra gentiles** was written around 1259 to 1265. It argues largely by reason, because non-Christians do not accept the Bible as an authority. His main work is the **Summa theologiae**, which remained unfinished. At the request of Pope Urban IV he wrote texts for the new feast of **Corpus Christi**, including the hymn “Pange lingua”.

In the year **1273** Thomas had a deep experience in prayer. Afterwards he stopped writing. He is said to have said that everything he had written seemed to him like **straw** in comparison. Thomas died in 1274 on the way to a council. In 1323 he was canonised, and later he was also named a Doctor of the Church.

gewusst: The Summa theologiae is so extensive that in print it fills many thick volumes.
Thomas is also called “Doctor angelicus”, the angelic teacher.

teile.einleitung: Mission means bringing the Christian faith to other people. The word comes from the Latin “missio”, meaning sending. The history of mission is long and has bright and dark sides, especially in the time of the colonies.
wichtigste: Christians appeal to Jesus's commission to bring the Gospel to all peoples.
In the colonial period, mission and conquest were often closely linked.
Bartolomé de Las Casas defended the rights of the indigenous people in America.
The Jesuits set up reductions for the Guaraní, protected villages of their own.
From 1828 the Basel Mission sent missionaries to the Gold Coast, today's Ghana.
Missionaries also founded schools and hospitals, but their work is also viewed critically.

abschnitte.text: Even the first Christians such as **Paul** travelled far to tell of the faith. Later monks from Ireland moved through Europe. One of them was **Gallus**, after whom the city of St Gallen is named. In this way Christianity gradually came to many countries. In the Middle Ages mission and politics were often linked, and kings had their peoples baptised.

From 1492 the Spanish and the Portuguese conquered large areas in America. Under the **encomienda** system, settlers were assigned indigenous people as workers and were supposed to Christianise them. In reality it led to forced labour and exploitation. With the **Requerimiento** of 1513 the indigenous people were called on to submit to the Crown and the Church, often in Spanish and without translation. Portugal organised the Church in its colonies through the **Padroado**, a right granted by the Pope.

The Dominican **Bartolomé de Las Casas** denounced the violence of the conquerors. In the Valladolid debate of 1550 he argued with Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda about whether indigenous people could be converted by force. Las Casas said no. In the area of present-day Paraguay, **Jesuits** founded reductions for the **Guaraní**. There they were protected from slave hunters, until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767/68.

In the Kingdom of Kongo, King **Afonso I** had Christianity spread from 1506 and at the same time complained about the slave trade of the Portuguese. In the 19th century many Protestant missionaries came to Africa. The **Basel Mission** worked from 1828 on the **Gold Coast**, and many of its first missionaries died of tropical diseases. The missionary **David Livingstone** summed up his programme as “Christianity, commerce and civilisation”. He hoped that legal trade would displace the slave trade.

Missionaries often built **schools and hospitals** and translated the Bible into many languages. At the same time they sometimes helped to suppress foreign cultures, and worked closely with colonial powers. That is why the history of mission is today being **critically re-examined**. Many churches now understand mission as partnership. In Switzerland the organisation **Mission 21** has emerged from the Basel Mission.

gewusst: The Presbyterian Church of Ghana arose from the work of the Basel Mission.
Afonso I of Kongo wrote letters to the Portuguese king that have survived to this day.

teile.einleitung: Pacifism is the attitude of rejecting war and violence on principle. In Christianity pacifists appeal to the words of Jesus about love of enemies. Other Christians think that violence can sometimes be permitted to defend against injustice.
wichtigste: Pacifists reject war and violence on principle.
The Schleitheim Articles of the Swiss Anabaptists of 1527 rejected the use of the sword.
Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren count among the historic peace churches.
Augustine developed the doctrine of the just war.
In 1992 Switzerland adopted a civilian alternative service.

abschnitte.titel: Peace after the Sermon on the Mount
abschnitte.text: In the **Sermon on the Mount** Jesus says: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” He also demands that people **love their enemies** and not answer violence with violence. Many Christians see in this a commission to **renounce violence**. The word pacifism comes from the Latin “pax”, peace. Pacifists reject war and violence on principle.

abschnitte.titel: The doctrine of the just war
abschnitte.text: Not all Christians think alike. The Church Father **Augustine of Hippo** asked under what conditions a war might be permitted, for example to defend against injustice. From this came the **doctrine of the just war**. Later **Thomas Aquinas** developed it further. This doctrine stands opposed to strict pacifism. The great churches long upheld it.

abschnitte.titel: The Anabaptists and the peace churches
abschnitte.text: In **1527** Swiss Anabaptists met in **Schleitheim** in the canton of Schaffhausen. Under the leadership of **Michael Sattler**, they adopted the **Schleitheim Articles**. In them they rejected, among other things, that Christians should use the sword. From the Anabaptist movement the **Mennonites** emerged. Together with the **Quakers** and the Church of the Brethren they count as the **historic peace churches**, which traditionally reject military service.

In Switzerland there is **compulsory military service** for men. For a long time men who refused service on grounds of conscience were punished. On **17 May 1992** the voters adopted a **civilian alternative service** in the constitution. The Civilian Service Act came into force in **1996**. Since then men who do not want to do military service can work, for example, in hospitals, homes or in nature conservation.

gewusst: The Mennonites are named after the Anabaptist leader Menno Simons.
In 1947 the Quakers received the Nobel Peace Prize for their help after the world wars.

teile.einleitung: The Book of Revelation is the last book of the Christian Bible. In visions, that is, in mysterious images, it describes the end of the old world and a new creation. Its other name is the Apocalypse.
wichtigste: Revelation stands at the very end of the Christian Bible.
According to his own account, John received his visions on the island of Patmos.
Apocalypse literally means “unveiling”.
At the beginning stand letters to seven communities in Asia Minor.
A lamb, the image for Christ, opens the scroll with the seven seals.
At the end John sees a new heaven and a new earth.

abschnitte.text: The author calls himself **John**. He writes that he was on the island of **Patmos** in the Aegean when he had his visions. There a grotto that recalls him is still shown today. Revelation was written in Greek, probably towards the end of the 1st century. At that time Christians in the Roman Empire were in part persecuted. The book wanted to give them courage and hope.

The other name of the book is **Apocalypse**. The Greek word literally means “uncovering” or **“unveiling”**. What is meant is that God shows what is hidden. Only later did the word become, in everyday speech, a term for terrible catastrophes. The word **Armageddon**, the place of the last battle, is also used in everyday speech today for a huge catastrophe.

At the beginning stand **letters to seven communities** in Asia Minor, among them Ephesus, Smyrna and Pergamum. The number **seven** keeps recurring: seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls. In the Bible it often stands for completeness. Only a **lamb** is worthy to open the scroll with the seven seals. The lamb is an image for **Jesus Christ**.

Revelation is full of **images**: angels, dragons, horsemen and beasts. In chapter 13 the number **666** stands as the “number of the beast” for a hostile power. Some old manuscripts have the number 616 instead. Many researchers think that the images allude to the power of Rome. The images are hard to interpret, which is why there are many different interpretations.

At the end John sees **a new heaven and a new earth**. He describes the **heavenly Jerusalem**, a shining city with twelve gates. There there is to be no more suffering, no tears and no death. So the Bible ends with a message of hope. Many artists have painted these images, for example Albrecht Dürer.

gewusst: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse from Revelation are a popular motif in art.
Revelation has 22 chapters.

teile.einleitung: The Luther Bible is Martin Luther's translation of the Bible into German. It made the Bible understandable for ordinary people and strongly shaped the German language.
wichtigste: Luther's New Testament appeared in 1522 as the “September Testament”.
Philipp Melanchthon helped him as an expert in Greek.
The first complete Luther Bible was printed in Wittenberg.
Luther wanted to write as people spoke.
The Luther Bible helped to shape a common written language.
In 2017 a revision appeared for the 500th anniversary of the Reformation.

abschnitte.text: After the Diet of Worms in 1521, **Martin Luther** was taken to the **Wartburg** for his protection. There in a few weeks he translated the **New Testament** from Greek into German. It appeared in **1522**. Because it came out in September, it is called the **“September Testament”**. In December an improved edition followed.

Luther did not work alone. **Philipp Melanchthon**, professor in **Wittenberg** and an outstanding expert in the ancient languages, checked the translation carefully. Afterwards Luther and his helpers also translated the **Old Testament** from Hebrew. In 1534 the first complete Luther Bible appeared in Wittenberg. Thanks to **printing** it spread quickly.

Luther wanted **ordinary people** to understand the Bible. In his own words he wanted to look at the people's mouths and so write as they spoke. In 1530 he explained in the **“Open Letter on Translating”** how he went about translating. In it he defended his understandable language against critics.

The Luther Bible was read in all German-speaking areas. Many words and expressions from it are still in use today. In this way it contributed much to the unification of **standard German**. In Switzerland, almost at the same time, the **Zurich Bible** came into being, on which Zwingli and his colleagues worked and which appeared complete in 1531.

The Luther Bible has been revised again and again so that it stays understandable. The latest version appeared in **2017** for the **500th anniversary of the Reformation**. In 1517 Luther had published his theses. In the Protestant churches of Germany the Luther Bible is still the most widely used translation. The **Einheitsübersetzung** (Standard Translation), on the other hand, is used mainly by Catholics.

gewusst: German words such as “Lückenbüsser” (stopgap) and sayings such as “hiding one's light under a bushel” go back to the Luther Bible.
Luther translated the New Testament at the Wartburg in only about eleven weeks.

t1nugwb3.t: Roman Catholic Central Conference of Switzerland

teile.einleitung: The Roman Catholic Central Conference of Switzerland, RKZ for short, is the association of the Catholic cantonal churches. It is a special feature of the Swiss church system.
wichtigste: The RKZ has existed since 1971.
It unites the cantonal church organisations.
Its general secretariat is in Zurich.
It understands itself as the counterpart to the Swiss Bishops' Conference.
The highest body is the plenary assembly with two delegates per member.
It co-finances church tasks that concern the whole of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the Catholic Church has two sides. The **bishops** and priests lead the Church in questions of faith. In addition, in most cantons there is a **cantonal church** with elected authorities. It collects church taxes and manages money and buildings. This coexistence is called the **dual system**. The RKZ understands itself as the counterpart to the **Swiss Bishops' Conference**.

The RKZ has existed **since 1971**. It unites the **cantonal church organisations** of Switzerland. Its general secretariat is in **Zurich**. On **1 December 2019** the cantonal church of **Schwyz** also joined as a full member. Before that it had only had guest status.

The highest body is the **plenary assembly**. Each member organisation sends **two delegates**. The assembly decides on important questions and the budget. In November 2019 **Renata Asal-Steger** became president of the RKZ.

The RKZ **co-finances church tasks that concern the whole of Switzerland**. These include work that a single parish or canton cannot bear alone, for example specialist offices, media work or the work of the Bishops' Conference. The cantonal churches pay contributions for this. In doing so the RKZ works closely with the bishops.

gewusst: The dual system with cantonal churches in this form exists almost only in Switzerland.
In Switzerland each canton itself regulates how it works together with the churches.

teile.einleitung: Notre-Dame-du-Haut is a pilgrimage chapel on a hill above the French village of Ronchamp. It was built by the architect Le Corbusier, who came from Switzerland. With its curved forms it is regarded as one of the most important buildings of the 20th century.
wichtigste: The chapel stands in Ronchamp in France, in the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté.
Le Corbusier was born in 1887 as Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in La Chaux-de-Fonds.
The chapel was built from 1953 to 1955 and consecrated on 25 June 1955.
The curved concrete roof recalls a shell or a ship's hull.
Through the thick south wall light falls through irregular, coloured openings.
Since 2016 the chapel has belonged to the UNESCO World Heritage.

abschnitte.text: **Le Corbusier** was really called **Charles-Édouard Jeanneret**. He was born in 1887 in **La Chaux-de-Fonds** in the Neuchâtel Jura. Later he lived in Paris and took French citizenship. He became one of the best-known architects in the world. He was shown on the **10-franc note** of the 8th series, which was in circulation from 1997.

On the hill above **Ronchamp** there had long been a pilgrimage chapel. It was destroyed in the **Second World War**. From 1953 to 1955 Le Corbusier built an entirely new chapel. It was consecrated on **25 June 1955**. It is dedicated to Mary, and “Notre-Dame” means “Our Lady” in French.

The massive, dark **concrete roof** is striking. It is curved and recalls a **shell** or a ship's hull. Le Corbusier is said to have been inspired by a crab shell. Between the roof and the walls there is a narrow gap through which light falls. So the heavy roof seems almost to float. The walls are plastered white and in part slanting.

The thick **south wall** is pierced by many openings of different sizes. They grow wider towards the inside, and coloured glass creates an atmospheric **light**. For large pilgrimages there is an **open-air altar and pulpit** on the east side. The projecting roof protects them, and the faithful gather on the meadow in front.

In **2016** seventeen buildings by Le Corbusier in seven countries were together added to the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The chapel of Ronchamp is among them. Two buildings in Switzerland are also included: the **Villa Le Lac** in Corseaux on Lake Geneva and the **Immeuble Clarté** in Geneva. Every year many people visit the chapel because of its special architecture.

gewusst: Le Corbusier built the Villa Le Lac in Corseaux for his parents.
The name “Le Corbusier” was a self-chosen artist's name.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the church parish (Kirchgemeinde) is the local community of the members of a national church. It is organised in a similar way to a political municipality. The members themselves decide on important questions.
wichtigste: The Kirchgemeinde is the local community of church members.
It is often allowed to levy church taxes.
At the parish assembly, the members entitled to vote decide on the budget.
In many Reformed parishes the leadership is called the Kirchenpflege (parish council).
The parish often elects the pastor.
In the Catholic Church there is, alongside the Kirchgemeinde, the Pfarrei (canonical parish): the dual system.
Because of falling membership, parishes often merge.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **Kirchgemeinde** is the local community of the members of a **national church**. It works in a similar way to a political municipality. It has members, a leadership and a budget of its own. It is often allowed to levy **church taxes**. With this money it pays, for example, salaries, buildings and services.

Important decisions are made by the **parish assembly**. There the **members entitled to vote** decide on the **budget** and other business. In many Reformed parishes, for example in the **canton of Zurich**, the elected leadership is called the **Kirchenpflege**. In other cantons it is called the parish council. In many parishes the members also **elect** their **pastor**.

In the Catholic Church there is, alongside the Kirchgemeinde, also the **Pfarrei**. The Pfarrei is the **unit under canon law** that is looked after by a **parish priest**. It takes care of services and pastoral care. The Kirchgemeinde is organised under state law and mainly manages money and buildings. This coexistence is called the **dual system**. It is a special feature of Switzerland.

A parish offers much more than services. Typical are **youth work**, religious education, services for older people and help for people in need. Today parishes often **merge**. One reason is **falling membership**. So, for example, in 2019 a single large Reformed parish arose in the city of Zurich.

gewusst: In many cantons, foreigners may also vote in the parish.
That the members of a congregation elect their own pastor themselves is rare worldwide.

teile.einleitung: The Zurich Bible is a German Bible translation from the time of the Reformation in Zurich. The impetus came from Huldrych Zwingli. It was revised several times, and most recently a completely new translation appeared in 2007.
wichtigste: Huldrych Zwingli gave the impetus for the Zurich Bible.
Leo Jud played a major part in the translation.
From 1524 the New Testament appeared first.
The version of 1931 was used for over 75 years.
In 2007 the new translation was handed over in the Grossmünster.
The Zurich Bible is known for its great closeness to the original text.

abschnitte.titel: The Bible in one's own language
abschnitte.text: The Reformer **Huldrych Zwingli** wanted the congregation to be able to read the Bible in its **own language**. He translated together with other Zurich theologians. **Leo Jud**, pastor of the church of **St Peter** in Zurich, played a major part. The Bible was printed by the Zurich printer **Christoph Froschauer**.

From 1525 there was a special school in Zurich, the **Prophezei**. There scholars read biblical texts every day in **Hebrew**, **Greek** and **Latin** and interpreted them. This work went directly into the translation. The Prophezei is regarded as a forerunner of the University of Zurich.

From **1524** the **New Testament** appeared first. The Old Testament followed step by step. In the end all the parts were united in one volume. This complete Bible appeared in 1531 and was thus finished earlier than the complete Luther Bible.

The Zurich Bible was revised again and again. The revision of **1931** was almost a new translation. It was read in the Reformed churches of Switzerland for over 75 years. Afterwards, experts worked for about two decades on a new translation. It was handed over in **2007** in the **Grossmünster**. In the first ten days, 11,000 copies were sold.

Today the **Reformed Church of the canton of Zurich** publishes the Zurich Bible. It is known for its great **closeness to the original text**. It translates very exactly from the Hebrew and Greek text. That is why it is often used for studying the Bible.

gewusst: The Zurich Bible of 1531 is illustrated with many woodcuts.
The Zurich Bible is older than the complete Luther Bible, which appeared in 1534.

teile.einleitung: “Sola scriptura” means “by Scripture alone”. For the Reformers, the Bible was the highest standard for faith and teaching. In Zurich, Huldrych Zwingli put this principle into practice with particular determination.
wichtigste: “Sola scriptura” means “by Scripture alone”.
The Bible is regarded as the “norma normans”, the highest guideline.
In 1521 at Worms, Luther refused to recant unless he was refuted from Scripture.
In 1546 the Council of Trent placed tradition on the same level as the Bible.
From 1519 Zwingli preached continuously on the Gospel of Matthew at the Grossmünster.
In 1516 Erasmus published the Greek New Testament in Basel.

abschnitte.text: The Reformers wanted to base faith on the **Bible** again. According to the principle **“sola scriptura”**, Holy Scripture is the only binding guideline for faith and teaching. It is called the **“norma normans”**, the standard that sets the norm and by which everything is measured. Confessions of faith, by contrast, count as “norma normata”, a derived norm. They carry weight only if they agree with the Bible.

In 1521 Luther had to appear before Emperor Charles V and the estates of the Empire at the **Diet of Worms**. He was asked to recant his writings. Luther declared that he would recant only if he were refuted by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reasoning. His **conscience** was captive to the word of God. Afterwards he was placed under the imperial ban.

On 1 January 1519, **Huldrych Zwingli** began his work at the **Grossmünster** in Zurich. He broke with the prescribed order of readings and expounded the **Gospel of Matthew** chapter by chapter. This continuous exposition is called “lectio continua”. In 1525 he set up the **Prophezei**, a theological school. There biblical texts were translated and explained together from Hebrew and Greek. The Zurich Bible also came out of it.

To read the Bible accurately, one needed the **original languages**. In 1516 **Erasmus of Rotterdam** published the New Testament in Greek with the Basel printer Johann Froben, together with a Latin translation. Luther and Zwingli worked with this edition. Printing helped Bibles to spread in large numbers. Many people could now read the Bible in their own language.

The Catholic Church saw this differently. The **Council of Trent** declared in 1546 that Holy Scripture and the unwritten traditions were to be received with equal reverence. So **church tradition** stands on the same level as the Bible. In this way the Catholic Church deliberately set itself apart from the Reformation principle of Scripture. To this day this is an important difference between the denominations.

gewusst: The Zurich Bible appeared in 1531 as a complete Bible with Christoph Froschauer, a few years before Luther's complete Bible of 1534.
The Grossmünster with its two towers is still a landmark of Zurich today.

teile.einleitung: Church windows are often made of coloured pieces of glass. They show pictures from the Bible and let coloured light into the church. Many are small works of art, and some were designed by famous artists.
wichtigste: A picture made of coloured pieces of glass is called stained glass.
Dark lines of lead hold the pieces of glass together.
Many church windows show stories from the Bible.
Gothic church windows are pointed at the top.
A large round window like a flower is called a rose window.
Marc Chagall designed windows in the Fraumünster in Zurich.
The colours shine most beautifully when the sun is shining.

abschnitte.text: A picture made of coloured pieces of glass is called **stained glass**. The artists cut coloured glass into many small pieces. With paint they add faces and folds. Then the pieces are joined with **lead cames**. These **dark lines of lead** hold the **pieces of glass** together and are part of the picture.

Many church windows show **stories from the Bible** or saints. In the past many people could not read. The pictures helped them to understand the stories and remember them. Such windows are therefore sometimes called a **Bible for everyone**. Often a window tells a whole story in several pictures.

In the **Gothic** period, in the Middle Ages, churches were built with large, tall windows. A **Gothic window** is **pointed at the top**, and this shape is called a pointed arch. Especially beautiful is the **rose window**, a **large round window** that looks like a **flower**. Rose windows are found, for example, in Lausanne Cathedral. The colours **shine most beautifully inside when the sun is shining**.

In the **Fraumünster** in Zurich the artist **Marc Chagall** designed five large choir windows. They were installed in **1970** and show stories from the Bible in glowing colours. Many people from all over the world visit the Fraumünster to see them. In the **Grossmünster** right next to it, **Sigmar Polke** created modern windows, some even made of thin slices of stone. **Augusto Giacometti** also designed well-known church windows in Zurich.

gewusst: For stained glass you need glass coloured with metals: this is how blue and red, for example, arise.
In Romont FR there is the Vitromusée, a museum devoted only to stained glass.

teile.einleitung: The early church was the first Christian community in Jerusalem. According to the Acts of the Apostles, it came into being at Pentecost. Its members prayed together, shared their possessions and told of Jesus.
wichtigste: Pentecost is regarded as the birthday of the Church.
After Peter's Pentecost sermon about 3,000 people were baptised.
The Acts of the Apostles tells of the life of the first Christians.
The members of the early church shared their possessions with one another.
Stephen is regarded as the first Christian martyr.
In Antioch the followers of Jesus were called “Christians” for the first time.

abschnitte.text: After the Ascension of Jesus, his disciples stayed in **Jerusalem**. At **Pentecost**, according to the Acts of the Apostles, the **Holy Spirit** came upon them. **Peter** gave a sermon, and about **3,000 people** were baptised. In this way the first congregation came into being. That is why Pentecost is regarded as the birthday of the Church.

The life of the first Christians is told above all in the **Acts of the Apostles**. It is the fifth book of the New Testament. Traditionally it is ascribed to the evangelist **Luke**. It is regarded as the second part of his Gospel. Both books are addressed to a certain **Theophilus**.

The believers met for prayer and for the breaking of bread together. According to the Acts of the Apostles, they had **everything in common**. This is called **community of goods**. Whoever owned something shared it so that nobody had to suffer need. Seven men were chosen to care for the poor.

One of these seven who cared for the poor was **Stephen**. He was stoned in Jerusalem and is regarded as the **first Christian martyr**. An important leader of the community was **James**, the brother of Jesus. Paul calls him one of the “pillars” of the Jerusalem church. He also played an important role at the Council of the Apostles.

Soon there were congregations outside Jerusalem too. In **Antioch** in Syria the followers of Jesus were called **Christians** for the first time. Around AD 48 the apostles met at the **Council of the Apostles** in Jerusalem. They decided that Christians from other peoples did not have to keep the whole Jewish law. This made mission work much easier.

gewusst: The passage about the roughly 3,000 baptised is in Acts 2:41.
Antioch is now called Antakya and lies in Turkey.

teile.einleitung: In the Bible the rainbow is a sign of a promise of God. After the story of the Flood, God sets the bow in the clouds and makes a covenant with Noah.
wichtigste: After the Flood Noah left the ark and built an altar.
God made a covenant with Noah and all living creatures.
God promised never again to send a great flood.
As a sign he set his bow in the clouds.
On seeing the rainbow, God himself will remember the covenant.
You see a rainbow when sun and rain come together.
