abschnitte.text: The story is in the first book of Moses (Genesis). After the **Flood** the water slowly sank. Noah, his family and the animals left the **ark**. The first thing Noah did was to build an **altar** and thank God that they had been saved.

God made a **covenant** with **Noah**, his descendants and all living creatures. A covenant is a solemn promise. God promised **never again to send a great flood** that destroys all life. As a sign he set his **bow in the clouds**. According to the Bible **God himself** will remember the covenant when he sees the rainbow.

In nature you see a rainbow **when sun and rain come together**. The sun must be behind you, the rain in front of you. The sunlight is refracted in the raindrops and split into its colours. So the coloured arc arises, from red through yellow and green to violet.

For many people the rainbow is still a sign of **hope** and of **peace**. You find it on children's Bibles, church windows and flags. The story shows: after a hard time, something good can begin again.

gewusst: Sometimes you even see a double rainbow, and in the outer bow the order of colours is reversed.
Similar flood stories are also found in very old tales from Mesopotamia.

teile.einleitung: The Pentecostal movement is a Christian movement that arose a good hundred years ago. It stresses especially the gifts of the Holy Spirit and today is among the fastest-growing currents of Christianity.
wichtigste: The name recalls Pentecost, when according to the Bible the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples.
An important beginning was the Azusa Street Revival of 1906 in Los Angeles.
It was led by the African American preacher William J. Seymour.
Typical are speaking in tongues and prayer for the healing of the sick.
The movement is growing especially strongly in Latin America and Africa.
In Switzerland the Schweizerische Pfingstmission (Swiss Pentecostal Mission) is a large association.

abschnitte.text: The movement is named after the feast of **Pentecost**. In the Acts of the Apostles it is told that the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples of Jesus. Afterwards they began to speak in different languages. The followers of the Pentecostal movement, the **Pentecostals**, believe that such experiences are possible today too. They speak of **baptism in the Spirit**.

An important starting point is regarded to be the **Azusa Street Revival**, which began in 1906 in **Los Angeles**. It was led by the African American preacher **William J. Seymour**. In a simple building, people of different skin colours met for years for long services. From there the movement spread quickly into many countries.

Pentecostals stress the **gifts of the Holy Spirit**. These include **speaking in tongues**, praying in sounds or languages that the person praying does not know himself. **Prayer for the sick** is also very important. The communities expect healing through God's power and appeal to accounts in the New Testament. The services are often lively, with modern music, clapping and free prayers.

Today there are Pentecostal communities all over the world. The movement is growing especially strongly in **Latin America** and **Africa**. One of the largest Pentecostal churches is the **Assemblies of God**. Since the 1960s, groups in Catholic and Reformed churches have also stressed the gifts of the Spirit. This is called the **charismatic movement**, after the Greek word “charisma” for gift of grace.

In Switzerland too there are many Pentecostal communities, often in cities and agglomerations. A large association is the **Schweizerische Pfingstmission**. Pentecostal communities belong to the **free churches**. They are not financed through church taxes, but mainly through donations from their members.

gewusst: The Pentecostal movement counts several hundred million followers worldwide.
The Greek word “charisma” means gift of grace or present.

teile.einleitung: The Zurich sausage meal took place in March 1522 in the house of the printer Christoph Froschauer. During Lent, some men deliberately ate sausage although meat was forbidden. The event is regarded as the beginning of the Reformation in Zurich.
wichtigste: The sausage meal took place on 9 March 1522.
It was Lent, and meat was forbidden.
The host was the printer Christoph Froschauer.
Zwingli was there but did not eat any sausage himself.
He defended the participants with the sermon “On the Choice and Freedom of Foods”.
The sausage meal is regarded as the beginning of the Reformation in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: On **9 March 1522**, some men met in the house of **Christoph Froschauer** in Zurich. It was **Lent**. According to the rules of the Church, one was not allowed to eat meat during this time. Even so, two **smoked sausages** were cut into thin pieces and shared among the guests. This was a deliberate breach of the **rule of fasting**.

**Christoph Froschauer** was a well-known **printer** in Zurich. Later he printed many writings of the Reformation and also the Zurich Bible. Before the council he excused the sausage meal: his journeymen had to work hard on an urgent **printing job**. So they needed hearty food.

**Huldrych Zwingli** was also present at the sausage meal. But he did not eat any sausage himself. Afterwards he defended the participants publicly. About two weeks later he gave a sermon entitled “**On the Choice and Freedom of Foods**”. “Erkiesen” is an old German word for choosing. Froschauer printed the text afterwards.

Zwingli argued from the **Bible**. There, he said, there is no commandment to give up meat during Lent. Rules of fasting were made by people. Every Christian may decide freely what to eat. But whoever fasts voluntarily should be allowed to do so.

The sausage meal triggered fierce discussions in Zurich. Soon it was no longer only about fasting but about the question of what should count in the Church. Only the Bible, or the rules of the Church too? In 1523 the **Zurich Disputations** followed. That is why the sausage meal is regarded as the **beginning of the Reformation** in Zurich.

gewusst: In this way a sausage became one of the best-known symbols of Swiss Reformation history.
Froschauer's printing house became one of the most important in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament of the Catholic Church for seriously ill and elderly people. The priest anoints them with blessed oil and prays for strength, comfort and peace.
wichtigste: In the past the Anointing of the Sick was mostly called Extreme Unction.
It appeals above all to the Letter of James in the Bible.
The priest anoints the forehead and hands with the oil of the sick.
Only a priest may administer it.
You can receive it several times in your life.
It does not replace medicine, but is meant to strengthen and comfort.

abschnitte.text: The Anointing of the Sick appeals especially to the **Letter of James** in the New Testament. In chapter 5 it says that the elders of the congregation should pray over the sick and **anoint them with oil**. Already in the Bible it is told that the disciples anointed the sick with oil. The Anointing of the Sick is one of the **seven sacraments** of the Catholic Church.

abschnitte.titel: From Extreme Unction to the Anointing of the Sick
abschnitte.text: For a long time this sacrament was administered mainly to **the dying**. That is why it was called **Extreme Unction**. The **Second Vatican Council** in the 1960s emphasised the name **Anointing of the Sick**. It wanted to show that the sacrament is meant for all seriously ill people, not only for the last hour. Elderly, frail people can also receive it.

Only a **priest** may administer the Anointing of the Sick. He lays his hands on the sick person in silence. Then he anoints the **forehead** and the palms of the **hands** with the blessed **oil of the sick** and speaks a prayer for strengthening. Often relatives are present. The celebration can take place at home, in hospital or in church.

Every year in **Holy Week** the bishop blesses three holy oils. This happens at the **Chrism Mass**. What is blessed are **chrism**, **the oil of catechumens** and **the oil of the sick**. The oil of the sick is then distributed to the parishes of the diocese. Chrism is needed, for example, at baptism and confirmation.

The Anointing of the Sick **does not replace medicine**. It is meant to strengthen sick people in their faith, comfort them and give them **peace**. You can receive it **several times**, for example when an illness gets worse or a serious operation is coming up. In many parishes there are also joint services with the Anointing of the Sick for older people.

gewusst: The oil for the oil of the sick is usually olive oil.
In many Swiss hospitals there are chaplains who can call a priest for the Anointing of the Sick.

teile.einleitung: “Messiah” is an oratorio by George Frideric Handel. With words from the Bible it tells of the life and the significance of Jesus. With its famous Hallelujah Chorus it is among the best-known musical works in the world.
wichtigste: George Frideric Handel came from Halle and lived for a long time in London.
He composed the “Messiah” in 1741 in only about 24 days.
The first performance was on 13 April 1742 in Dublin.
Charles Jennens put together the English text from the King James Bible.
The Hallelujah Chorus closes the second part.
An oratorio is performed without stage action and without costumes.

abschnitte.text: An **oratorio** is a large work for choir, soloists and orchestra. It tells a story, usually with a sacred text. Unlike in an **opera**, there is no stage action, no costumes and no scenery. The work is performed like a concert. Handel wrote many oratorios, and the “Messiah” is the most famous.

Handel was born in Halle in 1685 and from 1712 lived mainly in **London**. The text for the “Messiah” was put together by his friend **Charles Jennens** from verses of the English Bible. Handel composed the music from 22 August to 14 September 1741. That is only about three and a half weeks for over 50 movements. The work has three parts: prophecy and birth of Jesus, his suffering and resurrection, and finally redemption.

In 1741 Handel had been invited to Ireland. The first performance of the “Messiah” took place on **13 April 1742 in Dublin**. The concert was for a good cause: the proceeds went to charitable institutions. In London the work was heard only in 1743. There it was at first less successful than in Dublin.

At the end of the second part stands the **Hallelujah Chorus**. The word Hallelujah means “Praise God”. In Great Britain the audience traditionally stands up for this chorus. A legend tells that King George II rose to his feet at a performance. Whether that was really so, however, is **not documented**. The whole work ends with a great “Amen”.

From 1750 Handel performed the “Messiah” every year in aid of the **Foundling Hospital**. That was a home in London for abandoned and deserted children. With the money from the concerts the children could be looked after. Today the “Messiah” is often sung in **Advent and Christmas time**, although originally it was performed in the time before Easter.

gewusst: Handel was born in Germany and died in 1759 in London as a British citizen.
He is buried in Westminster Abbey in London.

teile.einleitung: The Assumption of Mary is a feast on 15 August. Catholic Christians believe that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was taken up into heaven in body and soul.
wichtigste: The Assumption of Mary is on 15 August.
In 1950 Pope Pius XII proclaimed Mary's assumption into heaven as a dogma.
Mary was taken up, whereas Jesus ascended into heaven himself.
In many regions bunches of herbs are blessed.
The Orthodox Church celebrates the Dormition of Mary.
In Ticino and other Catholic cantons the day is a public holiday.

abschnitte.text: On the **Assumption of Mary**, Catholic Christians celebrate that **Mary**, at the end of her life, was taken up into heaven in **body and soul**. It is one of the most important **Marian feasts** and is celebrated on **15 August**. This feast has existed for many centuries. The Bible itself says nothing about it; the belief comes from the tradition of the Church.

On **1 November 1950** Pope **Pius XII** declared as a **dogma**, that is, a binding article of faith, that Mary was taken up into heaven in body and soul. Since then this belief has been obligatory for Catholics. The Protestant churches do not usually celebrate the feast.

The **Ascension of Christ**, called **Auffahrt** in Switzerland, and the **Assumption of Mary** are two different feasts. In Latin the Ascension of Christ is called **Ascensio**: Jesus ascended into heaven by his own power. The Assumption of Mary is called **Assumptio**: Mary was **taken up** by God. In the **Orthodox Church** the feast is called the **Dormition of Mary**. It stresses Mary's death as a peaceful falling asleep.

In many Catholic regions the faithful bring **bunches of herbs** made of medicinal herbs and flowers to church on 15 August, where they are blessed. In Catholic cantons such as **Ticino**, **Valais** or **Uri**, 15 August is a legal public holiday. In **Italy** the day is called **Ferragosto**. It goes back to an ancient Roman feast in honour of Emperor Augustus, and many Italians then go on holiday.

gewusst: The name Ferragosto comes from the Latin “Feriae Augusti”, which means holidays of Augustus.
On 1 August Switzerland celebrates its national day, and two weeks later in some cantons there is another public holiday.

teile.einleitung: Pastors (Pfarrerinnen and Pfarrer in German) work for a Christian church parish. They lead services, accompany people in good times and hard times, and are for many an important contact person in the village or the neighbourhood.
wichtigste: The pastor usually leads the service.
They preach, pray and read from the Bible.
At baptisms, weddings and funerals they have an important task.
At the end of the service they speak the blessing.
A Catholic Pfarrer (parish priest) is a priest.
In the Reformed Church of Switzerland women can also become pastors.

abschnitte.text: The most important task is often the **service** on Sunday. The pastor prays with the congregation, reads from the Bible and gives a **sermon**. In the sermon she or he explains a Bible text and shows what it can mean for life today. At the end the pastor speaks the **blessing** and wishes everyone God's protection for the new week.

Pastors accompany people at important events. At the **baptism** a child or an adult is received into the Church. At a church wedding two people promise to stay together. This is called the **marriage ceremony**. At a funeral they comfort the relatives and say farewell together to the person who has died.

A large part of the work happens outside the church. Pastors visit **sick, old and sad people**, at home, in hospital or in the old people's home. They listen, give encouragement and pray with them. This accompaniment is called **pastoral care** (Seelsorge). Many also give religious education or prepare young people for confirmation.

In the **Reformed Church** many pastors wear a black **gown** (Talar), a long robe, at the service. There women and men may become pastors, and they may marry. In the **Roman Catholic Church** the Pfarrer is a **priest** who celebrates Mass at the altar. Only men become priests there, and they live without marriage.

Next to many churches stands a **parsonage** (Pfarrhaus). In the past the pastor often lived there, among the Reformed often with the whole family. In the parsonage there were also meetings, lessons and visits. Today not all pastors live in the parsonage any more, but the building still belongs to the look of many Swiss villages.

gewusst: To become a pastor, in Switzerland one usually studies **theology** for several years at a university.
The German word “Pfarrer” comes from “Pfarrei”, the territory of a church parish.

teile.einleitung: Candles belong in every church. For Christians their light is a sign of Jesus, who is called the light of the world. Many people light a candle in church to think of someone or to pray.
wichtigste: People light candles in church to think of someone.
Good church candles are often made of beeswax.
The Paschal candle is lit at the Easter Vigil.
The Eternal Light always burns in Catholic churches.
Candlelight stands for Jesus as the light of the world.
Candles are always put in a candlestick for safety.

abschnitte.text: In the Gospel of John, Jesus says: **“I am the light of the world.”** That is why the **light of a candle** is a sign of **Jesus** for Christians. A candle makes it bright where it is dark. This recalls hope and comfort. Candles therefore burn on the altar at almost every service.

Many people light a candle in church **to think of someone**. This may be a sick person, someone who has died, or a person in a difficult situation. The burning candle is like a silent **prayer**. For this there is often a **candle stand** with many small candles. Usually a small donation is put in a little box for it.

Good church candles are often made of **beeswax**. Beeswax burns calmly and smells pleasantly of honey. In the past it was regarded as especially precious and pure. Today there are also candles made of paraffin or vegetable wax. When lighting them you have to be **careful with fire**, so that nothing catches fire and nobody gets burned.

At the **Easter Vigil** the great **Paschal candle** is lit. It stands for the risen Jesus and afterwards burns at many services. In **Catholic churches** a **red light** always burns, the **Eternal Light**. It shows that Christ is present in the church. In Advent, one more candle is lit each week on the **Advent wreath**.

gewusst: On 2 February, Candlemas, the candles for the whole year are blessed in Catholic churches.
On the Paschal candle are often the year and the Greek letters alpha and omega.

teile.einleitung: The Christmas tree is an essential part of Christmas for many families. Usually it is a fir or spruce, decorated with lights, baubles and stars. The custom is a few hundred years old.
wichtigste: A fir or spruce is usually used as the Christmas tree.
The evergreen tree stands for life in winter.
In the past, real wax candles burned on the branches.
Classic Christmas baubles are made of thin glass.
Tinsel and straw stars are popular decorations.
On Christmas Eve the presents often lie under the tree.

abschnitte.text: A **fir** or **spruce** is usually used as the Christmas tree. These trees are green in winter too. When other trees are bare, the fir stays green. That is why the **evergreen** tree is seen as a sign of **life and hope**. In many Swiss homes, too, such a tree stands in December.

Even in the 15th and 16th centuries there are reports of decorated trees at Christmas time, for example from **Alsace**. At that time apples, nuts and baked goods were often hung on them. In the 19th century the Christmas tree spread to many countries. Today it is known all over the world.

In the past, real **wax candles** were stuck on the branches. It looked lovely but was dangerous, because a dry tree burns easily. Today many people use **electric fairy lights** because they are safer. Anyone who lights real candles should always keep water ready and never leave the tree alone.

Classic **Christmas baubles** are blown from thin **glass**. Today there are also baubles made of plastic. **Tinsel** is thin, shiny strips hung over the branches. **Straw stars**, made from drinking straws of straw, are also popular. They recall the straw in the stable in Bethlehem.

Many families fetch and decorate the tree only **shortly before Christmas**. Some do not decorate it until 24 December. Many people put the **presents** under the tree. After the celebration they are unwrapped. Often a small nativity scene stands next to the tree as well.

gewusst: The first glass Christmas baubles were made in the Thuringian town of Lauscha.
In the song “O Tannenbaum” the tree is praised because it stays green in winter.

teile.einleitung: A great many Catholic Christians live in Latin America. The faith came there with the Spanish and Portuguese conquerors from the 16th century. Today it shapes festivals, art and everyday life in many countries.
wichtigste: Brazil has the most Catholics in the world.
In 1531 the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared to Juan Diego near Mexico City.
Rose of Lima was canonised in 1671 as the first person from the Americas.
Gustavo Gutiérrez gave liberation theology its name in 1971.
Archbishop Óscar Romero was murdered in 1980 and canonised in 2018.
Francis was the first Pope from Latin America.
Leo XIV was for many years a missionary and bishop in Peru.

abschnitte.text: From the **16th century** Spain and Portugal conquered large parts of the Americas. With them came **missionaries** who spread the Catholic faith. For the native peoples this time was often very hard. Even so, Catholicism in time became part of their own culture. Today **Brazil** has the **most Catholics** in the world.

According to tradition, in **1531** the Virgin Mary appeared near **Mexico City** to the indigenous man **Juan Diego**. Since then she has been called the **Virgin of Guadalupe** and is very important for Mexico. Her basilica is among the most visited places of pilgrimage in the world. **Rose of Lima** from Peru was canonised in **1671** as the **first person from the Americas**. She helped poor and sick people.

Many people in Latin America lived in great poverty. The Peruvian theologian **Gustavo Gutiérrez** wrote a book in **1971** that gave **liberation theology** its name. It asks how faith can help the poor to free themselves from need and injustice. The movement was controversial in the Church. A well-known model is **Óscar Romero**, Archbishop of San Salvador. He was murdered during a Mass in **1980** and canonised in **2018**.

In **2013** the Argentine Jorge Mario Bergoglio became Pope and called himself **Francis**. He was the **first Pope from Latin America**. In **2025** the American Robert Francis Prevost was elected as **Leo XIV**. He had worked for many years as a missionary and bishop in **Peru**. In **Aparecida**, a large place of pilgrimage in Brazil, the Latin American bishops met in **2007** for their fifth General Conference.

gewusst: The image of the Virgin of Guadalupe is among the best-known religious images in the whole of the Americas.
The future Pope Francis led the group in Aparecida that wrote the concluding document.

teile.einleitung: A scriptorium was the writing room of a medieval monastery. Here monks carefully copied books by hand and decorated them with pictures. Without this work many old texts would have been lost.
wichtigste: In the scriptorium, monks copied books by hand.
The word comes from the Latin “scribere”, to write.
People wrote on parchment made from animal skin, usually with a goose feather.
Elaborately decorated first letters are called initials.
Carolingian minuscule is the basis of our lower-case letters.
The Codex Abrogans in St Gallen is regarded as the oldest book in the German language.

abschnitte.text: Before printing was invented, every book had to be written **by hand**. In many monasteries there was a room of its own for this, the **scriptorium**. The name comes from the Latin “scribere”, to write. The monks worked in silence and needed plenty of light, so they usually wrote by day. A thick book often took months or even years.

Paper was unknown in Europe for a long time. People wrote on **parchment**, which was made from the skins of calves, sheep or goats. The skin was cleaned, stretched and scraped thin. Writing was done with a **bird's feather**, usually a goose quill, which was cut at an angle and dipped in ink. Because parchment was expensive, old texts were sometimes scraped off and new ones written over them. Such a sheet is called a **palimpsest**.

Many manuscripts were splendidly decorated. At the start of a chapter there is often an **initial**, a large, elaborately decorated first letter. It is painted in colour and decorated with gold, tendrils or small figures. The art of decorating manuscripts with pictures is called **book illumination**. Some pages are real works of art.

In the time of **Charlemagne**, around the year 800, a new script came into being: **Carolingian minuscule**. It was clear and easy to read and spread throughout the Frankish Empire. Our **lower-case letters** of today developed from it. So whoever writes an a or a g today is using forms that are over 1,000 years old.

A famous scriptorium was in the **Abbey of St Gallen**. The **Abbey Library** of St Gallen still keeps many valuable manuscripts today. They include the **Codex Abrogans**, a Latin and Old High German dictionary from the 8th century. It is regarded as the oldest surviving book in the German language. The Abbey Precinct of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Monks sometimes wrote little complaints in the margin, for example that their hand hurt or that it was cold.
For one large book, the skins of many animals were needed.

teile.einleitung: The World Council of Churches is the largest association of Christian churches in the world. It has its seat in Geneva and works for unity, peace and justice.
wichtigste: The Council was founded in 1948, and its first general secretary was Willem Visser 't Hooft.
Over 350 churches from more than 120 countries belong to it.
The Ecumenical Institute is in the Château de Bossey on Lake Geneva.
The World Missionary Conference of Edinburgh in 1910 is regarded as the starting point of modern ecumenism.
The Lima Document of 1982 deals with baptism, Eucharist and ministry.
The 11th Assembly took place in 2022 in Karlsruhe.

abschnitte.text: The **World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh** in **1910** is regarded as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement. Missionaries noticed that the division of the churches hindered their work. Several movements arose from this. The Swedish archbishop **Nathan Söderblom** organised in **1925** in Stockholm the Conference on Life and Work. For this he received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1930. In 1927 the Faith and Order movement met in **Lausanne**.

From these movements the World Council of Churches emerged in **1948**. Its seat is in **Geneva**. The first **general secretary** was the Dutchman **Willem Visser 't Hooft**, who led the Council until 1966. Since **1946** there has been the **Ecumenical Institute** in the **Château de Bossey** in the canton of Vaud. There students from all over the world learn ecumenical theology together.

Over **350 churches** from more than **120 countries** belong to the Council. They are Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant and Old Catholic churches. By their own account they represent over 580 million Christians. The Roman Catholic Church is not a member, but cooperates. Every few years the members meet for an **Assembly**. In 2013 that was in Busan in South Korea, in **2022** in **Karlsruhe**, for the first time in Germany.

The Council works on questions of faith and on global problems. The **Lima Document** of **1982** showed how close the churches had come on **baptism, Eucharist and ministry**. From **1969** there was a programme against **racism**, which concerned especially **apartheid** in southern Africa. It was strongly disputed in some member churches. Since the beginning of **2023** the South African theologian **Jerry Pillay** has been general secretary (as of 2025).

gewusst: The founding idea is older than the Council itself: the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey existed two years before the official foundation.
With Lausanne and Geneva, Switzerland played an important role already in the early period of ecumenism.

teile.einleitung: The baptismal font stands in many churches and is the place where baptisms take place. At the top it has a basin for the baptismal water. Most often small children are baptised there and received into the Christian community.
wichtigste: At the font, people are baptised, mostly small children.
At the top it has a basin of water, sometimes also a lid.
It is usually carved from stone and often decorated.
The minister pours water over the child's head.
In Switzerland godparents are called Gotte and Götti.
The child receives a baptism candle.

abschnitte.titel: A special place in the church
abschnitte.text: As the name says, the **baptismal font** (German “Taufstein”, baptism stone) is usually carved from **stone**. At the top it has a **basin** into which the baptismal water is poured. Some fonts have a lid of wood or metal. They are often decorated with ornaments, figures or Bible verses. In many Reformed churches in Switzerland the font stands at the front, near the communion table and the pulpit.

At a baptism the family stands at the font with the child. The minister pours a little **water** over the child's head with her hand. As she does so she speaks the words: I baptise you in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Often she draws a small **cross** on the forehead. This shows that the child now belongs to Jesus Christ.

Baptism usually involves **godparents**. In Switzerland the godmother is called **Gotte** and the godfather **Götti**. They promise to be there for the child and to accompany it on its way through life. Often the Gotte and Götti remain important people for life. Many children receive special presents from them on birthdays and at Christmas.

At baptism the child receives a **baptism candle**. It is often lit from the large Easter candle. On the baptism candle there are often the child's name and the date of baptism, as well as signs such as a cross, water or a dove. The light recalls Jesus, who called himself the light of the world. Many families light the candle again every year on the baptism day.

gewusst: In the past, besides large churches there were separate baptismal churches, so-called baptisteries.
In some churches, teenagers and adults are also baptised at the font.

teile.einleitung: The cross is the most important sign of Christians. It recalls the death and resurrection of Jesus and meets us in churches, on mountain summits and even on flags.
wichtigste: The cross is the best-known sign of Christianity.
A simple cross consists of two beams.
A cross with a figure of Jesus is called a crucifix.
At the top there is often INRI, “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews”.
In the sign of the cross one draws a cross on oneself with the hand.
A Way of the Cross usually has 14 stations.

abschnitte.text: The **cross** recalls that Jesus died on the cross. For Christians, though, it is also a sign of hope, because they believe that Jesus rose again. A simple cross consists of **two beams**: a long vertical one and a shorter horizontal one. Many people wear a small **cross pendant** on a chain.

A cross on which a figure of Jesus hangs is called a **crucifix**. It is often found in Catholic churches. At the top of the cross the letters **INRI** often appear. They stand for the Latin words “Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum”, in English “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews”. According to the Bible, Pilate had this inscription put on the cross.

In the **sign of the cross** you draw a cross on your own body with your hand. You start at the **forehead**, go to the chest and then from one shoulder to the other. Often people say: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”. Many make the sign of the cross when praying or when entering a church.

On many mountain summits in Switzerland and in the Alps there are **summit crosses**. They mark the highest point of a mountain and are a Christian sign. Climbers like to be photographed next to them. At paths and crossroads, too, there are often wayside crosses.

A **Way of the Cross** tells of the suffering of Jesus, usually in **14 pictures**. Each picture, a so-called station, shows a moment on his way to the cross. Ways of the Cross are found in many churches and also outside on hills. Especially in the time before Easter, believers walk this way in prayer.

gewusst: The Swiss flag and the flags of the Scandinavian countries also show a cross.
The earliest Christians often used the fish rather than the cross as a sign of recognition; the cross only later became the most important symbol.

teile.einleitung: Theodicy is an old question of philosophy and theology: how can a good and all-powerful God allow suffering in the world? Many thinkers have given very different answers. There is still no final solution to this day.
wichtigste: “Theodicy” means “justification of God”.
The argument against God in the face of evil is attributed to Epicurus.
Augustine interpreted evil as “privatio boni”, the absence of good.
Leibniz thought that our world is the best of all possible worlds.
The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 shook this optimism.
In 1791 Kant held that all philosophical attempts at theodicy had failed.

abschnitte.text: The word **theodicy** is made up of the Greek “theos”, God, and “dike”, justice. So it means **justification of God**. The question is: if God is good and all-powerful, why is there suffering and evil? Even in antiquity an argument became known that is attributed to **Epicurus**: God cannot be both good and all-powerful if evil exists. It was handed down by the Christian writer Lactantius; whether it really comes from Epicurus is disputed.

In the Bible, the **Book of Job** puts this question at the centre. Job is righteous and still loses property, family and health. His friends and God himself wrestle with him for an answer. The Church Father **Augustine** saw evil as **“privatio boni”**, as the absence of good. For him evil has no being of its own, just as illness is a lack of health.

The German philosopher **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** coined the term theodicy. In his “Essais de Théodicée” of 1710 he wrote that an all-wise and all-good God had created the **best** of all possible worlds. Even evil has a meaning in it. This view suited the belief in progress of the **Enlightenment**. Many people found comfort in it; others thought it too smooth.

On All Saints' Day **1755**, an earthquake, a tsunami and fires destroyed the city of **Lisbon**. The disaster shook the optimism of the Enlightenment. Many asked anew how God could allow such suffering. In 1759, **Voltaire** mocked Leibniz's teaching in his novel **“Candide”**: the character Pangloss claims that despite all misfortunes everything is for the best. In 1791 **Immanuel Kant** wrote the treatise “On the Miscarriage of All Philosophical Trials in Theodicy”.

In the 20th century the American philosopher **Alvin Plantinga** put forward the **“Free Will Defense”**. He argued that a world with truly free creatures could be more valuable, even if they do evil. God could not give freedom and at the same time prevent every evil. Other thinkers do not consider this a sufficient answer, above all in the case of natural disasters. Theodicy remains an open question that believers and non-believers still think about today.

gewusst: The term “theodicy” only became known through Leibniz in 1710, although the question is much older.
Voltaire's “Candide” ends with the famous sentence that one must cultivate one's garden.

teile.einleitung: The Russian Orthodox Church is the largest Orthodox church in the world. Its history begins over a thousand years ago with the baptism of Kievan Rus and is closely linked with the history of Russia.
wichtigste: In 988 Grand Prince Vladimir I had himself baptised, and with him Kievan Rus.
In 1589 the Moscow Patriarchate was established.
In 1721 Peter the Great replaced the patriarch with the Holy Synod.
In 1917 the patriarchate was restored, and Tikhon became patriarch.
In the Soviet period the Church was heavily persecuted.
Since 2009 Kirill I has been patriarch (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: In the year **988** **Grand Prince Vladimir I** of Kiev had himself baptised. With him the realm of **Kievan Rus** became Christian. The faith came from **Byzantium**, today's Istanbul. That is why the Church celebrates the service on the Byzantine model, with icons, incense and much singing.

Later **Moscow** became the centre. In **1589** the **Moscow Patriarchate** was established, so the Church received its own patriarch as head. In the 17th century Patriarch **Nikon** introduced reforms in worship. Those who rejected them were called **Old Believers**. These groups still exist today. Tsar **Peter the Great** abolished the office of patriarch in 1721 and set up the **Holy Synod**, an authority under the control of the state.

In **1917** a national council restored the patriarchate, and **Tikhon** became patriarch. Shortly afterwards the Communists came to power. In the **Soviet Union** the Church was heavily persecuted, and many churches were closed or destroyed. The **Cathedral of Christ the Saviour** in Moscow was blown up in 1931 and rebuilt by 2000. Since 2009 **Kirill I** has been Patriarch of Moscow and All Rus (as of 2025).

Monasteries play a large role. Saint **Sergius of Radonezh** founded in the 14th century the **Trinity Monastery** north-east of Moscow. It became an important spiritual centre. Typical of Orthodox churches are **icons**, painted images of saints, and the **iconostasis**, a screen of images in front of the sanctuary.

gewusst: The Russian Orthodox Church celebrates Christmas according to the old Julian calendar, that is, on 7 January.
In Switzerland too there are Russian Orthodox churches, for example in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Around Epiphany on 6 January, children go from house to house as star singers. They are dressed as the Three Kings, sing songs, bring a blessing and collect money for children in need. The custom is widespread in Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
wichtigste: Star singers dress up as the Three Kings.
They carry a large star on a pole.
They are out and about around Epiphany on 6 January.
With chalk they write the year and C+M+B on the door.
C+M+B stands for “Christus mansionem benedicat”, Christ bless this house.
They collect donations for children in poor countries.

abschnitte.text: The Gospel of Matthew tells of **wise men from the East** who followed a star and found the child Jesus. They brought **gold, frankincense and myrrh**, very valuable gifts. The Bible gives no number and no names. Because there were three gifts, people later speak of three kings. According to old tradition they are called **Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar**.

Around **Epiphany** on 6 January, children and teenagers go through the streets in groups. They wear crowns and colourful cloaks. One carries a large **star** on a pole, which recalls the Star of Bethlehem. At every door they sing a song or recite a poem. Then they bring the blessing for the new year.

With blessed **chalk**, the star singers write a blessing on the door or above it. It consists of the year and the letters **C+M+B**. These stand for the Latin “Christus mansionem benedicat”, which means “Christ bless this house”. Many people also read the letters as the beginnings of the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. The crosses between the letters stand for the blessing.

The star singers collect **donations**. The money goes to projects that help **children in need** in poor countries, for example for schools, food or health. In Switzerland the Catholic aid agency **Missio** organises the campaign. Each year it puts a different country or theme in the centre. In this way the old custom becomes a big aid campaign by children for children.

In Switzerland, the **Three Kings' cake** goes with 6 January. It consists of sweet dough balls baked together into a ring. In one ball a small **king figure** is hidden. Whoever finds it may wear the crown and is king or queen for a day. Many families eat the cake together on Epiphany.

gewusst: The custom of the Three Kings' cake was revived in Switzerland in the 1950s by the bread researcher Max Währen.
According to old interpretation, gold stands for a king, frankincense for God and myrrh for the human being.

teile.einleitung: Scholasticism was the learning of the scholars of the Middle Ages. It tried to understand and justify the Christian faith with reason, often with the help of the philosopher Aristotle.
wichtigste: Scholasticism was practised in monastery schools and universities.
In “Sic et non”, Abelard set contradictory statements side by side.
The Sentences of Peter Lombard were for a long time the most important textbook.
Philosophy was regarded as the “handmaid of theology”.
Among the scholastics, Averroes was simply called “the Commentator”.
Well-known Franciscans were Bonaventure, Duns Scotus and William of Ockham.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “schola”, school. The scholars of Scholasticism taught at monastery schools and later at the first **universities**, for example in Paris and Oxford. They asked questions, collected reasons for and against, and looked for an answer. **Philosophy** was regarded as the **“handmaid of theology”**: it was meant to help people understand the faith.

In his work **“Sic et non”**, “Yes and No”, **Peter Abelard** set contradictory statements of the Church Fathers side by side. Students were to learn to resolve such contradictions. The **Sentences of Peter Lombard** were the basis of theological study for centuries. Many scholars wrote their own explanations of them.

In the 12th and 13th centuries, the works of the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** became newly known in the West. Much of it came through Arab scholars. The Andalusian philosopher **Averroes** wrote such important explanations of Aristotle that the scholastics simply called him **“the Commentator”**. The best-known scholastic is **Thomas Aquinas**.

For a long time the scholars argued about **universals**, that is, general terms such as “human being” or “tree”. Do they really exist, or are they only names? **Nominalism** holds that general terms are **mere names**. An important representative was the English Franciscan **William of Ockham**. **“Ockham's razor”** is named after him: explanations should not be made more complicated than necessary.

Many scholastics were given Latin honorary titles. The Franciscan **Bonaventure** was called **“Doctor seraphicus”**. **John Duns Scotus** was called **“Doctor subtilis”** because of his sharp thinking. He is linked with the term **“haecceity”**, the “thisness” that makes something exactly this one thing. Thomas Aquinas was called “Doctor angelicus”.

gewusst: In the 13th century the University of Paris was the most important centre of Scholasticism.
Ockham himself never used the expression “razor”; it only came into use later.

teile.einleitung: The Plan of St Gall is a drawing over 1,000 years old. It shows what an ideal monastery should look like in the early Middle Ages, and is among the greatest treasures of the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
wichtigste: The plan was made around 825 in the monastery of Reichenau on Lake Constance.
The dedication is addressed to a Gozbert, probably the abbot of St Gallen.
It is drawn on five pieces of parchment sewn together.
It shows a whole monastery complex with church, school, infirmary, workshops and gardens.
It is regarded as the earliest drawing of a monastery precinct from the Middle Ages.
Today it lies in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.

abschnitte.titel: A plan from the Carolingian period
abschnitte.text: The plan was made around 825/826, that is, in the time of the **Carolingians**. It was drawn on the monastery island of **Reichenau** in Lake Constance. From there it was sent to St Gallen. In the dedication a **Gozbert** is addressed. This is probably the St Gallen abbot Gozbert, who at that time was planning a new monastery church.

The plan consists of five pieces of **parchment** sewn together. Parchment is a finely processed animal skin on which people wrote in the Middle Ages. The sheet is about 112 cm high and 77.5 cm wide. The buildings are drawn in red ink and explained with many Latin labels. Because the inks are sensitive to light, the original is only rarely shown.

The plan shows not just a church but a whole **monastery complex**. This includes the monks' dormitory and refectory, a school, an infirmary, a guest house, workshops, stables, a herb garden and an orchard. A monastery was meant to supply itself almost completely. The monastery of St Gallen, however, was not built exactly according to this plan. It was more of an **ideal plan**, that is, a model.

The monastery plan is regarded as the **earliest drawn representation** of a monastery precinct from the Middle Ages. That is why it is very valuable for historians. It shows how people at that time imagined life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. The abbey precinct of St Gallen with its cathedral and Abbey Library has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage** since **1983**.

Near **Messkirch** in southern Germany a monastery has been built since 2013 according to the St Gallen plan. The project is called **Campus Galli**. The craftsmen work only with tools and techniques of the Middle Ages. Visitors can watch them and so experience how laborious building used to be.

gewusst: On the back of the plan, a life of Saint Martin was later written in the Middle Ages.
The building site of Campus Galli will probably last many decades, because everything is done by hand.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Bishops' Conference is the association of the Catholic bishops of Switzerland. It was founded as early as 1863 and is regarded as the first bishops' conference in the world.
wichtigste: The Swiss Bishops' Conference was founded in 1863.
It is regarded as the first bishops' conference in the world.
Its members are the bishops, the auxiliary bishops and the abbots of Einsiedeln and Saint-Maurice.
A term as president lasts three years.
Felix Gmür was president from 2019 to 2024; since January 2025 it has been Charles Morerod.
The general secretariat is in Fribourg.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Bishops' Conference** was founded in **1863**. It is regarded as the **first bishops' conference in the world**. Later, similar conferences came into being in many countries. There the bishops discuss together questions that affect the whole Catholic Church in Switzerland. The first president came from the diocese of **Sion**.

The conference includes the bishops of the six Swiss **dioceses** and the **auxiliary bishops**, who support a bishop. In addition there are the **abbots of Einsiedeln and Saint-Maurice**. These two old monasteries each lead a small church territory of their own, a **territorial abbey**. That is why their abbots are members like a bishop.

The conference elects a **president**. A term lasts **three years**. From 2019 to 2024 **Felix Gmür**, the Bishop of Basel, was president. Since **January 2025** the president has been **Charles Morerod**, Bishop of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg (as of 2025). The **general secretariat** is in **Fribourg**.

The Bishops' Conference speaks out on questions of faith, but also on social issues. Because in Switzerland the cantonal churches manage a lot of money, it works closely with the **Roman Catholic Central Conference**. Together they support tasks for the whole of Switzerland.

gewusst: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais has existed since the year 515 and is regarded as one of the oldest monasteries in the West with no break in its history.
Einsiedeln Abbey is an important place of pilgrimage with the famous Black Madonna.

teile.einleitung: Abu Bakr was one of the oldest and closest companions of the Prophet Muhammad. After Muhammad's death in the year 632 he became the first caliph, that is, the first successor at the head of the Muslim community. He ruled for only about two years.
wichtigste: Abu Bakr became the first caliph after Muhammad's death.
“Caliph” means successor or deputy.
His nickname as-Siddiq means “the truthful”.
His daughter Aisha was a wife of Muhammad.
In the Ridda wars he brought rebellious tribes back under Medina's rule.
He had the Quran collected for the first time.
He died in 634 and was buried beside Muhammad in Medina.

abschnitte.text: Abu Bakr was one of the first people to follow Muhammad. He believed him at once, even when others could hardly believe his reports. That is why he received the nickname **as-Siddiq**, “the truthful”. His daughter **Aisha** was one of Muhammad's best-known wives. Many traditions about the life of the Prophet go back to her.

When Muhammad died in **632**, the community chose Abu Bakr as his **successor**. The word **caliph** comes from the Arabic “khalifa” and means **successor** or deputy. It meant the leader of the community after the Messenger of God. The Sunnis count Abu Bakr among the **four rightly guided caliphs**. The Shia, by contrast, see Ali as Muhammad's rightful successor.

After Muhammad's death many **Arab tribes** broke away from Medina. They no longer wanted to pay levies. Abu Bakr fought the **Ridda wars** against them. “Ridda” means apostasy or turning away. In the end the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula were again under the rule of **Medina**.

abschnitte.titel: The first collection of the Quran
abschnitte.text: In the **Battle of Yamama**, many men who knew the **Quran** by heart were killed. People feared that parts might be lost. So Abu Bakr gave the order to collect the verses for the first time. **Zayd ibn Thabit**, who had earlier written down revelations for Muhammad, took on the task. He collected the verses from leaves, bones and from the memory of the believers.

Abu Bakr died as early as **634** in **Medina**, after only about **two years** as caliph. He was buried **next to the Prophet**. The tomb is now within the area of the **Prophet's Mosque**. His successor as caliph was **Umar**.

gewusst: The first collection of the Quran came about because many Quran reciters had fallen in battle.
Abu Bakr ruled for a shorter time than any of the other three rightly guided caliphs.

teile.einleitung: Palm Sunday is the Sunday before Easter. On this day Christians remember the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem. With Palm Sunday Holy Week begins.
wichtigste: Palm Sunday is one week before Easter.
On this day, according to the Gospels, Jesus entered Jerusalem.
The people waved palm branches and cried “Hosanna”.
Jesus came to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover.
Five days after Palm Sunday is Good Friday.
In Switzerland box branches are often used instead of palm branches.

abschnitte.text: According to the Gospels Jesus came with his disciples to **Jerusalem**, the city with the Temple. He rode into the city on a **donkey**. Many people greeted him with **palm branches** and laid clothes on the road. That is where the name of the day comes from. They cried **“Hosanna”**. Originally that means “Save us!” and became a cry of joy.

Jesus came to Jerusalem for the **feast of Passover**. For this Jewish feast many people travelled to the city. Passover recalls the **liberation of the people of Israel from Egypt**. That is why Jerusalem was then full of pilgrims. In this week Jesus also celebrated the Last Supper with his disciples.

Palm Sunday is **one week before Easter**. With it begins **Holy Week**, the week before the Easter feast. **Five days** after Palm Sunday comes Good Friday, on which Christians remember the death of Jesus. On the Sunday after that they celebrate Easter. So Palm Sunday is a cheerful day at the beginning of a serious week.

Palms do not grow outdoors here. That is why in Switzerland people often tie together **box branches** or other green branches. In church the branches are **blessed**. Many families afterwards put them at home behind a **cross** or hang them in the stable. They are meant to recall the blessing. In some Catholic regions children carry large **palm trees** decorated with ribbons to church.

gewusst: Some parishes burn the old palm branches and use the ash on the next Ash Wednesday.
In some places there is a procession on Palm Sunday, sometimes even with a wooden donkey.

teile.einleitung: The church tower is the tall tower of a church. You can see it from far away, and it is often the tallest building in the village. The bells hang at the top, and on the outside a clock shows the time.
wichtigste: The bells hang at the top of the church tower.
On many church towers there is a clock on the outside.
On many Reformed church towers in Switzerland sits a rooster made of metal.
You get to the top by a staircase.
From some church towers there is a wide view.
Bern Minster has the tallest church tower in Switzerland.
In Lausanne a tower watchman calls out the hours every night.

abschnitte.text: Church towers are mostly very tall, **so that they can be seen from far away**. They show from a distance where the church and the centre of the village are. In the past they also helped travellers to find their way. The tower points upwards, to heaven. In this way it is also a sign of faith.

At the top of the church tower hang the **bells**. They call people to the service and strike the hours. On the outside of many church towers you can see a **clock**. In the past most people had no clock of their own. The church tower clock showed everyone in the village what time it was.

On many **Reformed church towers** in Switzerland sits a **rooster made of metal**. It turns in the wind and so shows where the wind is blowing from. The rooster recalls the story of Peter in the Bible: before the rooster crowed, Peter had said three times that he did not know Jesus. The rooster also stands for watchfulness and for the new morning. On Catholic churches you often see a **cross** at the top.

In the church tower you get to the top **by a staircase**. Often it is narrow and has many steps. From some large church towers visitors have a **wide view** over the city and the countryside. The **tallest church tower in Switzerland** belongs to **Bern Minster**. It is about 100 metres high, and you can climb over 300 steps up it.

In **Lausanne** there is a special custom. Every night a **tower watchman** calls out the hours from the tower of the **cathedral**. From 10 pm to 2 am, after each stroke of the bell, he calls in all directions: “C'est le guet, il a sonné l'heure.” In the past the watchman kept a lookout for fire in the city. This custom has existed since the Middle Ages.

gewusst: Lausanne is one of the last cities in Europe where a tower watchman still calls every night.
The tower of Bern Minster was only finished in 1893, over 400 years after building began.

teile.einleitung: The Council of Trent was the response of the Catholic Church to the Reformation. It met from 1545 to 1563 in the city of Trent in northern Italy and renewed the Church profoundly.
wichtigste: The council lasted, with interruptions, from 1545 to 1563.
It confirmed the seven sacraments.
It declared the Latin Vulgate to be the authoritative Bible.
Every diocese was to have a seminary.
The renewal afterwards is called the Counter-Reformation or Catholic Reform.
Charles Borromeo also enforced the decisions in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: After the appearance of Luther and Zwingli the Western Church was split. Pope **Paul III** therefore summoned a council to **Trent**, a city in northern Italy. It met, with long interruptions, in **three periods** from **1545 to 1563**. The Protestants did not take part. So the council became above all a self-clarification of the Catholic Church.

The council held to the **seven sacraments**, such as baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist and marriage. The Reformed recognised only baptism and the Lord's Supper. The Bible and the tradition of the Church were to be authoritative. The binding biblical text was the **Vulgate**, the Latin translation that goes back to the Church Father **Jerome**.

The council also wanted to remedy abuses. Bishops were to live in their dioceses and care for the faithful. Every diocese was to have a **seminary**, a school for future priests. After the council a common catechism appeared, a book with the most important teachings of the faith.

The time after the council is called the **Counter-Reformation** or **Catholic Reform**. The Church wanted to renew itself and win back lost territories. New orders such as the **Jesuits** and the **Capuchins** played an important part. The renewal was also seen in art and architecture, for example in magnificent Baroque churches.

The Archbishop of Milan, **Charles Borromeo**, visited the Catholic areas of Switzerland and promoted the reforms there. At his suggestion a papal **nuncio** came to **Lucerne**. In Milan he founded a school for priests from Switzerland. Capuchins and Jesuits founded monasteries and schools in many Catholic places.

gewusst: Until the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s, the Catholic Mass was celebrated almost everywhere in Latin according to the rules from the time after Trent.
Trent is called Trento in Italian.

teile.einleitung: A church choir is a group of people who sing together in church. It sings in the service, at festivals and in concerts. In many Swiss villages and towns there is a church choir.
wichtigste: A church choir sings in church.
The choir director leads the choir.
The highest voice is called soprano, the lowest male voice bass.
Before a performance the choir practises in rehearsals.
At Christmas, church choirs like to sing songs about the birth of Jesus.
The word of praise “Hallelujah” appears in many church songs.
For children there are children's choirs.

abschnitte.text: A **church choir** sings in the **service**, at church festivals and sometimes in concerts. Its songs praise God, tell Bible stories or express joy and sorrow. The choir often sings together with the **organ**. Many church choirs have existed for over a hundred years. For many members the choir is also a pleasant fellowship.

A mixed choir usually has four voices. The highest voice is called **soprano**, which is often sung by women and children. Below it comes the **alto**. The men sing **tenor** and the lowest voice, the **bass**. When all the voices sound together, a full sound arises.

The choir is led by the **choir director**. She shows with her hands the beat and when it gets louder or quieter. Before the choir sings in the service, it **practises in rehearsals**, often once a week. First each voice learns its melody, then everyone sings together. That way it works on Sunday.

At **Christmas** many church choirs especially like to sing songs about the **birth of Jesus**. At Easter too there is festive music. In many songs the word of praise **“Hallelujah”** appears. It comes from Hebrew and means “Praise God”. For children there is a **children's choir** in many parishes, where they can sing and perform.

gewusst: A famous choral piece is the “Hallelujah” from the oratorio “Messiah” by George Frideric Handel.
Boys' choirs such as the Thomanerchor in Leipzig have existed for many centuries.

teile.einleitung: Easter Sunday is the most important feast of Christians. On this day they celebrate that, according to their belief, Jesus rose from the dead. Easter falls each year on a different date in March or April.
wichtigste: On Easter Sunday Christians celebrate the resurrection of Jesus.
Mary Magdalene and other women found the tomb empty on Easter morning.
The large stone in front of the tomb had been rolled away.
An angel told the women that Jesus lives.
Easter is on the Sunday after the first full moon in spring.
In most cantons Easter Monday is also a public holiday.

abschnitte.text: Jesus had died on Good Friday and been laid in a **rock tomb**. The tomb was closed with a heavy **stone**. Early on Sunday morning **Mary Magdalene** and other women went to the tomb. They saw that the stone had been rolled away and the tomb was empty. An **angel**, a messenger of God, told them: Jesus lives.

For Christians the **resurrection** is the core of their faith. They believe that Jesus was raised from death to new life. That is why Easter is the **most important feast** in the church year, even before Christmas. With Easter **Holy Week** ends, which begins with Palm Sunday. Every Sunday reminds Christians of this day.

According to the Gospels Jesus appeared several times to his disciples afterwards. The disciple **Thomas**, however, was not there. He did not want to believe that Jesus lives before he had seen the **wounds** himself. When Jesus appeared to him, he believed. That is why today one says of someone who doubts: **“doubting Thomas”**.

Easter is on the **Sunday after the first full moon in spring**. That is why the feast falls on a different date each year. Easter is at the earliest on **22 March** and at the latest on **25 April**. Other feasts such as Ascension (Auffahrt) and Pentecost also depend on the date of Easter. In most cantons **Easter Monday** is also a day off, so there is a long Easter weekend.

gewusst: The rule for the date of Easter was already discussed in the year 325 at the Council of Nicaea.
Orthodox Christians often celebrate Easter on a different Sunday, because they calculate with a different calendar.

teile.einleitung: The Coptic Orthodox Church is the church of the Christians in Egypt. It is one of the oldest churches in the world and has its own traditions, its own language in worship and its own head.
wichtigste: The Copts are the largest Christian community in Egypt.
The word “Copt” comes from the Greek word for Egyptian.
According to tradition, the evangelist Mark founded the church in Alexandria.
Its head is called the Pope of Alexandria, and since 2012 it has been Tawadros II.
After the Council of Chalcedon in 451 the Copts went their own way.
Coptic is still used in worship today.

abschnitte.text: The **Copts** are the largest Christian community in **Egypt**. The Greek word **“Aigyptios”** for Egyptian became “qibt” in Arabic. So originally “Copt” simply meant Egyptian. According to Coptic tradition the evangelist **Mark** brought the Christian faith to **Alexandria**. That is why the church is also called the Church of Saint Mark.

The head of the Copts bears the title **Pope of Alexandria** and Patriarch of the See of Saint Mark. Since **2012** this has been **Tawadros II** (as of 2026). He succeeded Shenouda III. By old custom he was chosen from three candidates by **lot**, drawn by a child. The seat of the Pope is today in Cairo.

abschnitte.titel: A way of their own since 451
abschnitte.text: At the **Council of Chalcedon** in the year 451 there was dispute over how divinity and humanity are united in Christ. The Copts rejected the decision. Since then they have belonged to the **Oriental Orthodox churches**, together with, for example, the Armenian and the Ethiopian church. In worship, alongside Arabic, **Coptic** is also used. It is the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language and is written with letters based mainly on the Greek alphabet.

In the desert of Egypt Christian **monasticism** began. **Anthony the Great** lived in the 3rd and 4th centuries as a hermit in the desert. Many followed his example. To this day there are old Coptic monasteries in Egypt that are inhabited by monks.

Many Copts wear a small **tattooed cross** on the inside of the wrist. Often it is tattooed on children already and shows their belonging to the church. The Copts also have their own way of counting years, the **Era of the Martyrs**. It begins in the year **284** with the start of the reign of Emperor **Diocletian**, under whom Christians were severely persecuted.

gewusst: The Copts too call their head Pope, and have done so for a very long time.
The Coptic language helped researchers to decipher the ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs.

teile.einleitung: For many people, carols are an essential part of Advent and Christmas. Some tell of the birth of Jesus, others of winter or the fir tree. The best known is “Silent Night, Holy Night”.
wichtigste: “Silent Night, Holy Night” was first sung in 1818.
That happened in Oberndorf near Salzburg in Austria.
The melody is by Franz Xaver Gruber, the text by Joseph Mohr.
The first time, the song was accompanied by a guitar.
Many songs are about winter, the fir tree or the Christ child.
In “Jingle Bells”, little bells jingle on a sleigh.

abschnitte.text: The song was first sung at Christmas **1818** in **Oberndorf** near Salzburg in **Austria**. That is a little more than 200 years ago. The melody was written by the teacher and organist **Franz Xaver Gruber**. The text was written by the priest **Joseph Mohr**. The first time, the accompaniment was played on a **guitar**. Today the song is known all over the world and sung in a great many languages.

In the German song “O Tannenbaum” it says: “how green are your **leaves**”. In fact a fir has **needles**. The song praises the tree for staying green in winter too. It is often sung when the family stands around the decorated Christmas tree.

Some carols tell of winter and of the anticipation. “Leise rieselt der **Schnee**” (“Softly the **snow** falls”) describes how snow falls and Christmas comes closer. In the English song “**Jingle Bells**”, **bells** jingle on a sleigh. “Bells” in German is “Glocken”.

Many songs tell of the birth of Jesus. “Ihr Kinderlein, **kommet**” (“O come, little children”) invites the children to come to the manger. In the song “Alle Jahre wieder” (“Every year again”), the **Christ child** comes down to earth every year. In “Kling, Glöckchen, klingelingeling” a little **bell** announces the Christmas season with its sound.
Carols are sung in families, schools and churches. Many choirs give concerts in Advent. In Switzerland there are songs in German, French, Italian and Romansh. Singing together creates a festive mood.

gewusst: In Austria “Silent Night” was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
In Oberndorf today a small Silent Night chapel stands on the site of the former church.

teile.einleitung: The “Novum Instrumentum omne” is a book by the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam. It appeared in 1516 in Basel and was the first published printed New Testament in Greek. It changed biblical scholarship and helped the Reformation.
wichtigste: The work appeared in 1516 in Basel from the printer Johann Froben.
It was the first published printed Greek New Testament.
Beside the Greek text stood a Latin translation of Erasmus's own.
Luther used the second edition of 1519 for his September Testament.
Erasmus published five editions in his lifetime.
From them came the Textus receptus, which prevailed until the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: **Erasmus of Rotterdam** was one of the most famous scholars of his time, a **humanist**. Humanists wanted to read the ancient texts in their original languages. **Basel** was then a leading place for printing and humanism. The printer **Johann Froben** published many works of Erasmus, and Erasmus lived for a time in his house. In 1516 the “Novum Instrumentum omne” appeared there.

Before that, people in Western Europe knew mainly the Latin Bible, the **Vulgate**. Erasmus brought the Greek text of the New Testament into print. In Spain a Greek New Testament had indeed already been printed in 1514, in the **Complutensian Polyglot**. But it was only delivered years later. So the edition of Erasmus was **the first to reach the market**.

Beside the Greek text Erasmus placed a **Latin translation of his own**. In addition there were detailed **notes**. Erasmus worked quickly and had only a few manuscripts. His manuscript of Revelation lacked the last verses, 22:16 to 21. He translated them from the Vulgate **back into Greek**, which created new readings.

Erasmus improved his text again and again. The editions appeared in **1516, 1519, 1522, 1527 and 1535**. In the third edition of 1522 he included the **Comma Johanneum**, a disputed addition about the Trinity in 1 John 5:7 to 8. It is missing in almost all Greek manuscripts. Erasmus included it only after he had been shown a manuscript with the addition.

**Martin Luther** translated the New Testament into German at the Wartburg in 1521 and 1522. He relied above all on the second edition of Erasmus of 1519. The **Textus receptus** is also based on the editions of Erasmus; the name comes from an edition of 1633. It means “the text received by all”. Until the 19th century this Greek text was dominant.

gewusst: Erasmus died in 1536 in Basel and is buried in Basel Minster.
Luther's September Testament is so called because it appeared in September 1522.

teile.einleitung: The Requiem in D minor is the last work of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. He died in 1791 before he could complete it, and the work was finished by others.
wichtigste: A requiem is music for a Mass for the dead.
Mozart worked on it in 1791 and died before it was finished.
Count Franz von Walsegg commissioned the work in secret.
The Requiem is in D minor.
Mozart's manuscript broke off after eight bars of the Lacrimosa.
His pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed the best-known version.

abschnitte.text: A **requiem** is a **Mass for the dead**, that is, a service for the deceased. The name comes from the first Latin word of the text: “Requiem aeternam”, eternal rest. Many composers have set this text to music. An important part is the medieval sequence **“Dies irae”**, the day of wrath. It is about the **Last Judgement** at the end of time.

In 1791 Mozart received a commission through a messenger. Behind the commission stood **Count Franz von Walsegg**. He wanted to perform the work in memory of his deceased wife and presumably to pass it off as his own composition. That is why he stayed in the background. Many legends later arose around this commission.

Mozart worked on the Requiem in the autumn of **1791**, but he became seriously ill and died in December. Only the first movement, the **Introitus**, was fully worked out by him and written for all the instruments. For further parts he left the vocal parts and important instrumental parts. At the **Lacrimosa** his manuscript broke off after only **eight bars**.

Mozart's widow Constanze wanted the work to be completed so that she would receive the fee. In the end it was completed by Mozart's pupil **Franz Xaver Süssmayr**. His version is still the best known and is performed most often. Later other musicians also wrote their own completions. The work is in the serious key of **D minor**.

gewusst: Parts of the Requiem were sung as early as at a memorial service for Mozart in December 1791 in Vienna.
Mozart lived to be only 35 years old.

teile.einleitung: Separation of church and state means that the state and the religious communities go their separate ways. In Switzerland each canton decides for itself how closely it is linked with the churches. Geneva and Neuchâtel take a special path.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the cantons regulate the relationship between church and state.
Most cantons recognise regional churches that may levy church taxes.
Geneva decided on the separation of church and state in 1907.
Neuchâtel introduced a far-reaching separation in 1941.
A federal popular initiative for complete separation clearly failed in 1980.
In Geneva a law of its own on the secularity of the state has applied since 2019.

abschnitte.text: In a **separation of church and state**, the state does not interfere in matters of faith, and the churches have no special state rights. Such a state is also called **secular** (French “laïque”). The word comes from French. The state is to be neutral and treat all religions equally. People are still free to believe what they like.

In Switzerland there is no single rule for the whole country. Each **canton** decides for itself how it deals with the churches. In many cantons the Reformed and the Roman Catholic churches are recognised as **regional churches**. They may then often levy church taxes. On 2 March 1980, voters rejected a popular initiative for complete separation with 78.9 per cent voting No. In the canton of Zurich, too, separation was clearly rejected in 1977 and 1995.

Geneva adopted separation as early as **1907**. Since then there has been no regional church recognised under public law there. The churches still receive money from their members: with the tax return one can make a **voluntary contribution**, which the canton collects. Because many people pay nothing, the Geneva churches have little money. Since 2019 this contribution has been called the “contribution religieuse volontaire” and is in principle also open to other religious communities.

On 10 February 2019, Geneva voters adopted a **law on the secularity of the state**, with 55.1 per cent Yes. It regulates, for example, religious symbols and religious events in public space. State employees who deal with the public are not to wear visible religious symbols. Supporters saw it as strengthening the neutrality of the state. Critics said it mainly affected women with headscarves, and there were complaints against individual articles.

Neuchâtel largely separated church and state in **1941**. But the canton is not entirely without a link. In a **concordat**, that is, an agreement, it recognised three churches in 2001 as institutions of public interest: the Reformed, the Roman Catholic and the Christian Catholic church. The cantonal constitution of 2000 confirms the secularity of the state.

gewusst: France separated church and state as early as 1905 with a law.
The Geneva secularity law is called “Loi sur la laïcité de l'État” in French.

teile.einleitung: The calming of the storm is a miracle story from the Gospels. Jesus and his disciples are caught in a dangerous storm on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus speaks to the wind and the water, and everything becomes quite still.
wichtigste: Jesus and the disciples cross the Sea of Galilee by boat in the evening.
A strong storm blows up, and the boat fills with water.
Jesus is asleep at the back of the boat on a cushion.
The disciples wake him, full of fear.
Jesus rebukes the wind and says to the sea: “Quiet! Be still!”
The disciples ask themselves: “Who is this man?”

abschnitte.text: In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus says **in the evening**: “Let us go over to the other side.” He gets into a **boat** on the **Sea of Galilee** with his disciples. Some of the disciples know the lake well, because they used to be fishermen. The lake lies deep in a hollow, and violent winds can suddenly rush down from the mountains. The story is also in Matthew and Luke.

In the middle of the lake a strong **storm** blows up. The waves break into the boat so that it fills with **water**. The disciples fear that they will sink. But Jesus is lying at the back of the boat, **asleep**. In the Gospel of Mark he is even sleeping on a cushion.

Full of **fear**, the disciples wake Jesus. They cry out that they are going under. Jesus gets up and **rebukes the wind**. To the sea he says: “Quiet! Be still!” Then the wind dies down, and it becomes **completely calm**. The Bible speaks of a great stillness.

Afterwards Jesus asks his disciples: “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?” He wants to strengthen their **trust**. The disciples are amazed and ask themselves: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” They sense that Jesus has a special **power**. Many Christians also understand the story as a picture: God is there when life becomes stormy.

gewusst: In 1986 a fishing boat about 2,000 years old was found on the shore of the Sea of Galilee.
The Sea of Galilee lies more than 200 metres below sea level.

teile.einleitung: Mother Teresa was a Catholic nun who devoted her life to the poorest of the poor. In Kolkata (Calcutta) in India she cared for the sick and the dying. She received the Nobel Peace Prize and was later canonised.
wichtigste: Mother Teresa was born in 1910 in Skopje, today the capital of North Macedonia.
Her birth name was Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, in English Agnes.
She came from a Catholic Albanian family.
In 1950 she founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta.
In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Pope Francis canonised her in 2016.

abschnitte.text: Mother Teresa was born in 1910 in **Skopje**. At that time the city belonged to the Ottoman Empire, and today it is the capital of **North Macedonia**. Her family was **Albanian** and Catholic. Her real name was **Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu**. Already as a teenager she wanted to become a nun and work in the mission.

At the age of 18 she joined the **Sisters of Loreto** and travelled to India. In the convent she chose the name Teresa, after the French saint **Thérèse of Lisieux**, the patron saint of missionaries. For almost 20 years she taught as a **teacher** at a girls' school in Calcutta. But every day she saw the great poverty outside the school walls.

Mother Teresa left the school in order to live directly among the poor. In 1950 she founded the **Missionaries of Charity** in Calcutta, today **Kolkata**. The sisters wear a simple **white sari with blue stripes**, like that worn by poor women in India. They opened homes for the dying, orphans and the sick. Today the sisters work all over the world.

In **1979** Mother Teresa received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. She asked that the money for the celebration banquet be given to the poor. She died in 1997 in Calcutta. Pope John Paul II beatified her in 2003, and **Pope Francis** canonised her on 4 September 2016 in Rome. There was also criticism of her, for example of the medical care in her homes.

gewusst: Mother Teresa became an Indian citizen and after her death received a state funeral in India.
In addition to the usual religious vows, her sisters take a fourth vow: to serve the poorest of the poor.

teile.einleitung: The organ is a large musical instrument that stands in many churches. Its notes arise in pipes through which air flows. Because it is so large and has so many sounds, it is called the “king of instruments”.
wichtigste: The notes of an organ come from pipes.
A blower pushes air into the pipes.
Small pipes sound high, large pipes low.
The low notes are played with the feet on the pedals.
With the stops one chooses which pipes sound.
Whoever plays the organ is called an organist.

abschnitte.text: An organ has many **pipes**, often hundreds or even thousands. They are made of metal or of wood. The **small** pipes sound **high**, the **large** ones sound **low**. Some pipes are only as small as a pencil, others several metres tall. Most of the pipes you cannot see at all, because they stand inside the organ.

For the pipes to sound, the organ needs **air**. Today an electric **blower** pushes the air into the organ. In the past helpers had to tread or pull a large **bellows** for this. When you press a key, a valve opens and the air flows into the matching pipe. So the note arises, as long as you hold the key down.

An organ often has several keyboards for the hands, the **manuals**. Below there is the **pedalboard** with wooden keys. On it one plays the low notes with the **feet**. With the **stops**, knobs or pulls beside the keys, one chooses which rows of pipes sound. So the organ can sound like a flute, like a trumpet or quite mighty.

In many churches the organ stands **up in the gallery**, a kind of balcony. From there its sound fills the whole church. The **organist** accompanies the hymns of the congregation at the service and plays music for listening. Many famous composers such as **Johann Sebastian Bach** wrote music for the organ. In many Swiss villages too the organ is the largest instrument in the place.
