In Sweden the Lucia festival is very popular.
The Lucia wears a white dress and a wreath with lights.
Lucia is regarded as the patron saint of the eyes.

abschnitte.text: Saint **Lucia** lived around the year 300 in **Syracuse**. This city lies on the island of **Sicily** in Italy. At that time Christians in the Roman Empire were persecuted under Emperor Diocletian. Lucia stayed true to her faith and died as a **martyr**. To this day she is the patron saint of Syracuse.

The name **Lucia** comes from the Latin word **lux**, which means light. It can be translated as “the shining one”. An old legend tells that Lucia secretly brought **food** to the Christians who were hiding in dark caves. So that she had her hands free, she is said to have worn a wreath with lights on her head.

Lucia is regarded as the **patron saint of the eyes** and of the blind. That fits her name, because without light we cannot see. People with eye troubles often pray to her. In pictures she is sometimes shown with a dish on which two eyes lie.

In **Sweden** the Lucia festival is celebrated on **13 December** in schools, churches and families. A girl plays Lucia. She wears a long **white dress** with a **red sash** around the waist and a **wreath of candles** on her head. Behind her walk other children with candles in a procession, singing songs. With it people eat yellow **saffron buns** called **Lussekatter**.

gewusst: According to the old calendar, 13 December fell almost on the shortest day of the year, which is why the festival of lights suits this date so well.
The well-known song “Santa Lucia” also comes originally from Italy, from Naples.

teile.einleitung: The Council of Constance was a great church assembly from 1414 to 1418 on Lake Constance, near today's Swiss border. It ended a time in which there were several popes at once.
wichtigste: The council met from 1414 to 1418 in Constance.
At that time three popes were quarrelling over the office, which is called the Western Schism.
King Sigismund campaigned strongly for the council.
With the decree “Haec sancta” the council placed itself above the Pope.
In 1417 Martin V was elected, which ended the Schism.
In 1415 the Confederates conquered Aargau.

abschnitte.text: Around 1400 the Western Church was split. At times there were **three popes** who did not recognise one another. This split is called the **Western Schism**. The Roman-German king **Sigismund** pressed for a council to resolve the crisis. So from 1414 bishops, princes, scholars and many guests came to **Constance** on Lake Constance.

In 1415 the council passed the decree **“Haec sancta”**. In it it declared that its authority came directly from Christ. Even the Pope had to obey it in matters of faith and church reform. The decree **“Frequens”** of 1417 demanded that general councils be held regularly in future. This idea is called **conciliarism**.

The three popes were deposed or resigned. On **11 November 1417** Oddo Colonna was elected. After the saint of the day he called himself **Martin V**. He was recognised by the whole Western Church. With this the Schism ended. The council also condemned the Bohemian reformer **Jan Hus**, who was executed in Constance in 1415.

Pope **John XXIII** fled from Constance in 1415. Duke **Frederick IV of Austria** helped him with this and was outlawed by the king for it. Sigismund called on the Confederates to occupy Frederick's territories. So in 1415 they conquered **Aargau**. It was afterwards administered as a common territory, above all by Bern.

gewusst: The building at the harbour of Constance in which the Pope was elected in 1417 is still called the Konzil today.
The antipope John XXIII of this time is not the same as Pope John XXIII of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: The sexton looks after the church building. He or she unlocks the church, prepares the service and tidies up afterwards. In other regions people say “Mesmer” or “Küster”.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the person who looks after the church is called a “Sigrist”, or “Sigristin” for a woman.
The sexton unlocks the church and prepares everything.
In the past he rang the bells by hand.
Before the service he often lights the candles.
For festivals he decorates the church with flowers.
In eastern Switzerland and southern Germany people also say “Mesmer”, in northern Germany “Küster”.

abschnitte.text: The **sexton** (German “Sigrist”) is responsible for the church building. He unlocks the church in the morning and locks it again in the evening. He turns on the lights, provides warmth in winter and keeps everything clean. The word comes from the Latin “sacrista”, someone who looks after holy things. The name **sacristy** comes from the same word, for the room where robes and equipment are kept.

Before the service the sexton prepares everything. He puts out the **hymn books** and puts the numbers of the hymns on the hymn board. He often lights the **candles** on the altar. For baptisms he gets water ready, for the Lord's Supper bread and wine. When people arrive, everything should be ready.

In the past, the **ringing of the bells** was one of the most important tasks. Every day the sexton climbed the tower and pulled the bell ropes. The bells called people to the service, showed the time of day and warned of fire. Today most bells ring electrically. But the sexton often still sets the ringing times.

For festivals such as Christmas, Easter or the harvest thanksgiving, the sexton decorates the church, for example with **flowers**. After the service he puts the hymn books back, puts out the candles and locks up. He also helps at weddings, baptisms and funerals. A woman in this job is called a **Sigristin**. Today many women work as sextons, often in a part-time post with the parish.

gewusst: In Switzerland the sexton is usually employed by the parish, not by the pastor.
In the past the sexton often lived right next to the church in the sexton's house.

teile.einleitung: Easter eggs are among the best-known customs at Easter. People dye or paint them, hide them and eat them together. The egg is a sign of new life.
wichtigste: In the past people ate no eggs during Lent, so at Easter there were many.
The Easter egg is a sign of new life and fits the resurrection.
Before dyeing, the eggs are hard-boiled.
Onion skins dye reddish brown, beetroot pink to red, red cabbage blue and turmeric yellow.
Red is the oldest colour for Easter eggs.
With a leaf and a stocking a leaf pattern is created.

abschnitte.text: In the past Christians were not allowed to eat eggs during **Lent** before Easter. But the hens went on laying eggs. To keep them from spoiling, people boiled them. At Easter there were then especially many eggs. The egg is also a **sign of new life**: a chick hatches from an egg. So it fits well with the feast of the **resurrection** of Jesus.

**Red** is the oldest colour for Easter eggs. It recalls the blood of Jesus and life. In the Orthodox Church Easter eggs are still often dyed red today. Before eggs are dyed or painted, they are boiled **hard**. Then they do not break so easily and keep longer.

You can dye eggs with **natural dyes**. **Onion skins** give a brown to reddish-brown tone. With **beetroot** the eggs become pink to red. The juice of **red cabbage** looks violet, but dyes the white shell blue. The spice **turmeric** makes the eggs a strong yellow. White eggs take the colour better than brown ones.

For a pretty pattern you lay a small **leaf** or a blossom on the egg. Then you tie the egg tightly into a piece of **stocking**. Where the leaf lies, no colour reaches. After dyeing, a pale **leaf print** remains. Finally the eggs are rubbed with a little oil, and then they shine.

In **Eiertütschen** (egg tapping), two people knock their eggs against each other at the tip. Whoever's egg stays whole has won. In Bern there is the **Zwänzgerle**: children hold out an egg, and adults try to throw a twenty-rappen coin into it. If the coin sticks, the egg belongs to the thrower, otherwise the child may keep the coin. In many places the eggs are also hidden in the garden to be searched for.

gewusst: Artfully painted Easter eggs are found especially in Eastern Europe, for example in Ukraine.
A hard-boiled egg spins like a top, a raw one hardly at all.

teile.einleitung: Ruth is a woman from the Old Testament. Her story stands in the Book of Ruth and tells of loyalty, friendship and a new beginning in a foreign land.
wichtigste: Ruth came from the land of Moab.
Her mother-in-law was called Naomi.
After Ruth's husband had died, she stayed with Naomi.
Ruth promised: “Where you go, I will go.”
In Bethlehem she gathered leftover ears of grain in the field of Boaz.
Her great-grandson was King David.

abschnitte.titel: A family in a foreign land
abschnitte.text: Because of a famine, a family moved from **Bethlehem** to the land of **Moab**. The mother was called **Naomi**. Her two sons married women from Moab, one of them was **Ruth**. Then Naomi's husband and both sons died. The three women were now alone.

Naomi wanted to return to her homeland. She told her daughters-in-law to stay in Moab. But Ruth wanted to stay with her and said: **“Where you go, I will go.”** She also promised that Naomi's people should be her people and Naomi's God her God. This sentence is still often read today at weddings or marriage ceremonies.

Ruth and Naomi went to **Bethlehem**. It was harvest time. Poor people were allowed at that time to gather the **leftover ears of grain** in the fields. Ruth gathered in the field of **Boaz**, a relative of Naomi. Boaz was kind to her because he had heard of her loyalty. He made sure that she could gather enough.

Later Boaz and Ruth married. They had a son named **Obed**. Naomi was very happy and took care of the child. Obed became the grandfather of **King David**. So Ruth, the foreigner from Moab, was the great-grandmother of the most famous king of Israel.

gewusst: The Book of Ruth is one of only two books of the Bible named after a woman; the other is Esther.
In the New Testament Ruth is mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus.

teile.einleitung: The Schleitheim Articles are an early confession of faith of the Anabaptists. They were adopted in 1527 in the village of Schleitheim in what is now the canton of Schaffhausen.
wichtigste: The articles were adopted on 24 February 1527.
Schleitheim is in what is now the canton of Schaffhausen.
Michael Sattler is regarded as the main author.
The confession has seven articles.
Christians should not swear oaths at all.
The congregation should keep apart from the world, which it regarded as evil.

abschnitte.text: The **Anabaptists** came into being in the 1520s in Zurich. They were part of the Reformation but wanted to go further than Zwingli. They rejected the baptism of small children and baptised only people who had decided for the faith themselves. The authorities persecuted them harshly. Later the **Mennonites** and the **Amish** grew out of them.

On **24 February 1527**, Anabaptists met in the village of **Schleitheim** in what is now the **canton of Schaffhausen**. There they adopted a shared confession with **seven articles**. **Michael Sattler**, a former monk, is regarded as the main author. He was executed for his faith in the same year.

One article deals with **separation**. It means that the congregation **separates itself from the world**, which it regarded as evil. The Anabaptists wanted to lead a life according to the Bible, apart from violence and worldly customs. Another article concerns the **oath**: Christians should **not swear at all**, because Jesus says so in the Sermon on the Mount.

In the article on the **sword**, the Anabaptists demand that Christians do **not hold any public office that uses the power of the sword**. So they should not become judges or soldiers. Other articles concern baptism, the Lord's Supper, excommunication and the shepherds of the congregation. Non-violence still shapes many Anabaptist congregations today.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are still Anabaptist congregations today, especially in the Emmental and in the Jura.
The Schleitheim Articles were printed quickly and spread widely.

teile.einleitung: The Crusades were military campaigns of Christian armies in the Middle Ages. They led above all to the Holy Land, where the crusaders wanted to bring Jerusalem under Christian rule.
wichtigste: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at Clermont.
The aim was above all Jerusalem with the tomb of Jesus.
In 1099 the crusaders conquered Jerusalem.
In 1187 Saladin recaptured the city.
Richard the Lionheart and Frederick Barbarossa took part in the Third Crusade.
In the Fourth Crusade, crusaders plundered Constantinople in 1204.

abschnitte.text: In the year **1095** Pope **Urban II** gave a speech at a church assembly in **Clermont** in France. He called on Christians to go to the Holy Land. The aim was **Jerusalem** with the tomb of Jesus, which was under Muslim rule. Many knights and ordinary people followed the call. They sewed a cross onto their clothes, which is why they were called **crusaders**.

In the **First Crusade** the crusaders conquered Jerusalem in **1099**. In the process a great many of the city's inhabitants lost their lives. After that they founded several **crusader states**. In the year **1187** **Saladin**, Sultan of Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusaders at Hattin and took Jerusalem again.

In response to Saladin's victory the **Third Crusade** began. Emperor **Frederick Barbarossa** drowned on the way in 1190 in the river Saleph in the south of present-day Turkey. The English king **Richard the Lionheart** fought against Saladin and conquered some coastal cities. But he did not win back Jerusalem. In the end the two concluded a truce that allowed Christian pilgrims to visit the city.

The **Fourth Crusade** never reached the Holy Land at all. Instead, in **1204** the crusaders attacked the Christian city of **Constantinople** and plundered it. This deepened the gulf between the Western and Eastern Church greatly. To this day this event is regarded as a heavy burden between Catholics and Orthodox.

In the time of the Crusades **military orders** arose. The **Templars** were founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims. They were both monks and knights. The **Hospitallers** also belong here. With the fall of the city of **Acre** in 1291 the rule of the crusaders in the Holy Land ended. Today the Crusades are viewed critically because of the many victims.

gewusst: Through the Crusades, new goods such as spices, sugar and silk came into wider circulation in Europe.
Altogether the Crusades lasted about 200 years, from 1096 to 1291.

teile.einleitung: Martin Luther King was an American pastor and civil rights leader. Without violence, he fought for black people in the USA to have the same rights as white people.
wichtigste: Martin Luther King was a pastor of a Baptist church.
The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 made him known.
He fought with nonviolent resistance, following the example of Gandhi.
In 1963 he gave the speech “I Have a Dream” in Washington.
In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1968 he was murdered in Memphis.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther King was born on **15 January 1929** in **Atlanta**. His father was pastor of the **Ebenezer Baptist Church**, where King was baptised. In 1954 King himself became pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in **Montgomery** in Alabama. From 1960 he preached again in Atlanta together with his father. His faith was the foundation of his commitment.

In the southern states of the USA, **racial segregation** applied at that time. Black people had to sit at the back of the bus, for example. In 1955 **Rosa Parks** in Montgomery refused to give up her seat for a white passenger, and was arrested. In response many African Americans boycotted the buses for over a year. King led the **Montgomery bus boycott**. In the end segregation on buses was banned.

King fought with **nonviolent resistance**. He relied on peaceful marches, boycotts and sit-ins. He rejected violence out of Christian conviction. An important model was **Mahatma Gandhi**, who had led India to independence with nonviolent resistance. In 1959 King travelled to India to learn more about Gandhi's ideas.

On **28 August 1963** the **March on Washington** took place. In front of the **Lincoln Memorial**, King gave his famous speech **“I Have a Dream”** to about 250,000 people. He described his dream of a country in which all people are treated equally. In 1964, at the age of 35, he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. He was then the youngest prizewinner.

On **4 April 1968** Martin Luther King was shot dead in **Memphis**. He was only 39 years old. But his ideas live on. In the USA, **Martin Luther King Day** has commemorated him since 1986. It is on the **third Monday in January**, close to his birthday.

gewusst: His father changed his own name and that of his son in honour of the Reformer Martin Luther.
Since 2011 there has been a large memorial to Martin Luther King in Washington.

teile.einleitung: On St Martin's Day, 11 November, people remember Saint Martin. He is known for having shared his cloak with a freezing beggar. In Switzerland there are lovely customs for it, such as lantern processions and Räbeliechtli (turnip lanterns).
wichtigste: St Martin's Day is on 11 November.
Martin cut his cloak with his sword and shared it with a beggar.
He was first a soldier and later Bishop of Tours.
According to the legend, cackling geese betrayed him.
At the Martin's procession children carry lanterns or Räbeliechtli.
In Sursee the Gansabhauet (goose cutting) takes place on St Martin's Day.

abschnitte.text: **Martin** was first a **Roman soldier**. On a cold winter's day he saw a **freezing beggar** at a city gate. Martin had nothing with him but his weapons and his cloak. So he cut the **cloak** in two with his **sword** and gave the beggar one half. This story shows how important it is to share with others.

Martin had himself **baptised** and later left the army. He lived as a monk and founded monasteries. The people of the city of **Tours** in present-day **France** wanted him as their bishop. A legend tells that Martin did not want to become bishop and hid in a **goose pen**. But the **geese** cackled so loudly that they betrayed him. So he did become Bishop of Tours after all.

On St Martin's Day children walk through the streets in the evening with glowing **lanterns** and sing songs. In Switzerland a **Räbeliechtli** is often carved for it. A **Räbe** is a white autumn turnip. It is hollowed out, patterns are carved into it, and a candle is put inside. Räbeliechtli processions take place in November in many municipalities.

In **Sursee** in the canton of Lucerne there is a special custom on St Martin's Day, the **Gansabhauet**. A dead goose hangs from a wire. Young people try, **blindfolded**, to strike it down with a blunt **sabre**. For this they wear a golden sun mask. In the past St Martin's Day was also a day on which interest was paid and people ate geese.

gewusst: The Räbechilbi in Richterswil on Lake Zurich is regarded as one of the largest Räbeliechtli processions.
Martin is the patron saint of many churches, and in Switzerland there are numerous churches of St Martin.

teile.einleitung: Sacraments are special celebrations in the Christian churches. They are regarded as visible signs of God's invisible grace. The Catholic Church knows seven sacraments, the Reformed Church two.
wichtigste: A sacrament is a visible sign of God's invisible grace.
The Council of Trent fixed the number seven as binding.
Baptism, confirmation and Eucharist are the sacraments of initiation.
Penance and anointing of the sick are called sacraments of healing.
Baptism, confirmation and ordination are received only once.
The Orthodox Church usually calls the sacraments mysteries.

abschnitte.text: A **sacrament** is often described as a **visible sign of God's invisible grace**. Words and signs belong together here, for example water at baptism or bread and wine at communion. The word comes from the Latin “sacramentum”, sanctuary or mystery. The **Orthodox Church** usually calls the sacraments **mysteries**.

The **Council of Trent** in the 16th century fixed the number of **seven sacraments** as binding. The three **sacraments of initiation**, that is, sacraments of admission, are **baptism, confirmation and Eucharist**. **Penance** and **anointing of the sick** are called **sacraments of healing**. In addition there are **marriage** and **ordination**, which are devoted to serving others.

**Baptism, confirmation and ordination** can be received only **once in a lifetime**. According to Catholic teaching they mark a person for ever. **Baptism** may in an emergency even be validly administered by a person who is not ordained, for example for a newborn in danger of death. In the sacrament of marriage, according to Catholic teaching, **the couple give the sacrament to each other**, and the priest is a witness.

The sacrament of **ordination** has three degrees: **deacon**, **priest** and **bishop**. Only a bishop may administer it. Deacons help in pastoral care and at celebrations. Priests celebrate Mass, and bishops lead a diocese.

The Reformers such as Luther and Zwingli recognised only **two sacraments**: **baptism** and **communion**. Only these, they held, were instituted by Jesus himself. That is why the Reformed churches in Switzerland do celebrate confirmation and weddings too, but do not count them among the sacraments.

gewusst: The Council of Trent met, with interruptions, from 1545 to 1563.
For an emergency baptism, water and the baptismal formula in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are enough.

teile.einleitung: Alongside the Catholic and Protestant churches, the Orthodox Church is one of the great churches of Christianity. It is widespread above all in Eastern Europe, Greece and the Middle East. Its name means “right belief”.
wichtigste: Orthodoxy means “right belief” or “right praise”.
Since the East-West Schism of 1054 the Eastern and Western Church have been separated.
The Patriarch of Constantinople has a primacy of honour, but is not a head like the Pope.
The Russian Orthodox Church has the most believers.
The main service is called the Divine Liturgy.
Many Orthodox Christians celebrate Christmas on 7 January.

abschnitte.text: The word **Orthodoxy** is made up of the Greek “orthos” for right and “doxa” for opinion or praise. The Church sees itself as the guardian of the original faith. In **1054** representatives of Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other. This **East-West Schism** is regarded as the beginning of the separation of the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

The Orthodox Church consists of several **self-governing churches**, for example the Greek, Serbian or Romanian. The **Russian Orthodox Church** has by far the most believers and is led by the Patriarch of Moscow. The **Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople**, today Istanbul, is regarded as “first among equals”. He has a primacy of honour, but is not a head like the Pope.

The main Sunday service is called the **Divine Liturgy**. The best-known form goes back to **John Chrysostom**. There is much singing, often without instruments, and incense fills the room. **Icons**, painted holy images, are important. A screen of images, the **iconostasis**, separates the sanctuary from the space of the faithful.

Many Orthodox churches calculate their feasts according to the old **Julian calendar**. Today this lies 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar, which we use in everyday life. That is why many Orthodox Christians celebrate Christmas on **7 January**. Easter, too, often falls on a different date. In Switzerland many Orthodox Christians live today, for example from Serbia, Romania or Greece.

On the peninsula of **Athos** in Greece, Orthodox monks have lived for over 1,000 years in about 20 monasteries. Women may not enter the peninsula. Orthodox **priests** may be married if they marry **before ordination**. **Bishops**, on the other hand, are chosen only from unmarried monks. In Chambésy near Geneva the Ecumenical Patriarchate has an Orthodox centre.

gewusst: Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross from right to left, Catholics from left to right.
Many Orthodox churches have onion domes or cupolas.

teile.einleitung: Before Jesus began to preach in public, he had himself baptised in the Jordan. He was baptised by John the Baptist. The Gospels tell that the heavens opened and a voice spoke.
wichtigste: Jesus was baptised by John the Baptist.
The baptism took place in the Jordan.
John immersed people in the river.
The heavens opened, and the Spirit of God came down on Jesus.
A voice said: “This is my beloved Son.”
Afterwards Jesus went into the desert to fast and pray.

abschnitte.text: **John the Baptist** lived simply in the desert and preached to people. He called on them to change their lives and make a new start with God. Whoever wished could be baptised by him in the **River Jordan**. John **immersed** people in the water. The water was a sign of a **new beginning** with God.

One day **Jesus** also came to the Jordan to be baptised. John was surprised and at first did not want to. He said: “I ought to be baptised by you.” But Jesus asked him to baptise him. Then John baptised him in the river.

As Jesus came up out of the water, **the heavens opened**. The **Spirit of God** came down on him like a **dove**. A voice from heaven said: “This is my beloved Son.” In this way God showed that Jesus belongs to him. That is why the dove is still a sign of the Holy Spirit today.

Directly after the baptism, Jesus withdrew into the **desert**, to a lonely place. There he **fasted** and prayed for forty days. Afterwards he began to preach in public and gather disciples around him. So the baptism stands at the beginning of his ministry. All four Gospels tell of it.

The **Jordan** flows from north to south through the Sea of Galilee and runs into the **Dead Sea**. To this day pilgrims come to the river to be baptised there. In churches too, people are baptised with **water**. In this way Christians recall the baptism of Jesus by John. Many churches celebrate the feast of the Baptism of the Lord in January.

gewusst: The Dead Sea, into which the Jordan flows, is so salty that you almost float in it by yourself.
The place where Jesus is said to have been baptised is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Vulgate is the Latin translation of the Bible that the Western Church used for over a thousand years. It goes back above all to the scholar Jerome. Its name means “the commonly used one”.
wichtigste: Jerome began the work around 382 at the request of Pope Damasus I.
He translated large parts of the Old Testament in Bethlehem.
He translated from Hebrew and spoke of the “hebraica veritas”.
In 1546 a council declared the Vulgate authentic.
The Gutenberg Bible reproduces the text of the Vulgate.
In 1979 the Nova Vulgata appeared as a new official edition.

abschnitte.text: In the first centuries there were many inconsistent **Old Latin translations** of the Bible. Pope **Damasus I** wanted to change that. He commissioned the scholar **Jerome** to revise the Latin Gospels. Jerome began this work around **382**. The name **Vulgate** comes from “vulgare”, to make common, and means the commonly used version.

In **386** Jerome moved to **Bethlehem** and lived there in a monastery. There he translated large parts of the Old Testament. He learned Hebrew from Jewish scholars. For him the Hebrew original was more authoritative than the Greek translation, the **Septuagint**. He called this the **hebraica veritas**, the Hebrew truth.

The Vulgate became the Bible of the Western Church throughout the Middle Ages. Around 1454, **Johannes Gutenberg** printed his famous 42-line Bible in Mainz with the text of the Vulgate. In 1546 the **Council of Trent** declared the Vulgate **authentic** for teaching, preaching and disputation. In this way it became the authoritative Latin text of the Catholic Church.

After the Second Vatican Council, the Vulgate was revised. It was compared with the Hebrew and Greek original texts. In 1979 Pope **John Paul II** published the **Nova Vulgata** as the new official edition.

The Vulgate also had consequences for art. In Exodus 34:29 there is a Hebrew word that means “to shine” but is related to the word for “horn”. The Vulgate says that the face of Moses was **“cornuta”**, that is, horned. That is why Michelangelo's famous **statue of Moses** shows Moses with horns on his head.

gewusst: Jerome is often painted with a lion because a legend tells that he pulled a thorn out of a lion's paw.
The Gutenberg Bible is regarded as one of the first great books printed with movable type.

teile.einleitung: For centuries the Ottoman sultans also bore the title of caliph. After the First World War the Republic of Turkey came into being, and the parliament in Ankara abolished the sultanate in 1922 and the caliphate in 1924. This triggered great discussion in the Islamic world.
wichtigste: On 1 November 1922 the sultanate was abolished in Turkey.
On 3 March 1924 the Grand National Assembly abolished the caliphate.
The last Ottoman sultan was Mehmed VI.
The last Ottoman caliph was Abdulmejid II.
In 1924 Abdulmejid II first went into exile in Switzerland.
In British India the Khilafat movement campaigned for the caliphate.

abschnitte.text: The rulers of the **Ottoman Empire** were **sultans**, that is, worldly rulers. They also bore the title of **caliph**, which stands for leadership of the Muslim community. After the **First World War** the empire fell apart. In Ankara a new government formed under **Mustafa Kemal**, later called Atatürk, with the **Grand National Assembly**.

On **1 November 1922**, the National Assembly separated the sultanate from the caliphate and abolished the **sultanate**. The last sultan, **Mehmed VI**, left Istanbul on a British warship. He died in 1926 in exile in Sanremo. **Abdulmejid II** was elected caliph, now with only a spiritual office and no political power. On **3 March 1924** the parliament also abolished the **caliphate**.

The members of the Ottoman dynasty had to leave the country. **Abdulmejid II**, the last caliph of the House of Osman, first travelled to **Switzerland** in 1924. In the same year he moved on to **Nice**. He died in **1944** in **Paris**.

In **British India**, the **Khilafat movement** had campaigned since 1919 for the preservation of the Ottoman caliphate. It combined Muslim concerns with the struggle against British rule, and **Mahatma Gandhi** supported it for a time. In March 1924, **Sharif Hussein** of Mecca had himself proclaimed caliph but found little recognition. In 1925 the Egyptian scholar **Ali Abd al-Raziq** argued that the caliphate was not a religious duty. His book triggered violent protests at **al-Azhar**.

gewusst: After his deposition the last Ottoman caliph lived briefly in Switzerland.
Since 1924 there has been no caliphate that is generally recognised by many Muslims.

teile.einleitung: Rerum novarum is a famous encyclical of Pope Leo XIII from the year 1891. It is regarded as the beginning of Catholic social teaching and deals with the situation of workers.
wichtigste: Pope Leo XIII published the encyclical in 1891.
“Rerum novarum” means “of new things”.
It deals with the situation of workers during industrialisation.
It defends private property as a natural right.
It demands just wages and allows workers' associations.
The Fribourg Union around Bishop Gaspard Mermillod provided preparatory work.

abschnitte.text: An **encyclical** is a circular letter of the Pope to the whole Church. It is named after its first Latin words. **“Rerum novarum”** means “of new things”. Pope **Leo XIII** published it in the year **1891**. It is regarded as the first great document of **Catholic social teaching**.

In the 19th century **industrialisation** changed the lives of many people. In factories men, women and also children often worked for very long hours for little pay. People spoke of the **labour question**. Rerum novarum dealt above all with the **situation of workers** and demanded that they be treated with dignity.

The encyclical defends **private property** as a natural right and rejects socialism. At the same time it demands **just wages**, protection from excessively long work and rest on Sunday. Workers may join together in **associations**. The state should also care for the weak. In this way the Pope sought a path between the opposites of his time.

The **Fribourg Union**, a circle of Catholic experts, also worked on the ideas. It met in Fribourg under the chairmanship of the Swiss bishop **Gaspard Mermillod**. Its reflections on the social question flowed into Rerum novarum. In Switzerland Christian social workers' associations also came into being in this period.

gewusst: Later popes wrote their own social encyclicals for anniversaries of Rerum novarum, for example in 1931 and 1991.
In 2025 Pope Leo XIV chose his name also with a view to Leo XIII and his social teaching.

teile.einleitung: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell much of the story almost identically, but some things differently. That is why they are called the Synoptic Gospels. The Synoptic Problem is the question of how these three Gospels depend on one another.
wichtigste: “Synopsis” means “seeing together”.
In 1776 Johann Jakob Griesbach published a synopsis of the three Gospels.
Material that appears in all three is called triple tradition.
Material that appears in only one Gospel is called special material, for example the prodigal son in Luke.
There are several solutions, such as the Augustinian, the Griesbach and the Farrer hypotheses.
Today many researchers support the Two-Source Theory with Mark and the sayings source Q.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **“synopsis”** literally means **seeing together**. A synopsis sets out the similar texts of the Gospels in columns **side by side**. In 1776 **Johann Jakob Griesbach** published such a synopsis of the first three Gospels. In this way agreements and differences could be compared at a glance. Since then Matthew, Mark and Luke have been called the **Synoptics**.

Some stories appear in all three Gospels, for example the baptism of Jesus or the story of the Passion. This is called **triple tradition**. Other material appears in only one Gospel; this is called **special material**. An example is the parable of the **prodigal son**, which is only in Luke 15. Often even the wording and the order agree. This suggests that the evangelists copied from one another or from shared sources.

The Church Father **Augustine** already thought about the order. In “De consensu evangelistarum” he described Mark as the companion and abbreviator of Matthew. The order Matthew, Mark, Luke is therefore called the **Augustinian hypothesis**. In the 18th century Lessing and Eichhorn suspected a lost Aramaic gospel as a shared source. This idea is called the **original gospel hypothesis**.

Griesbach himself assumed that **Matthew** wrote first and Luke used him. Mark then summarised both and was therefore the youngest of the three Gospels. This is the **Griesbach hypothesis**. In 1955, in the essay “On Dispensing with Q”, the Englishman **Austin Farrer** proposed a different way. According to the **Farrer hypothesis**, Mark wrote first, and Luke used both Mark and Matthew directly.

The solution most widely held today is the **Two-Source Theory**. According to it, **Mark** is the oldest Gospel, which is called Markan priority. Matthew and Luke used Mark and, in addition, a collection of sayings of Jesus. This lost source is called the **sayings source Q**, after the German word “Quelle”, source. The Synoptic Problem has still not been completely solved to this day.

gewusst: The sayings source Q has never been found as a manuscript; it is only inferred from Matthew and Luke.
The Gospel of John does not belong to the Synoptics because it tells much quite differently.

teile.einleitung: The Annunciation tells how the angel Gabriel comes to Mary. He tells her that she is to become the mother of Jesus. The story is in the Gospel of Luke and is celebrated as a feast on 25 March.
wichtigste: The story is told in detail in the Gospel of Luke.
The angel Gabriel comes to Mary in Nazareth.
Mary was frightened by the angel's greeting.
The angel said that her child would be called Son of the Most High.
In the end Mary said yes to God's plan.
The prayer “Hail Mary” begins with the angel's greeting.

abschnitte.text: The **Gospel of Luke** in the New Testament tells the story in detail. God sent the **angel Gabriel** to the town of **Nazareth** in Galilee. A young woman named **Mary** lived there. She was engaged to Joseph. The angel greeted her with the words: “Greetings, you who are highly favoured, the Lord is with you.”

Mary was **frightened** by these words. She wondered what this greeting could mean. The angel said: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” Then he explained to her that she would have a son. She was to give him the name **Jesus**.

The angel said that the child would be great and would be called **Son of the Most High**. By the Most High, God is meant. His kingdom would have **no end**, that is, it would last for ever. When Mary wondered, the angel answered: “**Nothing is impossible with God.**”

In the end Mary agreed. She said: “May it happen to me as you have said.” With this **yes** she accepted God's plan. For many Christians, Jesus is the Son of God. That is why they also call Mary the **Mother of God**.

The Church celebrates the Annunciation on **25 March**. The well-known prayer **Hail Mary** came from the angel's greeting. In Latin it begins “Ave Maria”. Many painters have painted the scene: often you see Mary reading and the angel with a lily in his hand.

gewusst: In art the lily is regarded as a sign of Mary's purity.
In Catholic regions, the ringing of bells for the “Angelus” recalls the Annunciation three times a day.
